title: Grading Ravens Defensive Position Groups Through Six Weeks
full_text:
With Week 6 in the rearview and Week 7 on the horizon, the 2026 NFL regular season is a third of the way in the books. The Baltimore Ravens currently find themselves in a three-way tie for the best record in the AFC North at 4-2, and the defense has been a work in progress while still contributing to the team's overall success.
Under new head coach and defensive play-caller Jesse Minter, they came into the season expected to be one of the best units in the league, and while they've dominated entire halves and sometimes three quarters of games, they've yet to put together a full four quarters of excellence.
The talent that general manager Eric DeCosta amassed on the defensive side of the ball has shown flashes of dominance and could round into a strength for this year's team as the offense continues to get healthy and keep being explosive . Here's how each position group has graded out thus far.
Gradual ramp-ups in training camp and delayed regular-season debuts prevented this talented bunch from hitting the ground running. However, over the past two games, they've begun to play up to their immense potential collectively instead of as individuals in spurts. The trio of multi-time Pro Bowlers Nnamdi Madubuike and Calais Campbell and budding star Travis Jones gives the Ravens one of the best interiors in the league.
In the four games since Madubuike returned from a serious neck injury that cut his 2025 season short, he looks more and more like his game-wrecking pre-injury form. Campbell remains the ageless wonder and has looked great the past two weeks and Jones as been a stud from the start of the season when it comes to making plays against the run at and behind the line of scrimmage. Behind them, veterans John Jenkins, Broderick Washington and third-year pro Aeneas Peebles have provided solid depth but haven't really stood out in a noticeable or consistent way.
This group has been the most pleasant surprise of the entire defense thus far this season, with how consistently disruptive they've been down in and down out each week, especially at the top of the depth chart. After a down year in 2025 that still saw him get voted to his fourth straight Pro Bowl, veteran Roquan Smith is back to playing at an All Pro level, leading the team with 47 total tackles, tying for the second-most sacks with two and making plays on the ball with an interception, forced fumble and two pass breakups.
At the WILL spot, fourth-year pro Trenton Simpson, is finally putting it all together in a contract year and has been enjoying quite the breakout campaign. He's recorded the third-most total tackles on the team with 41, including tying for the most tackles for loss with six, and he also has an interception to go along with a fumble recovery and a pass breakup. Second-year pros Teddye Buchanan and Jay Higgins have predominantly played special teams, with Buchanan seeing some limited snaps on defense in base personnel packages.
This is another group that has been hindered by health to a degree, with four-time Pro Bowl veteran and prized free agent acquisition Trey Hendrickson sustaining a finger injury that required surgery and caused him to miss two games. Yet in four games, he has still managed to record a pair of sacks, four quarterback hits and a 22.7% pressure rate, the highest rate among defenders with at least 25 pressures this season, according to NextGenStats .
Leading the Ravens with 3.5 sacks through six games is Tavius Robinson, another fourth-year pro making the most of his extended playing time in the final season of his rookie deal. He also leads the team with eight quarterback hits, batted down two passes and forced a fumble. Second-year pro Mike Green is tied with Hendrickson for the second-most sacks on the team with a pair and stepped up in a big way during the two games he was out. He ranks second on the team with six quarterback hits and has been playing the run well with four tackles for loss.
The Ravens also have a pair of rookies who have been playing regularly , with second-rounder Zion Young's snaps coming on defense during early downs while undrafted free agent Ethan Burke has primarily played on special teams but was the first of the two to record a sack.
The Ravens have gotten a mixed bag of results from this position group, with some impressive plays and missed opportunities to make more impactful ones despite constantly being in good position in coverage. They've been playing third-year pro Nate Wiggins and four-time Pro Bowl veteran Marlon Humphrey on the perimeter and deploying both second-year pro Keyon Martin and fifth-round rookie Chandler Rivers at nickel for stretches.
As a group, they've struggled to contain No. 1 wide receivers from both inconsistent and highly efficient passing offenses and haven't been making enough plays on the ball, with no interceptions and just nine pass breakups between them. Wiggins has been the best of the bunch, allowing just a 51.7 % completion rate and an opposing passer rating of 65.7. Neither he nor Humphrey has given up a touchdown this year yet and will need to raise their game even more during the next third of the season with tougher opponents yet to come.
The saving grace keeping this grade from being flat-out 'D' or 'C-' at best is the fact that three-time All Pro Kyle Hamilton is playing like a well-deserving Defensive Player of the Year candidate right now, and second-year pro Malaki Starks has shown signs of improvement over the past couple of weeks. What was being billed as potentially the best trio in the league all summer has fallen well short of expectations to start the season.
Collectively, they have not only failed to consistently come up with big plays in key moments but have also been the main culprits in some very detrimental breakdowns in coverage late in games and on third downs, especially.
Starks appears to be turning a corner, making plays both in coverage and as a forceful player against the run. However, the same can not be said about veteran free agent acquisition Jaylinn Hawkins, who has disappointed thus far. He has no pass breakups, interceptions, tackles for loss or plays on the ball of any kind. He'll need to start turning it around before the Ravens' coaches are forced to find a configuration that works better without him, possibly one that utilizes second-year undrafted gem and special teams ace Keondre Jackson.
Coming into the regular season after a disastrous end to his rookie year and a discouraging performance in the preseason, a lot of eyes were on and remain on second-year placekicker Tyler Loop. He's drilled some impressive kicks in high-leverage situations, including the walk-off winner in Rio de Janeiro in Week 3 to beat the Dallas Cowboys in a thriller and setting a new home-field record for the longest successful attempt. However, he's still struggled with consistency when it comes to making clutch kicks in the second half of games. Both of the Ravens' losses have featured missed kicks by Loop from under 50 yards, and this year, he's 10-of-13 on field goals, with one blocked attempt and two bad misses. The Ravens signed veteran kicker Jake Moody to the practice squad at the onset of the season to give Loop some competition and recently brought him back earlier this week in the wake of his recent struggles.
Rookie punter Ryan Eckley has been the field-flipping weapon that the Ravens envisioned they were getting when they selected him in the sixth round of this year's draft. Half of his punts have pinned the opposing team's offense inside its own 20-yard line; he's averaging 46.9 yards per punt and his longest has been 62 yards. As far as the return game goes, the Ravens haven't gotten much juice from second-year pro LaJohntay Wester, who's returned 10 punts for 91 yards with a long of 24. He's one of three players who have returned kicks, and none have broken one longer than 42 yards (Chris Moore in the season opener.
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On SI…

title: Ravens Injury Report Reveals Major Development For Lamar Jackson
full_text:
Baltimore Ravens two-time MVP Lamar Jackson continues to make tangible signs of progress in his return from a two-week absence.
On Thursday, for the first time since suffering an ankle injury late in the first half in Week 4, Jackson was with the team for the start of practice, and he was moving quite well . Even better than on the video that emerged of him Wednesday taking part in what head coach Jesse Minter refereed to as a “little” bit of limited work in that session. Jackson was interacting with teammates in an overt manner Thursday that certainly gave the appearance of the starting quarterback preparing to be back at the helm. Seemed to be a spring in his step.
Minter, like all NFL coaches, does not meet with the media on Thursday and offensive coordinator Declan Doyle spoke prior to the practice session. The Ravens listed Jackson as limited at practice on Wednesday and gave him a limited designation on Thursday. The final injury report will be revealed on Friday, but this is clearly multiple days of progress after none for weeks.
This much is obvious – Minter is virtually certain not to come out tomorrow and rule Jackson out as he did the previous two Fridays. Jackson has finally made significant progress from the injury after Minter referred to it as “day-to-day” for over two weeks and Jackson will continue to get treatment and test the ankle out through the weekend. Barring a setback, based on over 20 years of covering this stuff, it certainly looks to me like the Ravens are preparing for Jackson to return for a vital AFC North game against the Bengals to open what is a difficult middle stretch of the schedule.
It also would not be surprising in the least to see Jackson, and not Huntley, meeting with the media on Friday, which would be another obvious indication of where this is going. We originally circled Week 7 as the first team return date as we gathered information on Jackson’s original injury, and were a little alarmed when Minter spoke so cryptically about the star’s potential return on Monday.
If indeed this is Jackson’s return, it comes at the ideal time. Back-up Snoop Huntley is very limited in how he can attack a defense and Jackson’s absence was also becoming a drain on the run game as opponents did not have to concern themselves with defending Huntley’s legs much. A suspect offensive line was also an issue and new center Cam Jurgens is practicing fully and on track to make his Ravens debut Sunday. (The possibility for other trades does still exist ).
Jackson is 11-2 vs the Bengals in his career and 7-2 against them when Joe Burrow starts. The Ravens average 29 points per game against Cincy with Jackson at the helm – the Bengals defensive line is markedly improved this season  – and he averages over 220 rushing yards and 64 rushing yards.
Jackson has 837 rushing yards in his career against the Bengals, the most any QB has against any team in NFL history. A lot of that was when coordinator Lou Anarumo was at the helm (Jackson carved him up in Indianapolis in Week 1 – but the Bengals still have major issues defending outside runs and their linebackers tend to struggle with tackling; areas Jackson can exploit.

title: One Ravens Player Who Could Surprisingly Be Traded Before the Deadline
full_text:
The Ravens have already made their trade deadline splash.
Giving up a ransom for an offensive lineman with a deep injury, while still in concussion protocol, and taking on $17M a year in salary a few weeks back drew criticism around the NFL for Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta. And as we have explained, for a team already running a franchise-record payroll and with the least cap space in the NFL, the options for further moves are limited.
Unless, of course they shed significant salary and cap in a transaction that then allows them to add elsewhere in a more meaningful way. It’s complicated for sure, and, most likely, DeCosta maybe tries to pick up a veteran kicker on the cheap (as always we know who they would be looking at ), but the Cam Jurgens trade was certainly a shocker, so maybe team president Sashi Brown and DeCosta have more tricks up their sleeve.
And, assuming they are getting a little heathier at a certain position, and if things don’t improve with certain highly-paid players soon, maybe they could manage to sell and buy something else significant in what could be two-time MVP Lamar Jackson’s final season here and before an inevitable purge of longtime starters that will be coming in 2027.
So, who do we have in mind?
DeCosta is cornerback Marlon Humphrey’s No. 1 fan. He gushed about him before the season started, justifying his $19.3M in total compensation in the final year of his deal (10th among all NFL corners) and how he would bounce back in a big way. Yeah, well, he’s a decent enough player but the Ravens corners still don’t make plays on the ball and their corners and safeties don’t have a pick all season despite being thrown all as much as anyone.
Humphrey, a man-coverage guy for the most part, spoke about how he was “garbage” at times in the preseason and the Ravens are always talking up TJ Tampa, and that oft-injured corner is working his way back from Injured Reserve. Maybe Humphrey moves to the slot and they get better there – the slot has been the abyss and Ja’Marr Chase might be able to go off there Sunday – but if not, even with the corner play being suspect, moving this contract could open up significant wiggle room.
When Humphrey has wanted the other team's best receiver this season, it has not gone well.
With Baltimore less than $3M under the cap, not having many ideal restructure candidates and still needing space to cover additions along the way due to injury and otherwise, including Humphrey in a package would make sense.
Humphrey has been a Pro Bowl performer in the past, going through a walk year doesn’t always bring out the best (especially when you have spent your entire career in one place), and there is always an acute need around the league and people willing to take risks (like DeCosta with Jaire Alexander not that long ago!).
By the deadline, Humphrey will basically be owed $7.7M for the second half of the season, and would save that much in cap if dealt. It’s a lot of money to be sure, but the Ravens already paid him $4M in the offseason in a bonus and if they believe as much in rookie head coach Jesse Minter’s scheme as they should, and believe in their youth at this position (and maybe if they ate a few million of Humphrey’s deal to save $5M) they could have the ability to maneuver in a more meaningful way at the deadline.
If they want to win a Super Bowl, they need to be creative and keep an open mind. There are plenty of Ravens not playing to their contract, but most are untradable; Minter didn’t need a $19M corner to have a top three pass defense with his zone schemes with the Chargers, and this could be addition by subtraction in numerous ways.
Minter knows the Chargers corners incredibly well, and knows how they fit the scheme, and LA is 0-6 and will make trades and shed salary. They wouldn't want Humphrey but the Ravens clearing his salary and opening up a starting spot at corner would seem to make a lot of sense (and personnel guys have expressed as much to me), moving Marlon as a precursor to bringing another corner in.
I seem to recall the Ravens and Chargers making a trade a year ago at this time that worked out damn well for Minter when he got Odafe Oweh (and didn't do much of anything for the Ravens at all).

title: Grading Ravens Offensive Position Groups Through Six Weeks
full_text:
With Week 6 in the rearview and Week 7 on the horizon, the 2026 NFL regular season is a third of the way in the books. The Baltimore Ravens currently find themselves in a three-way tie for the best record in the AFC North at 4-2, and the offense has been a major catalyst for the team's overall success.
Under new offensive coordinator and first-time play-caller Declan Doyle, they've fielded one of the most explosive and innovative units in the league, although the overall health of the roster has been an issue and kept them from performing at a high level in all four quarters in most of their games.
The talent that general manager Eric DeCosta amassed on the offensive side of the ball has shown flashes of brilliance and dominance and could be the driving force for this year's team as the defense continues to round into shape. Here's how each position group has graded out thus far.
As with several other position groups on this team, health is the only obstacle keeping the Ravens' most gifted signal-caller from helping the offense reach its full potential. The differences in explosiveness, efficiency, and overall production with and without Lamar Jackson are beyond stark.
In the 14 quarters with the two-time league MVP under center, the Ravens have scored 116 points, 14 touchdowns, 967 passing yards and 1,464 total yards. He suffered an ankle sprain midway through the Ravens' Week 4 game against the Tennessee Titans and in the 10 quarters without him, they've only mustered a third of those figures with 40 points, four touchdowns, 429 passing yards and 742 total yards. Jackson was playing at an MVP level before he went down and has more than enough time to catch up with Brock Purdy and Josh Allen and emerge as a frontrunner down the stretch.
While the Ravens rank second in the league in rushing yards and they've eclipsed 100 yards on the ground in all but one game, this position group has been more than solid but not spectacular. Five-time Pro Bowler Derrick Henry leads the team in rushing by a mile with 534 yards, which ranks fourth in the league. He's only had two 100-plus-rushing-yard performances and is coming off his least productive game, where he was held to a season-low 58 yards and committed a costly fumble in the fourth quarter.
Fellow veteran Justice Hill has been a nice change-of-pace option, averaging 7.4 yards per rush and is still excelling in his primary pass-catching-and-blocking role. Third-year pro Rasheen Ali has yet to play a single snap on offense but has been a staple on special teams, covering and returning kicks.
Given Doyle's background as a former tight ends coach, there were heightened expectations for this remodeled bunch coming into the season. Injuries have impacted this group as well, with veteran blocking specialist Durham Smythe suffering a season-ending torn Achilles and both three-time Pro Bowler Mark Andrews and fourth-round rookie Matt Hibner sustaining minor hand injuries. Andrews has struggled with drops and had a slow start to the season with 23 catches on 33 targets for 181 receiving yards and one touchdown, while Hibner and fellow rookie Josh Cuevas have shown some promising flashes and have combined to record 12 catches on 13 targets for 154 receiving yards and two touchdowns.
This is yet another group that's been hit hard by the injury bug, with two-time Pro Bowler Zay Flowers missing a game and a half and being hampered in another with a hamstring strain. Standout third-round rookie Ja'Kobi Lane had his debut cut short in Week 1 with a fractured wrist that kept him out until this past Sunday, but he's looked good when healthy with five catches on eight targets for 51 receiving yards and four first downs.
Veteran Rashod Bateman has been a reliable chain-mover and stepped up when Flowers was hobbled and out of commission, but he is dealing with a nagging shoulder injury. Third-year pro Devontez Walker leads the team with 18.8 receiving yards per catch and has recorded four catches for 75 receiving yards and a touchdown. Fourth-round rookie Elijah Sarratt has been a regular healthy scratch and has recorded one catch on two targets for 13 yards and a first down.
No position group has been hit harder by injury than this group, dating back to the summer when they lost projected starting center Danny Pinter for the year in a joint training camp practice. They lost their next two top centers in the same game in Week 3 and were forced to slide stud rookie right guard over the past three weeks and have had to play third-stringer Emory Jones in his spot the past two weeks. All that shuffling prompted DeCosta to make the bold move to trade for two-time Pro Bowl center Cam Jurgens from the Philadelphia Eagles. Two-time Pro Bowl left tackle Ronnie Stanley missed a game with a toe injury, and this Sunday will mark their fifth different starting configuration this season.
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On SI focusing primarily on original content and reporting. He provides analysis, breakdowns, profiles, and reports on important news and transactions from and about the Ravens. His professional resume as a sports reporter includes covering local events, teams, and athletes in his hometown of Anchorage, Alaska for Anchorage Daily News. His coverage on the Ravens and other NFL teams has been featured on Heavy.com/sports, Maryland Sports Blog and most recently Baltimore Beatdown from 2021 until 2025.

title: Ravens-Bengals Matchups: Any Reason To Think Ja'Marr Chase Won't Feast Again?
full_text:
The Ravens have a number one problem with No. 1 wide receivers.
Even by the lowest of standards in terms of what a “No. 1 WR” really is they have it bad. Rookie Carnell Tate (Titans) was at his best against them and true proven go-to guys like Drake London (Falcons) and George Pickens (Cowboys) and CeeDee Lamb (Cowboys) and Chris Olave (Saints) ate them up. And many of them were relying on a suspect quarterback to get the ball and not Joe Burrow, who leads the NFL in completion percentage and can operate at the highest levels.
And Burrow is never more at his best than when he is feeding his top target, Ja’Marr Chase, and Chase has never been better throughout his career than when he faces the Ravens. And this edition of Baltimore’s secondary is having all kinds of issues in the second half of games and on third down and especially making any sort of dynamic plays on the football. And they can’t slow down the main cogs in any functional passing attack.
So, yeah, Sunday is going to be a quite a challenge for rookie head coach Jesse Minter, who has done a fine enough job overall but has been getting worked as a defensive coordinator in the second half of games, and who might just need his cornerback-obsessed general manager to go try to find him one before the trade deadline because his corners and safeties are getting picked apart in coverage on third-and-long when the opposition is desperate to make a play downfield (just happened again in Cleveland Sunday).
They best come correct this weekend hosting the Bengals who are coming off a bye with a QB who usually doesn’t really heat up until mid October.
“It is a work in progress,” Minter said of his defense after Wednesday’s practice. “I do see improvement, and I do appreciate the way the guys are chasing improvement. I think there's just a level that we can get to from a pure confidence and conviction standpoint in what we're doing that you can play things aggressively, that you can anticipate things that are about to happen, that when things happen on the fly, the adjustments and things like that happen in real time.
“We're getting closer and closer to that. So, to the guys' credit, they're working at it. Again, it's six games in. Let's try to keep climbing and keep getting better and better, so that we're at our best as we keep going."
They better a lot closer to their best on Sunday. Chase is uniquely equipped to exploit their weaknesses and the soft spots in this zone defense and he’s been torching these defensive backs his entire career.
In case you haven’t been paying attention to what Chase does to these guys, I’ll refresh your memory. He has 1204 yards in 10 career games, that is the most by any player against any opponent in NFL history over at least 10 games. Let that sink in.
Chase is already fourth all-time in receiving yards against the Ravens, a franchise prided on its defense for a generation, behind only Jimmy Smith, Hines Ward and Chad Ochocinco. Chase already has three games of 190 yards or more against Baltimore, that is the most such games any person has against any team in the history of this league.
“It starts with Burrow,” defensive lineman Calais Campbell said, “he's a general out there. He knows how to check all the right plays and check into the right runs based off how people play them. And you have to give the attention to the receivers. They are the best in the game. Chase is probably No. 1, or arguably the best receiver in the game, and then you have Tee Higgins who's Top 10 at the worst; he's a really elite receiver as well.”
Chase is being used a little differently this season, as even more of a deep ball guy and little less moving the chains in the slot.
But that could change Sunday given how atrocious the Ravens have been defending the slot (more on that in a minute). His YAC per reception is at just 2.7 this season (5.7/catch in his career), but Chase has his second-best Expected Points Added/Target of his career (0.47) and is over 9 air yards per target (second-best) with elite route depth, too.
The EPA is still up there even though he is getting just seven targets per game thus far because his explosive play rate is soaring (over 18%) and Burrow is going to tight end Mike Gesicki more to keep things moving in the slot.
Ravens corners and safeties do not have an interception on the season (Kyle Hamilton’s came as a linebacker) they only have about a half-dozen pass breakups combined and none of them has had much success against this receiver. Chase is a size speed monster, he can run through defenders like a running back, and with how shaky the Ravens deep safeties have been, just putting a top over him likely won’t be enough.
Chase has been in the slot less than a quarter of the time this season, but given Baltimore’s film I bet that changes Sunday. As we have been chronicling in depth , young slot corners Keyon Martin and Chandler Rivers, who couldn’t handle Chase’s size and power, both have an opposing passer rating of 119 when thrown on in the slot. Overall, here’s where Baltimore’s slot defense ranks:
Passer Rating: 117.7 (27th) Comp %: 74.1% (26th)    Y ards: 510 (27th) Yds/Att: 8.8 (23rd)
Gesicki will need attention in the slot, too. Baltimore has faced the fewest passing attempts to TEs in the NFL per game, but is allowing a 121.5 rating when they are targeted (26th). Gesicki in the slot this season has 11 catches on 14 targets at 14.3 yards/catch(!) with three touchdowns.
Baltimore really needs starting QB Lamar Jackson (ankle) back for this game to likely keep pace with the Bengals, but that is anything but a sure thing. Minter better be ready to mix and catch corners and he needs a huge revenge game out of former Bengal pass rusher Trey Hendrickson, because it’s hard to fancy his defensive backs against this group.
And if nothing else, probably see what Nate Wiggins can do. In four games against the Bengals Wiggins has allowed just 13 completions on 28 attempts for a 62.5 passer rating, no TDs and just two plays over 20 yards.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Bills Paired With Eagles For Trade That Would Fix Defensive Problem for Buffalo
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills' defense has been a major problem during the 2026 season and general manager Brandon Beane needs to be aggressive to help that side of the ball out.
In the first year under new defenisve coordinator Jim Leonhard, the Bills sport one of the worst defenses in the NFL. Buffalo has been especially bad against the pass, with the Bills ranking 31st.
One major cause of their struggles against the pass has been the Bills' cornerbacks room, which has seen lackluster play from both Maxwell Hairston and Davison Igbinosun, with the former getting benched recently. Things have been so bad that the Bills brought Tre'Davious White back in the hopes he can help improve things.
The Bills still have a few more weeks before the trade deadline to assess where they stand, but if things keep going the way they have been, a cornerback trade is needed.
With the Philadelphia Eagles in rough shape following a 2-4 start and the loss of Jalen Hurts for the rest of the season, general manager Howie Roseman could start selling at the deadline.
One player The Athletic's Daniel Popper believes could be for sale is cornerback Riq Woolen, and he thinks the Bills could be a fit.
"Woolen won a Super Bowl with the Seahawks last season. He then hit free agency and, rather surprisingly, a market did not materialize for him. Woolen ended up signing a one-year deal with the Eagles. Although he has given up two touchdowns, Woolen has played well in coverage down-to-down for Philadelphia. He was in tight coverage on the Parker Washington one-handed touchdown in the Eagles’ loss to the Jaguars in Week 5. The combination of size and speed will always make Woolen an intriguing piece," Popper said.
"Best fits: Lions, Steelers, Bills, Jaguars," he added.
The Eagles signed Woolen to a one-year , $12 million contract, which means he could leave in free agency in 2027 for nothing. With Philly going nowhere fast, it makes sense to unload him to make sure that doesn't happen.
According to Pro Football Focus , Woolen's coverage grade in 2026 is a healthy 68.3, which ranks 25th at the position.
That mark ranks higher than both Igbinosun's (48.2) and Hairston's (36.4), and even No. 1 cornerback Christian Benford's (53.6).
While Woolen's raw coverage numbers haven't been great (53.3% completion rate, 108.5 passer rating), he is still doing better than all three of the Bills' top-three cornerbacks in completion rate allowed, and he has a superior passer rating permitted than Benford and Hairston.
Another plus with Woolen is his experience, something he has more of than Hairston and Igbinosun combined. He also has a Super Bowl ring, which is particularly intriguing for a Bills team gunning for that exact thing in 2026.
While we'd love for the Bills to swing a bit higher in their pursuit of a cornerback addition, the elite of the elite rarely become available.
Woolen would be a fine consolation prize who will come at the reasonable price of a Day 3 pick.

title: Bills Could Be Destined for Record-Breaking Season in Many Ways
full_text:
It’s already been a good week for the first-place team in the AFC East, and that club won’t be taking the field until a week from this Sunday.
On Thursday evening at Soldier Field, the Chicago Bears cooled off the New England Patriots. Ben Johnson’s team came away with a 30-24 triumph in a contest which saw New England’s Drake Maye and Chicago’s Caleb Williams both throw for 300-plus yards.
That means Joe Brady’s 5-1 Buffalo Bills have extended their lead in the division as the Pats dropped to 4-3. Of course, there’s still a lot of football remaining in the league’s 107th campaign.
Buffalo's drives this season: #1 of 32 in points per drive (3.13) #1 in drives ending in a score (57%) #1 in EPA per drive (1.15) #1 in series conversion rate (80.2%) punts on 19% of drives, the lowest in the NFL
Six weeks and one game into the 2026 NFL season and one thing is abundantly clear: Putting 30-plus points on the board is becoming more of a common occurrence. Last night’s performance by the Bears marked the 55th time a team reached that figure this season.
How did Josh Allen make this TD pass to Keon Coleman? BUFvsLV on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/CNLw6KW2tC
Such is the case with Brady’s Bills. An offensive unit led by the tag team duo of quarterback Josh Allen and running back James Cook has already produced 23 touchdowns in six contests. Buffalo leads the NFL in average points per contest (32.8) and has reached the 30-point mark in four games.
That’s the good news. When it comes to the other side of the football, new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard is still looking for answers. The Bills are giving up 28.5 points per contest and only the Detroit Lions are allowing more total yards and passing yards per contest. Leonhard’s unit has surrendered 21 offensive TD—15 of those through the air. In the four games that Buffalo has reached at least 30 points, they have also permitted 30-plus points.
So where are we headed with this? There’s still 11 games remaining on the Bills’ schedule, and who they play doesn’t seem to matter these days. Allen and company are finding their way to the end zone, and so are their opponents.
It was just two years ago that the Bills set a team record for points scored (525) in a season. That happened to be the year that Allen was named the league’s MVP. Now ponder this. The franchise mark for the most points allowed in a season is a brisk 454 (28.4 points per game), which came in a 16-game campaign in 1984.
That club finished 2-14 under head coach Kay Stephenson, but that was bad enough for the team to earn the first overall pick in the ’85 NFL draft— selecting future Hall of Fame defensive end Bruce Smith.
The average Buffalo Bills’ game this season averages 61.3 points. That adds up to a lot of entertaining football. But if this club has any kind of aspirations of reaching and then winning Super Bowl LXI, Leonhard needs to come up with some solutions on his side of the football.

That includes television, as he spent more than two decades at ESPN, and was part of shows that garnered five Emmy Awards. He also spent the 2015 NFL season with Thursday Night Football on CBS/NFLN.

title: Bills' Jim Leonhard Getting Hot Seat Buzz Amid Buffalo's Defensive Struggles
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are 5-1 as they enter the bye this week, but that does not mean their season hasn't been without issues.
The biggest issue, by far, is the performance of the defense, which has been woefully disappointing over the first six games , leading to no shortage of scrutiny for new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard.
In per-game averages, the Bills rank 31st in total yards and passing yards, and 28th in points.
As a result of Buffalo's rough start, USA TODAY's Michael Middlehurts-Schwartz thinks Leonhard is one of the NFL's coordinators who is under the most pressure .
"Unlike some others on this list, Leonhard probably isn't facing questions of job security as he oversees a fairly significant shift in adapting former coach Sean McDermott's defense to a radically different scheme. But with Buffalo otherwise looking capable of competing for its first title, he's hardly off the hook," he said.
While there is no doubt plenty of pressure on Leonhard to turn things around, especially given the Bills' status as a Super Bowl contender, we just don't see his job being in any real danger.
It isn't easy to change schemes and have success in the first year, and making that harder is the fact that the Bills had to work in multiple new starters.
It also doesn't help that the Bills have seen lackluster play at multiple position groups, including linebacker, cornerback and safety, so part of the blame rests on general manager Brandon Beane swinging and missing on players at those positions.
The Bills have shown remarkable patience with coaches, and even with Beane himself, so there's a good chance Leonhard won't be shown the door, even if the defense's issues continue.
To his credit, Leonhard hasn't minced words about the performance of the defense.
“It’s time to start being good at something, right? I mean . . . that’s our struggles right now. It’s too inconsistent to pretend that we’re building, and working, and making improvements," he said.
When it comes to where the issues lie, Leonhard has pointed the finger at the secondary more than the defensive front.
“Significantly more on the back seven than there is on the front,” he said.
The safety pairing of C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Cole Bishop has not panned out overall, and now the Bills are going to be without Gardner-Johnson for a game, which will force Damar Hamlin and Jalon Kilgore into bigger roles. We know Hamlin's limits and the rookie remains unproven.
At cornerback, Maxwell Hairston has not taken the step forward the Bills were expecting, and rookie Davison Igbinosun is still raw and in need of more work.
All of this adds up to Beane needing to do something at the trade deadline to help his defensive coordinator out. The Bills general manager will have more than two weeks to get that done.

title: CJ Gardner-Johnson Debacle Exposes Bills' Free Agency Failures Under Brandon Beane
full_text:
It's seems safe to say that safety Chauncey Gardner-Johnson is another swing-and-miss in free agency by Buffalo Bills ' general manager Brandon Beane.
In addition to subpar performance, Gardner-Johnson's circus act has already produced multiple distractions dating back to training camp . His one-game suspension for spitting at an opponent last time out in Week 6 should re-open the conversation about Buffalo's multiple free agency failures in recent years under Beane's watch.
Granted salary cap space has been far from plentiful, it's more than fair to question the Bills' use of limited resources over the past few free agency cycles.
With Gardner-Johnson continuing the trend into 2026, Buffalo has suffered from at least one costly free agent bust three years in a row.
The 2025 free agent class looks highly troubling with two of the four key members already off the roster but still accounting for significant portions of this year's salary cap space.
Here's a quick look at the Bills' last three underwhelming free agent classes and the dead salary cap money that remains. All figures are provided by Spotrac .
Edge rusher Bradley Chubb and slot cornerback Dee Alford have been nothing better than average thus far.
Chubb represents the biggest investment of the class, signing for three years and $43.5 million. He has only 1.5 sacks, but he's been solid against the run. Buffalo realistically must keep him through at least the 2027 season. Cutting him would cost $16.8 million in dead money on next year's cap.
Alford, who inked a three-year deal for $15.75 million, is also likely to stick around for at least two seasons, unless Buffalo is willing to eat $5.07 million in dead money on the 2027 spending limit.
While Gardner-Johnson is only under contract for one season, his deal contains void years in 2027 and 2028. He'll cost $1 million against the cap next year and $500K the following season. If the Bills release him now , they face a $3.08 million dead cap charge.
Joey Bosa and Larry Ogunjobi were both one-year propositions that failed , and in the latter's case failed miserably.
After opening the season with a six-game suspension due to a substance policy violation, Ogunjobi totaled 19 tackles and no quarterback hits over 215 defensive snaps. In the playoff loss to the Denver Broncos, he committed an awful offsides penalty that negated a Bills' fumble recovery.
Meanwhile, Bosa made a few noteworthy plays , but failed to consistently affect the opposing passer. He made 5.0 sacks over 15 games, and he was practically invisible against the run all year.
Unfortunately, the Bills are still paying the price for both players. Bosa is on the book for $7.2 million in dead cap space this year while Ogunjobi costs $2.35 million.
That's before mentioning Josh Palmer's disappointing 2025 season , and the fact that it doesn't look like the wide receiver will live up to his contract value this year, either. Palmer, who is on a three-year deal worth $30 million, has only 26 receptions in 17 appearances as a Bill.
Palmer is occupying $11.75 million of cap room this season, and he carries a $4.8 million dead money charge in 2027 if cut. Furthermore, Buffalo is on the hook for void years in 2028 ($3.2m) and 2029 ($1.6m).
Wide receivers Curtis Samuel and Mack Hollins were the two most significant free agent additions in 2024 with the latter only on a one-year contract.
The Samuel signing is the one that is truly mind blowing on multiple levels. He mysteriously failed to come close to the production level he enjoyed under offensive coordinator Joe Brady in 2020, and he wound up being a healthy scratch on multiple occasions in 2025 when he caught seven passes for 81 yards over six games.
Samuel, who initially signed on for three years and $24 million, counts $3.45 million against Buffalo's cap this year after being released during the offseason.

title: Bills Safety Sam Franklin Has Suspension Reduced After Spitting Incident
full_text:
Sam Franklin Jr. was suspended for one game after the league determined the Buffalo Bills safety spit at an opponent during the fourth quarter. Franklin appealed that ruling and according to Adam Schefter, his punishment has been reduced.
Franklin will no longer be suspended for a game and will not lose a game check. Hearing officer James Thrash apparently still felt Franklin's actions during the game deserved a punishment as he will receive a $14,926 fine for unsportsmanlike conduct.
Buffalo is on a bye this week , and will host the Baltimore Ravens in Week 8 on November 1. Franklin will be eligible to play in that game, making this ruling a win, even though he is still going to be hit with the fine.
The Bills defeated the Raiders in Week 6, but had a couple of unfortunate incidents from that game lead to punishments, and both were related to spitting.
During the second quarter, safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson was ejected, and later suspended , when he spit at Las Vegas tight end Brock Bowers. He initially refused to take full ownership of his actions, and never admitted to spitting . Still, the league had enough evidence to not only suspend Gardner-Johnson for one game, but they upheld his punishment on appeal .
Unlike Gardner-Johnson, Franklin was not penalized or ejected during the game. That made his suspension far more shocking, and Franklin was also surprised when the news broke. Shortly after the suspension was announced, Sal Capaccio of WGR 550 reported that Franklin would appeal.
"I'm told Franklin vehemently denies this ever happening and will be appealing," Capaccio reported .
Capaccio also shared a slow-motion video that Franklin shared on his social media, which showed that he was kicked during the alleged incident. Franklin also said he still wouldn't spit on anyone despite the contact.
As for the fine, this is the second time this season Franklin will be hit with one by the NFL. He was fined $9,425 for a blindside block in Week 1 . That penalty qualifies for the new "Three-Strike Suspension Rule."
Under that rule a player would be suspended if they receive three penalties for one of the following penalites: " hip drop tackle, horse collar tackle , launching, hit on a defenseless player and blindside block."

title: Bills-Commanders Trade Could Solve Major Secondary Concern in Buffalo
full_text:
Through six games, the Buffalo Bills have proven to have one major concern: pass defense.
Buffalo has surrenderd 1,715 yards through the air, sending them into their Week 7 bye ranked 31st overall against the pass . First-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard is focused on finding answers , but only so much can be done with the current secondary.
We've covered in depth recently about the Bills' need for help at safety , but their coverage issues at cornerback have been just as problematic. They can try and add more help ahead of the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline and The Athletic's Daniel Popper believes they shoud go after Amik Robertson of the Washington Commanders.
Washington signed Robertson this offseason and while he's been one of the few bright spots in their defense, the Commanders are just 1-4-1 and could be headed toward a major overhaul with head coach Dan Quinn on the hot seat. What should really intrigue the Bills when it comes to Roberston is his ability to play the slot as well as the boundary.
"Robertson signed a two-year, $16 million deal with the Commanders in free agency. He has been one of the few bright spots from Peters’ offseason. Robertson does not have any fully guaranteed money on his deal in 2027," Popper wrote.
"The Commanders would take on $3 million in dead money in 2027 if they trade him before the deadline. Robertson is a capable man coverage corner who could help a number of teams in the secondary. He can play inside and outside."
A fourth-round pick out of Louisiana Tech in 2020, Robertson has often been overlooked due to his size. At 5-foot-9 and 183 pounds, he's one of the shorter defensive backs, but he's never let that hold him back. In seven years, he has 253 tackles, 43 pass defenses, and five interceptions. This year, he has 40 tackles and has already broken up eight passes.
He has a 69.8 overall grade from PFF , but what is really impressive is his 86.8 grade in run defense, which is proof that he plays much larger than his 183-pound frame would indicate. Robertson would make sense as a nickel for the Bills, where he can help slow down opposing slot receivers while also improving their run defense.
If Washington is ready to stockpile picks, Buffalo general manager Brandon Beane should be willing to make a move and bring in the versatile Robertson, who could truly shore up their greatest weakness.

title: Dalton Kincaid Teams Up With Pat McAfee During Bills' Bye Week
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills might be on their bye week , but that doesn’t mean Bills Mafia has to suffer through an entire weekend without seeing at least one of their favorite Bills’ players on their screens.
Coming off back-to-back wins over the last two weeks out West against the Los Angeles Rams and Las Vegas Raiders, players and coaches of the Western New York franchise have been on a little hiatus from the daily grind of the National Football League since last Sunday’s 33-30 victory over the Raiders at Allegiant Stadium in Paradise, Nevada.
Fourth-year tight end Dalton Kincaid , however, won’t be resting much longer as he’ll be shifting gears on Saturday morning from NFL player to “celebrity guest picker” for ESPN ’s College Gameday , which begins at 9:00 a.m. ET and will be broadcast live from The University of Utah campus in Salt Lake City prior to Saturday night’s collegiate matchup between the hometown team and the University of Houston at 10:15 p.m. ET.
The announcement was made when the Bills' tight end made an appearance on The Pat McAfee Show earlier in the week. Kincaid will join McAfee, a former NFL punter, on the picks panel.
The Utes are currently ranked 10th in the nation, while the Cougars sit in the 14th spot.
🚨BREAKING NEWS🚨 @_DaltonKincaid will be the @CollegeGameDay guest picker this Saturday at Utah #PMSLive pic.twitter.com/jxZyUDipJn
It will be a homecoming of sorts for Kincaid, who attended the school in Utah from 2020 to 2022, totaling 107 receptions for 1,414 yards and 16 touchdowns in 31 games played for the Utes after previously attending the University of San Diego in 2018 and 2019.
Undoubtedly, returning to a place where he once dominated as a First-Team All-Pac-12 player after posting 70 catches for 890 receiving yards and eight touchdowns in 2022 will be special for Kincaid.
And, it’s just the icing on the cake after he recently celebrated his 27th birthday with a victory at Allegiant Stadium—less than 20 miles from his hometown of Summerlin, Nevada—on October 18 where he had 7 receptions for 38 yards, which is the most receptions he’s had since Week 2 of the 2026 campaign.
For that reason, it’s probably been an exciting whirlwind of a week for the Bills’ playmaker, who has 23 catches for 315 yards and one touchdown reception so far this season, which currently places him sixth in the NFL for yardage at his position through six weeks.
His 13.7 yard-per-catch average also ranks third out of the top-25 tight ends for this season behind only New England’s Eli Raridon (14.0 YPC) and Kansas City’s Travis Kelce (15.0 YPC).
It’s been quite the ride for the Nevada native in what is arguably his most important season since entering the league as a 2023 first-round pick as he’s currently on pace for a stat line of 65 catches for 893 yards and three touchdowns, which would be the most yards of his young career, as well as the second most receptions and touchdowns.
Considering all of the injury battles and struggles with consistency that he’s battled through over the past two seasons, the turnaround that Kincaid’s had from September into the middle of October has been a great sight to see.
Now, he’ll get the chance to continue that journey of joy on Saturday, and Bills’ fans who are locked into the collegiate football landscape will surely recognize his face if they tune into the College Gameday program this weekend.
Can Kincaid get every game pick right in front of the nation?

title: Four Buffalo Bills With Most to Prove Following Week 7 Bye
full_text:
At 5-1, the Buffalo Bills are off to an excellent start under first-year head coach Joe Brady . While the record is what ultimately matters, there are some concerns for the Bills that need to be addressed during their Week 7 bye .
The most pressing concern is the defense as a whole. Defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard has helped players such as Greg Rousseau excel , but they've had major problems, especially against the pass.
While Leonhard will be hard at work trying to get things corrected on his end, there are also multiple players who need to step up once the Bills leave their bye week. That being the case, here are the three players with the most to prove.
Jackson Hawes was one of the biggest steals in the NFL draft last season. He finished as the fourth-highest rated tight end in the league, earning a PFF grade of 83.2 . He was essentially a sixth offensive lineman, but had some moments as a receiver, hauling in 16 receptions on 19 targets for 187 yards and three touchdowns.
In 2026, he seems to be having a bit of a sophomore slump. Hawes has no receptions and has been targeted just once in six games. He's also seen his grade drop to 41.4 overall. The good news is that he's still been a solid blocker, but the Bills need him to return to the form they saw during his rookie season.
Terrel Bernard was excited about working under Leonhard and he has 45 tackles in six games. Those numbers can be misleading, however, as Bernard has a PFF grade of just 53.9 which is 60th out of 75 qualified linebackers.
Bills On SI's Ralph Ventre has been critical of Bernard , saying he looks slow and confused at times this season. He also admits his spot is likely safe due to his contract. That means any improvements at the position will be solely on Bernard living up to expectations. For that to happen, he needs to use this week off to refocus and get back on track.
Early in the season, Dalton Kincaid was Buffalo's most dynamic receiver. He had 130 yards on six receptions in Week 1 and 95 yards on eight catches in Week 2. Since then, he's recorded 38 yards in two games and seven yards in two others.
Kincaid is a versatile weapon in the passing game and when he's at his best, it truly opens up the offense. When Buffalo gets out of its bye, they need to see Kincaid return to the form he showed at the beginning of the season. If he can do that, the Bills' offense would be able to take a huge step forward.
It's hard to find anyone in Buffalo whose stock has fallen as much as Maxwell Hairston's . The 2025 first-round pick was benched in favor of Davison Igbinosun and there's a growing feeling that Leonhard could eventually phase him out of the plans completely.
The good news for Hairston is that he's young and has all the tools to succeed. What he really needs is to rediscover his confidence. Perhaps he will be able to figure that out during the bye week, because he could be running out of time.

title: Bills' Potential Safety Solution Former Ravens' INT Leader Ready on Practice Squad
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills will be down one safety when they come off their bye week to host the Baltimore Ravens on November 1.
Starter Chauncey Gardner-Johnson must serve a one-game NFL-imposed suspension for violating the conduct policy by spitting on an opponent during the October 18 road game against the Las Vegas Raiders.
As a result, veteran Damar Hamlin will presumably start alongside Cole Bishop at safety in Week 7 with fifth-round rookie Jalon Kilgore providing insurance off the bench. Kilgore saw his first career defensive snaps as a dime safety in the wake of  Gardner-Johnson's ejection last Sunday.
Although they could likely get away without making the move, especially if versatile defensive back Jordan Hancock, the Bills may opt to call up veteran safety Geno Stone from the practice squad for game day against the Ravens.
Rather than placing Stone in a standby role, Buffalo should give him enough snaps for an in-game evaluation. There's certainly a chance he can provide more of what the Bills need from that position group, especially against the pass.
Putting aside the extracurricular nonsense, Gardner-Johnson's performance has been subpar at best. He owns a 21.6 percent missed tackle rate while opposing passers are averaging 13.8 yards per completion when targeting him in coverage. In fact, the Bills should consider cutting Gardner-Johnson and giving his roster spot to Stone.
As a whole, the Bills' safeties are part of the reason why the team ranks next to last in pass defense (285.8).
Before thinking about a potential trade to upgrade the secondary, why not turn to someone who is already in the building and has experience producing at the NFL level? It certainly isn't the sexiest option, but it may yield better results than any external addition could at this point in time.
The Bills added Stone in March after two seasons, and 34 consecutive starts, with the Cincinnati Bengals.
Stone, who signed a modest veteran contract reportedly worth $1.4 million, was drawn to Buffalo for a number of reasons, including an endorsement from fellow Iowa Hawkeye Micah Hyde .
Prior to spending back-to-back seasons as a Bengals' starter, Stone, a 2020 seventh-round draft pick, played out his rookie contract with the Baltimore Ravens. In 2023, Stone made a team-high seven interceptions to lead all NFL safeties.
While the 27-year-old Stone, who has 85 career appearances (53 starts) under his belt, struggled with his tackling and coverage last season, he has a versatility that gives him a chance to succeed in defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard's scheme.
“I was always a Swiss Army knife that kind of did a lot of different things and that's what I like my safety group to be," said Leonhard, who spent 10 years as a NFL safety. "There's going to be a lot of different roles and a lot of different positions and techniques they're asked to do."
Stone has earned starts as both a free safety and a strong safety since being drafted in 2020.

title: Key Stat That Explains NFL Leader Keon Coleman's Redemption Arc  With Bills
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills had high hopes for Keon Coleman when they drafted him in 2024. It may have taken some time, but he looks to be living up to their expectations.
In fact, Coleman's third year in the NFL looks like it could be his best yet. He was selected as a riser in the Bills On SI Bye Week Stock Report .
After scoring four touchdowns in each of his first two seasons with the Bills, Coleman has needed only six games to get to three on the year this season.
But one metric has shown that Coleman may be playing even better than a casual fan may expect. What it shows is that Coleman's development is fully in effect as he plays through his age-23 season.
𝗪𝗢𝗪: Keon Coleman leads the ENTIRE NFL in EPA per target 🤯 Is the Keon breakout REAL? #Bills | #GoBills | #BillsMafia pic.twitter.com/eOB2WlTufn
One may be wondering: what exactly is EPA? It's Expected Points Added. The metric represents how much a single play increases or decreases a team's likelihood of scoring. So, in essence, no receiver in the NFL this season is enhancing his team's chances of scoring more than Coleman.
Other metrics back this up and show how well Coleman has played thus far. The Florida State product has the highest success rate (70.8 percent) and catch rate (79.2 percent) of his career. Coleman also has zero drops this year and has garnered a 138.0 passer rating when targeted (another career high).
The play of Coleman really seems to be tied to the fact that head coach Joe Brady has heavily invested in his development.
Brady's backing of Coleman when he was named Bills' head coach seems to be paying dividends. Especially as the Buffalo receiving corps dealt with injuries to D.J. Moore and Josh Palmer.
Brady elaborated on the maturity his third-year  wideout is showing and how that has helped his play on the field.
"His play has never been his issue," said Brady. "And right now, there's not issues off the field. He's where he needs to be, he's handling everything like a pro."
It's encouraging to see just how strong Coleman has played in 2026. But like his head coach alluded to, his best days still look to be ahead.
"There's so much trust we have for him as the player, the development, and he continues to just make plays," said Brady.
