title: Grading Every Colts Position Group Through Six Weeks
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are six games into the 2026 season, and at 2-4, there is plenty of blame to go around.
Most of it belongs on the defensive side of the ball, but there are still a few bright spots keeping this team competitive. Here is my position-by-position report card through six weeks.
Daniel Jones has been underwhelming, throwing for 1,290 yards, four touchdowns and six interceptions while completing just 59.6% of his passes.
His legs have also been a complete non-factor with only 55 rushing yards, but there are two important caveats: he is still working back from a torn Achilles, and this receiving corps has given him very little help.
Jonathan Taylor is once again proving he is one of the best running backs in football.
He has 492 rushing yards and seven rushing touchdowns, tied for the most among NFL running backs through six weeks. But Seth McGowan and the rest of the room have provided very little offensive impact behind him.
Injuries have crushed this room, but the production has still been nowhere near good enough.
No one has consistently created separation or provided the explosive element this offense desperately needs, allowing defenses to key in even more on Taylor.
Tyler Warren is carrying this room.
The tight end room has accounted for three of Indianapolis' four passing touchdowns, but five different tight ends have combined for only around 275 receiving yards.
This is one group I am not putting much blame on.
Indianapolis owns PFF's third-best run-blocking grade at 74.0 and seventh-best pass-blocking grade at 71.1, and the offensive line has given this offense enough to be much better than it has been.
The Colts rank 31st in run-defense grade via PFF, and the pass rush has not been much better.
This group simply has not gotten to the quarterback consistently, which has made life even harder on an already shaky secondary.
This has been one of the worst position rooms on the roster.
Akeem Davis-Gaither has had some strong moments against the run, but the coverage has been poor, the run defense has been inconsistent and the rookie linebackers have done very little to inspire confidence moving forward.
Indianapolis owns PFF's 28th-ranked coverage unit at 43.6, and the corners have struggled against both the pass and the run.
Sauce Gardner has been decent overall, but quarterbacks have had far too much time in clean pockets, exposing this secondary repeatedly.
Cam Bynum and A.J. Haulcy have both fallen short of expectations.
Bynum finally recorded his first interception against Tennessee, but both safeties have been inconsistent in coverage and against the run.
Special teams has easily been the most reliable unit on this team.
Spencer Shrader continues to deliver, and Rigoberto Sanchez remains one of the league's best punters. The blocked punt against Tennessee was a disaster, but this unit has still been one of the few consistent positives through six weeks
Six weeks in, the Colts have far more questions than answers, and the grades reflect exactly that.
Jonathan Taylor, the offensive line and special teams have done their part, but the rest of this roster needs to step up in a hurry. If Indianapolis has any hope of turning this season around, the defense has to start pulling its weight.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: What Shane Steichen Must Do to Save His Job With the Colts
full_text:
Chris Ballard is gone. And if this season keeps trending the way it has, I have a hard time believing Shane Steichen will be far behind.
Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon made her expectations clear when she fired Ballard on Monday. The standard is to compete for championships, and at 2-4, Indianapolis is nowhere close right now.
Steichen still has 11 games to change that. Here is what I think he needs to do to remain the Colts' head coach in 2027.
First and foremost, Steichen has to start winning football games.
This roster is too talented to finish under .500 again. Indianapolis went 8-9 in each of the last two seasons, and after Irsay-Gordon preached urgency all offseason, another losing record should not be enough.
At 27-30 through his first 57 games, Steichen has yet to make the playoffs. He needs to show signs this team is moving forward.
A winning season might not be enough by itself. The Colts need to find a way into the postseason.
Jacksonville sits two games ahead at 4-2, so winning the AFC South will require a serious turnaround. But whether it comes through the division or a wild-card spot, Indianapolis needs to be playing meaningful football in January.
This is where I need to see Steichen take more ownership.
The Colts allowed 24.2 points per game in Lou Anarumo's first season and are allowing 27.3 through six games this year. Those results are not good enough for a team that has invested heavily on defense.
Steichen has always been known for offense, but being a head coach means owning all three phases. If this unit continues to struggle, he has to be willing to make changes.
Jones looked completely different in 2025, completing 68% of his passes with 19 touchdowns, eight interceptions and a 100.2 passer rating. Through six games this season, those numbers have fallen to 59.6%, four touchdowns, six interceptions and a 71.1 rating.
Steichen was hired in large part because of what he helped build around Jalen Hurts in Philadelphia. That 2022 Eagles offense leaned on an elite offensive line and dominant rushing attack to make life easier on its quarterback.
The Colts have Jonathan Taylor, a strong offensive line and enough weapons to do something similar. Steichen has to find that version of his offense again.
Lastly, this team has to stop beating itself.
The Colts just blew a 13-0 halftime lead to an 0-5 Titans team, with a blocked punt helping swing the game. Irsay-Gordon specifically talked about finishing games when she brought Steichen back after last season.
Bottom line: Steichen needs to win, make the playoffs, fix the defense and prove the offensive creativity that got him this job is still there.
If he cannot do that over the next 11 games, I would expect the Colts' next general manager to be hiring a new head coach.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts' Injury Woes Continue as 16 Players Appear on Week 7 Report
full_text:
Just when it seemed things couldn't get much worse for the Indianapolis Colts, Wednesday's injury report brought another headache.
Sunday's embarrassing 26-20 loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans dropped Indianapolis to 2-4. A day later, owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon fired general manager Chris Ballard, ending his tenure in his 10th season.
Now, with undefeated Minnesota waiting on Sunday, 16 players from the Colts' 53-man roster appeared on the first injury report of the week.
That's almost a third of the roster, and this team is only six games into the season.
Eleven players did not practice, while five were limited. Three listings were for rest — Keenan Allen, Charvarius Ward Sr. and Jonathan Taylor — and defensive tackle Jerry Tillery was absent for personal reasons.
That leaves 12 players dealing with actual injuries. For a team desperate to turn things around, it's a troubling list.
Tight end Tyler Warren is the name I'm watching most closely. Warren did not practice Wednesday due to the groin injury suffered late last week, which already cost him Sunday's game against Tennessee.
Matt Goncalves (ankle), Drew Ogletree (ankle) and Rigoberto Sanchez (right foot) also sat out, while Jalen Travis (foot) was limited.
Sanchez suffered his injury against Tennessee, prompting Indianapolis to add veteran punter Thomas Morstead to the practice squad.
Wide receiver Anthony Gould missed practice with a concussion, while Ashton Dulin was limited with a hamstring injury.
On defense, things aren't looking much better.
Rookie Bryce Boettcher missed Wednesday's practice with a groin injury, and Jaylon Carlies was limited as he continues recovering from the rib injury that has kept him out of the last two games.
Austin Ajiake was also limited while undergoing a concussion evaluation.
If Carlies cannot return, Indianapolis could have to lean even more heavily on rookie CJ Allen, while recently re-signed veteran Germaine Pratt may become an option. And with Boettcher now on the report, this group is running out of healthy bodies.
Then there's the cornerback room, where Sauce Gardner (calf), Justin Walley (knee) and Ward all missed practice.
Ward's absence was rest-related, but Gardner is considered week-to-week after injuring his calf against Tennessee. Losing him for any length of time would be a massive blow to an already struggling secondary.
The Colts are allowing 27.3 points per game, and facing a 5-0 Vikings team isn't exactly an ideal opportunity to navigate this many injuries.
This injury bug always seems to find its way back to Indianapolis. With jobs on the line and the season slipping away, the Colts need that trend to stop quickly.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 3 Colts May See Increased Workloads Moving Forward
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' 2026 season is all but over, and the organization needs to start looking ahead.
With the playoffs no longer a realistic expectation, the rest of the remaining schedule should focus on evaluating the roster and determining which players deserve a role beyond this season .
Rather than continuing to rely on the same personnel, Indianapolis should use this stretch to explore its options and give more opportunities to players who could factor into the team's future. There is little reason to leave potential answers on the sideline when the Colts have so many questions to address.
Here are three Colts who should see more playing time for the remainder of the season.
As the Colts use the rest of the season to parse through their roster and identify pieces they can build around for the future, CJ Allen will be one of those players.
The Colts’ top draft choice from a year ago has found playing time hard to come by thus far in his rookie season as the Colts have opted to play more experienced veterans instead.
Allen's 46 snaps through six games are the least among all Colts linebackers, and there's almost no reason not to increase his workload.
But the season is basically a wash at this point, and Indianapolis may as well give Allen an extended run to see if he’s truly someone they can lean on moving forward, or if he’ll have to find a new NFL home when the housecleaning inevitably begins.
Will Mallory made his season debut on Sunday after spending the first five weeks on injured reserve. While filling in for the injured Tyler Warren, it was immediately apparent that Mallory could be a contributor on the Colts offense moving forward.
Mallory caught only two passes for 20 yards, but was targeted six times, third-most on the team and the most of any non-wide receiver. So clearly, Daniel Jones knows he can trust Mallory in the passing game.
As the season moves along, look for Mallory to be more involved in the passing attack, even when Warren is back healthy. As Indianapolis uses the remaining schedule to evaluate its roster before entering a rebuilding phase, Mallory is likely to stand out as a player they can count on going into the reset.
Daniel Jones has not been good enough to keep the Colts from reconsidering their quarterback situation.
With the previous regime gone and the season slipping away, there is no better time to see what Anthony Richardson can do for the Colts . Richardson had lost the faith of the coaching staff during the 2024 season, but there’s virtually zero reason to not let him loose at some point in 2026.
Even if Richardson stinks it up, the Colts can move into the offseason with the knowledge that their search for a franchise quarterback continues. But, if Richardson shows significant improvement and promise, then Indianapolis may elect to extend his leash a little bit and see what he can do in a full season next year.
Playing Richardson at some point is a no-brainer. Jones clearly is a shell of his 2025 self and the Colts season is all but lost.
But there’s nothing to lose by giving Richardson a shot.

title: Week 7 Power Rankings: Indianapolis Plummets After Disastrous Week
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' collapse has officially changed the national conversation around the franchise.
After a disastrous loss to the Tennessee Titans and the firing of general manager Chris Ballard , Indianapolis finds itself facing mounting questions about the direction of the organization. With the season taking a troubling turn, let's take a look at where the Colts stand in the eyes of the national media.
Sports Illustrated: 28th (Week 6: 24th)
No sugarcoating from Sports Illustrated’s Conor Orr . He dropped the Colts four places in his updated rankings after their embarrassing loss in Week 6.
“Losing to the Titans will absolutely break you as a person,” he wrote, keeping analysis very brief this time around.
I’m sure the fans will agree with you, Conor.
ESPN’s team of beat reporters voted to drop the Colts just two spots, the shortest fall by any publication this week.
Colts reporter Stephen Holder wrote that Daniel Jones’ poor play is the most problematic offensive issue for Indianapolis, though there are reasons explaining why.
“The team's receivers are very underwhelming without Alec Pierce ( heel ), and the offensive line isn't consistently handling blitzes well. But Jones is not able to rise above those issues, ranking near the bottom of the league in QBR (30th), yards per attempt (29th) and completion rate (29th).”
After six weeks last season, Jones ranked in the top five in all three categories. Quite a regression.
Pro Football Talk: 27th (Week 6: 23rd)
Pro Football Talk’s Mike Florio has just one question for the Colts: Is a fire sale coming?
Reports indicate a complete dismantling of the roster at the upcoming Nov. 10 trade deadline is unrealistic, but the Colts could still absolutely make some moves to expedite their rebuilding process.
But in the meantime, a bottom five ranking is definitely reasonable considering the current state of the franchise.
The Athletic: 30th (Week 6: 25th)
Chad Graff and Josh Kendall slid Indianapolis down five slots this week and into the bottom three in the NFL, one of two publications to do so.
“Things are getting ugly in Indy,” they wrote, referencing both the horrendous loss and the decision to fire Ballard.
The pair has some praise for Jonathan Taylor, who “keeps chugging along,” Taylor is on pace to rush for 1,300 yards for the third straight season.
Fox Sports: 23rd (Week 6: 20th)
A three-spot slide for Indianapolis in Ralph Vacchiano’s newest rankings, down to 23rd from its previous place at No. 20.
Vacchiano wrote that Colts CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has “waved the white flag” on the 2026 season by getting rid of Ballard, getting the wheels started on a new chapter in franchise history.
“That’s a pretty clear signal that they’re heading for a rebuild and a new vision next season, which means coach Shane Steichen is probably next to go, and QB Daniel Jones shouldn’t get too comfortable either,” he wrote, adding that Sunday’s loss to Tennessee is indicative of where the franchise is headed: towards rock bottom.
NFL.com: 30th (Week 6: 24th)
NFL.com’s Nick Shook is the second of two media members to rank the Colts outside the top 29 teams, pushing them six spots down from No. 24, the longest drop by any major outlet this week. After firing their general manager, Shook doesn’t expect much from Indianapolis the rest of the season.
“Firing a GM midseason usually doesn’t produce sudden improvement, meaning the Colts are what their record says they are, and fans shouldn’t expect much more,” he wrote.
Shook pointed to a few familiar issues: turnovers, failure to capitalize on scoring chances and an underperforming defense as reasons for the devastating collapse.
Bleacher Report: 27th (Week 6: 23rd)
Bleacher Report’s team of NFL writers collectively placed the Colts at 27th in the NFL, four spots down from last week.
“The Colts look far removed from the team that started 8-2 last season, with little sign of a return to that form in 2026,” Kris Knox wrote. “(They) are spiraling, and things could get worse with road games against the Minnesota Vikings and Jacksonville Jaguars on deck.”
Daniel Jones has been poor, too poor to overcome injury problems at wide receiver. The defense has been too inconsistent and ineffective through six games.
And things are likely to get worse before they get better. Gear up for a long few months, Colts fans.

title: Colts Interim General Manager Makes First Moves in New Role
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have made their first roster moves under interim general manager Ed Dodds .
In his first full day as interim, Dodds made two additions to the Colts practice squad, signing wide receiver Mecole Hardman and punter Thomas Morstead, releasing wide receiver Eli Pancol from the practice squad in a corresponding move.
Dodds is taking over the Colts' personnel department for the remainder of the 2026 season following the firing of longtime general manager Chris Ballard on Monday. The longtime assistant GM will oversee Indianapolis' roster decisions as the franchise navigates what remains of a disappointing season.
Hardman and Morstead address two areas of concern for the Colts following Sunday's 26-20 loss to the Tennessee Titans, although neither practice squad addition represents an immediate solution.
Hardman's arrival comes as Indy continues searching for answers at wide receiver.
Injuries and inconsistent production have left the Colts without a reliable downfield threat outside of their injured options, limiting quarterback Daniel Jones' ability to stretch opposing defenses.
Alec Pierce, arguably Indianapolis' most dangerous deep threat, remains on injured reserve with a heel injury. Ashton Dulin has also dealt with injuries, missing four games so far this year. Indy kicked the tires on Darius Slayton, but that experiment failed spectacularly, with Slayton never suiting up for a game. Quez Watkins has been another option the team has explored, but the Colts still lack the consistent vertical presence their passing game needs.
Hardman brings a different skill set to the group. The veteran wide receiver is best known for his speed and ability to create explosive plays, giving Indianapolis another potential option to threaten defenses downfield. He also brings considerable NFL experience, seven seasons of it, including multiple Super Bowl championships with the Kansas City Chiefs.
The signing is a low-risk opportunity for the Colts to see whether Hardman can contribute to an offense that has struggled. His speed could provide a refreshing new dimension to the passing game that desperately needs a field-stretching presence with Pierce sidelined.
However, Hardman's addition is nothing more than a short-term trial run. Hardman will be 29 years old at the start of next season and is unlikely to be a part of the Colts plans as they navigate the next chapter in their franchise’s history.
Dodds also added veteran punter Thomas Morstead following a difficult afternoon for its special teams unit against Tennessee.
Rigoberto Sanchez endured a rough outing Sunday, having had a punt blocked and returned for a touchdown. On that same play, Sanchez suffered an apparent foot injury, leading Dodds to add another experienced punter in Morstead.
The 40-year-old punter has spent more than a decade in the NFL and has played for several teams, including the New Orleans Saints, New York Jets and Miami Dolphins. His experience could provide Indianapolis with additional depth and insurance as it evaluates its special teams personnel.
Because Morstead is joining the practice squad, the move does not necessarily signal an imminent change at punter, meaning the addition is more than likely a precautionary measure if Sanchez does have to miss any time in the short term.
For Dodds, these signings represent an early opportunity to address two weaknesses exposed during the Colts' most recent loss. Neither addition moves the needle, but both give Indianapolis veteran options as it attempts to stabilize a season that has quickly veered off course.

title: 5 Colts Who Could Be Traded Following Chris Ballard's Firing
full_text:
The Chris Ballard era is officially over in Indianapolis, and it didn't take long for the trade hypotheticals to start flying.
After Sunday's embarrassing 26-20 loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans dropped the Colts to 2-4, owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon fired Ballard Monday morning. Assistant GM Ed Dodds will oversee the personnel department for the remainder of the season.
Indianapolis doesn't own its 2027 first-round pick after sending it to the Jets in the Sauce Gardner trade, so I understand the talk about recouping draft capital. But I am not in favor of tearing this roster down to the studs.
Jonathan Taylor and Quenton Nelson are the type of players I would build the next version of this team around.
Still, if Indianapolis decides to make major changes before the Nov. 10 trade deadline or next offseason, these are the five names that make the most sense.
Nelson is in the final year of his contract and is scheduled to hit free agency after the season.
Big Q is still playing at an elite level, and that's exactly why teams would call. If someone puts a premium pick on the table, Indianapolis would have to listen.
But it would take a massive offer for me to move him.
Buckner is another veteran in the final year of his deal, and this one feels more realistic.
At 32, Buckner has four sacks through six games. If the Colts don't plan on bringing him back in 2027, getting something for him now makes sense.
This is where I start pushing back on the full-rebuild conversation.
Taylor signed an extension in August, led the NFL with 20 total touchdowns last season and already has seven rushing touchdowns this year.
He's one of the best players in franchise history, has publicly said he wants to be a Colt for life, and it would take a MASSIVE return to even consider moving him.
To me, Taylor and Nelson are a package deal. They should be pillars of whatever comes next.
Stewart probably isn't bringing back premium draft capital, but teams will call.
He's been a staple of Indianapolis' run defense for years, and as another veteran with an expiring contract, a contender looking for interior help could make him an attractive deadline target.
Ward is an interesting name to consider, especially with the Colts potentially looking to recoup some draft capital.
Indianapolis signed Ward to a three-year, $54 million deal in 2025, and while he's still a capable starting cornerback, his availability and production haven't quite lived up to that investment.
At 30 years old, Ward probably isn't bringing back a premium draft pick, but a contender looking for experienced secondary help could come calling.
If Indianapolis can get a reasonable return and create some future cap flexibility, this is one move I wouldn't be completely against.
Ultimately, Ed Dodds and Colts ownership have some difficult decisions ahead. But there's a difference between building for the future and trading away the very players this franchise should be building around.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Why Colts Should Consider a Change at QB: The Carousel's Last Ride
full_text:
As is tradition in the Ballard era, the Indianapolis Colts have not been good enough at quarterback so far this season.
After six weeks, it's undeniable that starting quarterback Daniel Jones has regressed into a shell of himself instead of picking up where he left off last season.
Former longtime general manager Chris Ballard put all of his eggs into Jones's basket, hoping that the former New York Giants quarterback would replicate the recent trend of former top draft picks finding success with a much-needed change of scenery.
The experiment started strong, as Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen combined to create an offense that perfectly complements Jones as a quarterback. The 2025 Colts offense got off to an unexpected start, playing like one of the most efficient offenses in league history.
However, after Jones broke his fibula in mid-November, things started to go off the rails. He wasn't nearly as mobile or decisive, but Jones was still playing honorably given the circumstances.
It was during a Week 14 AFC South matchup against the Jacksonville Jaguars when Jones tore his Achilles, and the one-year experiment looked to have run its course.
Instead of rolling with either Anthony Richardson or Riley Leonard for what was expected to be Ballard and Co.'s final chance, the Colts re-signed Daniel Jones to a two-year, $88 million deal, which essentially meant that the fate of the regime was in Jones's hands .
All it took was six games to prove that this roster was not going to get the job done, and Ballard has been shown the door as a result.
Ballard's early-season exit is a clear response from Colts Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon that proves she wasn't kidding when she said the sense of urgency has never been higher for Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen in the 2026 offseason.
Irsay-Gordon gave the regime one last shot, especially since Ballard was entering the final year of his contract, but enough is enough.
Steichen will be the head coach for the rest of the season, barring a never-before-seen collapse, but it remains to be seen if he'll see his contract through, which runs through the 2028 season.
We have relieved Chris Ballard of his duties as General Manager. pic.twitter.com/BleD6bfTsG
Parting ways with Ballard allows the Colts to get ahead of their general manager search, while also giving them a golden opportunity to shop their most valuable assets to maximize the next regime's first-year outlook .
One of the only downsides to making such a drastic move this early in the season is that it suggests the organization has given up on the current season.
Even though the Indianapolis Colts have all but punted on the 2026 regular season, their players still have to compete. The Colts must consider any move, and that includes the quarterback position.
I'm not suggesting a move be made right now, but the idea should at least be on the table if things continue to go south, regardless of how expensive a pill it may be to swallow.
The Colts' offensive woes through six weeks aren't all on Daniel Jones, but he hasn't been part of a potential solution either.
Lou Anarumo's defense has been hot-and-cold, and so has Shane Steichen's offense, but it's the latter's shortcomings that have been most concerning - and that's saying something considering the Colts gave up the second-most yards (1,029) through the first two weeks in NFL history, and currently sport the league's worst pass rush unit.
The Colts' offense has not only taken a step back from last year's early-season success, but they've fully reverted to being just another offense that Chris Ballard built.
In terms of personnel, the offense remains largely the same as a season ago. Lingering and/or aggravated injuries and a collective regression have crushed their outlook, but at the end of the day, the offense has not been good enough.
Daniel Jones deserves some nuance, as Indy's aforementioned lack of firepower on offense, particularly at wide receiver , has shrunk the field and forced his hand at times, but that still doesn't excuse his poor performance.
The Colts' starting quarterback has largely returned from his infamous Achilles tear, but it's evident that he's not the same player he was a season ago.
Jones has been pressured at the T-7th-highest rate (42.1%) among all starting quarterbacks, and it's brought out the worst in him. The offensive line, specifically at tackle, is doing him no favors, and his confidence is shot as a result.
Jones ranks near the bottom of the league in numerous statistical categories and is one of three starting quarterbacks who have thrown more interceptions (6) than touchdowns (4) after six weeks of play.
Among qualified quarterbacks, here's where Jones ranks league-wide in those aforementioned key statistical categories entering Week 7:
30th in passer rating (71.1) T-30th in QBR (38.2) 29th in completion percentage (59.6%) 29th in yards per pass attempt (5.9 YPA)
Jones is being paid to be an average quarterback, as his $44 million per year average salary ranks 15th at the position, but he's been much worse than the middle of the pack.
The passing attack has become so unsustainable that it's lowered the rushing game's ceiling, despite Jonathan Taylor's best efforts (6th in rushing yards, 2nd in rushing touchdowns).
Daniel Jones was never expected to single-handedly save the day. He's always been a quarterback who can only thrive if the situation around him is borderline perfect, and the group around him has proven that it's not ideal.
While Jones's future in Indianapolis is up in the air, what about his status for the rest of the 2026 regular season?
Colts head coach Shane Steichen said on Monday that Daniel Jones will remain the team's starting quarterback for the foreseeable future, but at what point do they entertain the idea of turning back to the player they'd seemingly given up on ? And should they, at least in some capacity?
Steichen has showcased extreme loyalty to Jones over their year and a half together. Jones earned his head coach's trust with the offense by embodying what it means to be a starting quarterback in the NFL, both on and off the field.
The two managed to put together an efficient operation that was fascinating to watch at its peak.
But that honeymoon phase is over, and the Colts' offense doesn't appear to be headed anywhere anytime soon.
The Indianapolis Colts decided the Anthony Richardson experiment had run its course after Daniel Jones won the starting job entering the 2025 regular season, leading to the fourth-year quarterback requesting a trade in the following offseason, but there's now a reality where Richardson could start in the final year of his rookie contract.
If nothing else, we should at least see the Colts use Richardson's otherworldly athleticism to open up the playbook a bit. Jones has noticeably lost some of his mobility after tearing his Achilles, so the offense could use some fresh legs from time to time.
Shane Steichen is known for his creative playcalling, and I'm sure he's got plenty of tricks up his sleeve for the QB run game. Richardson could be eased into the offense as a rushing threat, whether that be in the red zone or in a short-yardage QB-designed run package.
Maybe it becomes a regular part of the offensive philosophy moving forward, or perhaps it just comes out in gotta-have-it situations where you want to put a hat on a hat and trust that your guys are tougher than theirs.
The Colts' offense is truly broken through six weeks of play, and with a blitz-heavy Brian Flores defense being the next test, and an impressive 4-2 Jacksonville Jaguars squad on the horizon, it's fair to predict that they'll continue their downward trajectory.
One thing's obvious: if Daniel Jones continues to struggle, you have to consider the change to Richardson full-time .
In 2024, in his second season as the Colts' starting quarterback, Anthony Richardson was benched. But instead of being strictly performance-based, Richardson's…

title: The Jaguars' Top 2027 Roster Need Just Became Crystal Clear
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars still have a lot of football left in 2026, but that doesn't mean they can't always keep an eye on the future.
The future became a bit more clear for the Jaguars this week, at least as it pertains to what the Jaguars' top need might be in the 2027 offseason. With Jaguars' left tackle Anton Harrison now out for the year with an ACL injury, the Jaguars' biggest draft need a year from now has become crystal clear: the Jaguars need a young tackle to develop and bring into their system, and they need one badly.
The Jaguars have the ability to sustain Harrison's injury without much disruption to the offense thanks to Walker Little, who will now slot in at left tackle. Losing Harrison is obviously not ideal, especially because it takes the Jaguars from a great offensive tackle depth chart to one that has second-year guard Wyatt Milum an injury away from stepping in. But the Jaguars should be OK.
With that said, it is the long-term ramifications of Harrison's injury, both for himself and the Jaguars, that now make offensive tackle the team's biggest need before the 2027 offseason is even close to kicking off. The Jaguars' present at tackle looks fine, but Harrison's injury has made the future a lot murkier at a key spot.
Harrison was thought to be the best candidate to be the Jaguars' long-term answer at the left tackle spot, though he needed to prove himself this season to truly land the kind of big-money deal that would have made him a franchise pillar. Harrison started just six games at left tackle in his first four seasons, all of which came this season, which means the Jaguars' sample size of him on the blindside isn't exactly enough to feel confident in picking up extension talks.
Had Harrison stayed healthy and played well to end 2026, he likely would have been a prime extension candidate, either at the end of the season or at some point while playing on his fifth-year option. If he stayed healthy and was inconsistent, as he had been in six games this year, he likely would have entered next year as the starting left tackle for at least one more season as he attempted to prove himself again. That would have at least given the Jaguars some time to figure out left tackle.
But, that didn't happen. Harrison's season is over after only six games, and the Jaguars have no better idea now of whether he is their future at tackle than they did when the season began. That won't change with Harrison sidelined for the rest of the season, and the Jaguars will likely look to simply get by at left tackle until then, at least in terms of the long-term view.
That then brings 2027 into focus. The Jaguars' tackle situation will be Harrison coming off an ACL injury and still being a relative long-term unknown; Little entering a contract year; Cole Van Lanen in his age-29 season. The Jaguars would likely feel fine with rolling into the season with those as their top-3 options because it would be very similar to what they entered 2026 with.
But they also entered 2026 with the hope, perhaps even the expectation, of Harrison entrenching himself as the left tackle of the future. They likely can not enter 2027 with the same expectations, which means finding that tackle is critical. And for all of the positions the Jaguars have added to over the last two drafts, a young tackle is one thing they haven't found.
The only two offensive/defensive positions the Jaguars haven't drafted since James Gladstone took over as general manager are quarterback (duh) and offensive tackle, since Wyatt Milum was drafted as a guard. They have taken a center, running backs, receivers, tight ends, linebackers, safeties, a cornerback, defensive ends, and a defensive tackle ... but no offensive tackle.
The Jaguars need one they can develop, and Harrison's injury has made it clear that finding that tackle should be a top priority. An even bigger one than finding defensive line depth or secondary pieces. Instead, the Jaguars need to find a talented tackle who they can develop for at least a year before turning over the left tackle spot to him in the future.
Jacksonville might have needed the tackle even if Harrison stayed healthy. But now, there is no question. The Jaguars need to find some insurance at tackle, and it should happen within the first two rounds of the 2027 NFL Draft.
John Shipley has been covering the Jacksonville Jaguars as a beat reporter and publisher of Jaguar Report since 2019. Previously, he covered UCF's undefeated season as a beat reporter for NSM.Today, covered high school prep sports in Central Florida, and covered local sports and news for the Palatka Daily News. Follow John Shipley on Twitter at @_john_shipley.

title: One Trade Deadline Move the Jaguars Must Prioritize ASAP
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are a good team. A really good team, even. But, like any team, they could still use some help.
Help normally comes in the form of a trade around this time of the year, with the trade deadline just a few weeks away and rumors and interest starting to heat up. For the Jaguars, there is no reason this year's deadline can't be a productive one.
But what type of moves should the Jaguars prioritize with the deadline around the corner? Should they look for swing tackle help after Anton Harrison's season-ending injury? Should they add more pass-rushers or defensive backs? All of these moves would make some sense, but there is one player who stands out above all the other options: Los Angeles Chargers pass-rusher Khalil Mack.
The Jaguars have bigger needs than the edge position; at least from my view. The Jaguars' secondary has been banged up all season and there is a real and true need for cornerback depth. The secondary is why the Jaguars lost in the Wild Card last season, and it is facing some of the same issues today despite Travis Hunter being a true lockdown No. 1 cornerback.
But there is a reason that Mack is the top target the Jaguars should focus on landing, and one they should work to do so as quickly as possible. The Jaguars have a talented pair of edge defenders in Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen, but they have not gotten much production from the rest of the pass-rush unit on a down-to-down basis.
The Jaguars rank No. 9 in pressure rate this season at 39.1%, about a 4% increase from their 2025 number. But the Jaguars have had to blitz at a high clip to make that happen. When the Jaguars blitz, they have a pressure rate of 49.3%, which would rank No. 1 in the NFL this year in terms of standard pressure rate. But when the Jaguars do not blitz, their pressure rate drops to 33.6%. That is still 10th-best of all teams when they are just rushing four, but it is clear the Jaguars are getting more pressure when they send the house.
The reason for that is simple: the Jaguars are not getting any pass-rush from anyone not named Hines-Allen or Walker. Arik Armstead has had some big games inside, but also some quiet ones. And out of 130 qualifying rushers, Dennis Gardeck, Bryan Thomas Jr., and Danny Striggow rank No. 90, No. 123, and No. 129 in pass-rush win-rate.
This means that the Jaguars have two players on their roster providing pressure, and they have to scheme the rest of it up. To fix this, the Jaguars should offer the Chargers a fifth-round pick for Mack. Mack's win rate ranks just No. 70, but that is as the Chargers' No. 2 guy. He would be the No. 3 guy in Jacksonville, a better fit for where he is at in his career and a better fit for what the Jaguars truly need in their edge rotation.
Mack, who would be a cheap rental, would also allow Dennis Gardeck to be more rotational of a pass-rusher than he is now, a better role for his skill-set. It would also allow Walker to slide inside on more passing downs which is, you guessed it, a better role for his skill-set as well. It would make several members of the defense better, improve the pass-rush depth, and give the Jaguars a chance to not have to rely solely on two players to provide that spark.
The Jaguars could also recoup whatever they send over for Mack depending on where he signs in free agency next season. Getting a few months of production from Mack and then getting some kind of future compensatory pick for his services would be a big win in terms of team-building. With that said, the Jaguars would have to move with some quickness.
Mack will likely be a sought-after target on the trade market due to his position, years of production, and the fact that it is clear he will only take a Day 3 pick for the winless Chargers. A lot of teams are bound to be interested in a player like that, with the Chicago Bears already being tied to a potential move.
The Jaguars should move quickly to prevent anyone else from getting in on renting out Mack and then getting a future pick for him, because it is a smart move to move.

title: The Jaguars Only Have 3 Post-Bye Week Options For Brian Thomas Jr's Future
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have some big decisions to make after the bye week, and more than a few center around wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr.
The former first-round pick is the most embattled member of the roster through the first six weeks of the season, and the question now is what the Jaguars will do with their former No. 1 wide receiver.
So, what are t he Jaguars' options with Thomas as they near the end of their bye week? We break down each potential path below, starting with ...
The Jaguars trading Thomas , of course, is the most logical (and to me, probable) scenario for a few reasons. Jacksonville made it clear by benching him against the Texans that they are more or less done with trying to help him out of his slump, and the Jaguars have the depth that would make it possible to unload him in a deal. They didn't have that proven depth this offseason when his value was at its highest, but things have changed since then.
The fact that Marvin Harrison Jr. went for a second and a Day 3 pick swap suggests Thomas could net the Jaguars similar value, and there are several teams that would make sense as landing spots for the former LSU product. Washington Commanders with his college quarterback? A banged-up Los Angeles Rams team that is running short on wide receivers? A Las Vegas Raiders team that has a young quarterback and a middling receiver room?
The possibilities are all there for the Jaguars, and we should know sooner than later whether the Jaguars will be ready to part with the uber-talented Thomas.
Liam Coen set a bit of a precedent with the way he handled Thomas a week ago against the Houston Texans, which brings his post-bye week plans into focus. The Jaguars did not have Thomas play a single snap in the second-half last week against the Texans despite the Jaguars trailing for much of the game. Even with the Jaguars chasing points with a pass-first attack while facing a deficit, the Jaguars prefered to have Travis Hunter, Josh Cameron, or multiple tight ends on the field over Thomas in a key game.
The Jaguars could enter Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts with the same idea; either making him a healthy scratch or just simply not playing him or playing him in a marginal role. The fact he has no special teams value suggests there is a real scenario he might simply be inactive, but this path would have a few issues for the Jaguars. Namely, it would tank any kind of value Thomas has on the trade market or, at the least, tank any leverage the Jaguars have in trade talks.
If Thomas isn't seeing any playing time, there is no real reason for teams to offer premium picks for his services. His traits and pedigree suggests the Jaguars could still land a second-round pick for him, but that idea likely goes out the window if he doesn't see the field anymore. Still, the Jaguars will have to weigh what is in their best interests to win on each Sunday, which means sitting him might end up being the only real answer.
This is what the Jaguars have been doing for a while , and it just hasn't worked. Thomas became the clear third-fiddle for the Jaguars in the passing game last season after the Jaguars added Jakobi Meyers: in the six regular-season games Thomas played last year for the Jaguars alongside Meyers, he had one game with a target rate above 20%, compared to four games before Meyers was traded for. He was still playing, but he wasn't seeing the ball thrown his way. After being the undisputed No. 1 entering 2025, he clearly fell down the pecking order.
As a result, it was clear entering the season that Thomas would be a part of the passing game's equation, but far from its clear focus. But after a ho-hum Week 1 where he caught three passes for 40 yards, Thomas has caught three passes for 25 yards and a touchdown on eight targets over the last month. That is less than what Travis Hunter and Josh Cameron have produced in single games this season, and Thomas' playing time didn't really start dipping until this past week against the Texans, sans a reduced role in Week 3.
The Jaguars could still have Thomas on the field and keep trying and hoping that something suddenly clicks. But this path, which is the one of least resistance, has cost the Jaguars some real points and first-down conversions in critical moments this season. Maybe the Jaguars let Thomas try to get his groove back, but this feels unlikely.

title: Bye Week NFL Power Rankings Roundup: How Much Do Jaguars Get Dinged for Texans Loss?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' bye week came at just the right time.
The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 at the bye week, fresh off a close 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans and two games played overseas in the United Kingdom. And even after a loss to the Texans that exposed the Jaguars' few shortcomings, the Jaguars should still feel good about where they are.
"I got a lot of confidence in this team. We didn't get the result we wanted. We're not going to change a thing about our process? Do we have to evaluate and clean up areas in which we need to, specifically in some areas that we just talked about? Absolutely. But I have a lot of confidence in this team," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after last Sunday's loss to the Texans.
"I'm extremely proud of this team and the way they kept fighting today, going down ten points, ten points, ten points. Kept fighting. Kept fighting. Gave ourselves a chance in a quasi two-minute drill to go win the game. We end up kicking it. Settling, Cam [K Cam Little] makes a huge kick to put us in a position to tie that football game. I'm extremely proud of this team and confident in this group moving forward."
So, where do the Jaguars fall in this week's power rankings across the NFL after their Week 6 loss? We break it down below.
The line is held on this one, though Conor Orr does not that the Jaguars could very easily rise if Travis Hunter keeps up his high level of play. After seeing what Hunter did for the Jaguars against the Houston Texans, it is tough to disagree with Orr.
No changes here, which is interesting considering the Jaguars started off the year quite low in ESPN's rankings. They have since climbed into the top-5, though, and they do not appear to be going away.
I can understand putting most of the teams that are ahead of the Jaguars in their spot here, but the Cincinnati Bengals being multiple spots ahead of the Jaguars is curious considering the Jaguars were the clearly better team when the two faced off in the Bengal's home stadium in a Jaguars win a few weeks ago.
The Seahawks is the name I would dispute here when it comes to putting them above the Jaguars, but I think that this likely has as much to do with them being the most recent Super Bowl champions as it does anything else. With that said, the Jaguars are still able to find a decent spot within the top-10.
Moving the New England Patriots over the Jaguars here is certainly a choice. Perhaps there was a way we could see the Jaguars and Patriots on an even playing field against one another so we could use that as a reference point. That would have made a lot of sense. Alas!
The Jaguars did remain in the top-5 of these rankings, though they were leaped in the rankings by the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings. The argument can easily be made for the Bills ahead of the Jaguars, but having the Vikings ahead of them still seems foolish until they put together conseuctive weeks of strong offensive play.
These rankings take the Jaguars down a peg after having them in the top-5 a week ago, and it is clear that the Texans game is not the only factor. Instead, the Jaguars also took a few steps down these rankings due to their collective struggles in London, which also saw them barely defeat a wounded Philadelphia Eagles team in a miracle 19-17 win in Week 5.
Despite the loss to the previously 1-4 Texans, the Jaguars only dropped one spot in these rankings. The Jaguars ended up swapping places with the Buffalo Bills, who now sit at the No. 3 spot. It can be debated whether the Bills have been as consistently impressive as the Jaguars this season, but the Bills and Josh Allen did beat the Jaguars in last year's Wild Card round, so fair play for now.

title: 3 Trades Jaguars Must Consider to Bolster Offensive Line After Anton Harrison's Injury
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars suddenly have a very big need along the offensive line.
No, not at left tackle. The loss of Anton Harrison for the season due to an ACL injury is clearly a loss for the Jaguars' offense, but the Jaguars do have a reliable option in swing tackle Walker Little who can step in at left tackle and give the Jaguars quality snaps.
But with Little moved to a starting spot at left tackle, the Jaguars now have a massive question mark looking at the swing tackle spot. Most teams are one offensive tackle injury away from a nightmare, but the Jaguars took their one injury on the chin and can sustain the blow. But the Jaguars could not sustain a second loss.
So with the Jaguars being one snap away from one of their deep reserves having to step in at offensive tackle , the Jaguars should naturally look to the trade market to find a new swing tackle option. But, what names would make sense?
We have discussed Dylan Cook before , and for good reason. The backup offensive tackle played good football for the Steelers during the first two games of the season and has since stepped back into a depth role. He could be a quietly excellent swing tackle option who has legit starting potential down the road, which would give the Jaguars quite the piece to have on their roster as they move forward with Anton Harrison's uncertain post-injury future.
Why would the Steelers trade away such a good depth piece at such an important position, especially in a tight AFC North? Well, that is what draft picks are for. The Jaguars would likely have to overpay a bit considering Cook would still be a backup in Jacksonville, but he is a talented enough swing tackle option that he would be worth the risk. He would likely cost more than what Daniel Faalele cost the Jaguars this summer for that reason, but comfortable depth in a contending season is worth that.
It will be worth keeping tabs on the Steelers over the next few weeks. If they start losing games, perhaps they become more open to a potential deal closer to the deadline next month. But for as things stand today, Cook is the most attractive trade option if the Jaguars are looking to add a true swing tackle.
Austin Jackson is a former first-round pick who is on a cheap deal, has a decent amount of experience (65 career starts) and is on a bad team that would love nothing more than to get some draft picks. He seems like a player who a team could easily trade for without having to give up too much, which would make a difference to a team like the Jaguars that likely would not want to give away all that much.
Jackson has also played multiple spots along the offensive line, taking snaps at both tackle spots and also inside at guard. The Jaguars have stressed players with experience at multiple positions when it comes to the offensive line, and Jackson would certainly fall into that same category considering all we have seen him play at the NFL level.
The caveat, of course, is that Jackson, well, has not been very good in Miami. With that said, this is about depth, an even a below-average player with 60+ starts is better depth than the unknown that the Jaguars may be facing at the swing tackle spot moving forward with Little at left tackle and Harrison out for the year.
While Jackson is a player who could help fill a few different depth roles, there is no denying what Cleveland Browns' offensive lineman Dawand Jones is: he is an offensive tackle through and through, and he also has a bit of experience with 20 career starts since entering the NFL in 2023. He does have some reliability issues in terms of missed time over the years, but he has been active for all six games this year and would be a cheap addition on his contract year.
The Browns and Jaguars' front offices have also done deals with one another before, with general managers Andrew Berry and James Gladstone working together first on the Travis Hunter trade last April before the Tyson Campbell/Greg Newsome trade that took place after Week 5 last season ... close to the same timeline we are on in the 2026 season.

title: Anton Harrison's Injury Could Have Major Repercussions for These 4 Jaguars
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Anton Harrison is done for the rest of the season.
The Jacksonville Jaguars were dealt a tough blow on Friday, with reports stating the Jaguars' left tackle is set to miss the rest of the 2026 season due to an ACL injury.
The domino effect from Harrison's injury could be significant for a number of members on the roster as a result. Which Jaguars are set to be most impacted by Harrison's injuty, and why? We break it down below.
This one is clear. Harrison was entering an absolutely pivotal 2026 season, not just because he was made the team's blindside protector for the first time but because of the timing of his switch to left tackle. Harrison, who had his fifth-year option picked up for next season, was set to be a potential benefactor from the move to left tackle considering what a strong season could have meant for him when it came to his contract and what the talks at the table look like.
Harrison will of course return in 2027, but he will be coming off an ACL injury and will have just a six-game sample size as an NFL left tackle entering the season. This doesn't mean Harrison can't still play himself into a big-time deal with the Jaguars moving forward, but the situation has seen a major wrench thrown into it. The Jaguars needed this season to see if Harrison was worth extending, and Harrison needed this season to prove he should be one of the NFL's highest-paid tackles. Now, neither side is going to get much clarity entering the 2027 season.
It feels unlikely that the Jaguars will play Daniel Faalele much at the tackle position since he is a more natural guard and has subsequently taken more snaps at the guard position over the course of his career. But Faalele, who the Jaguars traded for during training camp as they sustained a rash of offensive line injuries, has been a healthy scratch for the Jaguars in each game this season as they entered each contest with eight active offensive linemen. With Harrison out, Faalele now becomes OL8.
Does this mean Faalele is set to enter the Jaguars' starting lineup soon post-bye? No, not really. But he will at the very least be active and be closer to stepping onto the field than he was before. Faalele is unlikely to be needed unless the Jaguars sustain more injuries along the offensive line, but he should now at the least be an option for the Jaguars to turn to on game day, especially in jumbo packages since Wyatt Milum's role as the No. 6 lineman may now change.
This could be an interesting development for Jaguars offensive lineman Patrick Mekari, who Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said was getting closer to returning from injured reserve after missing all of training camp and the first six games of the season with a back injury. Mekari has dealt with injuries for most of his time with the Jaguars, but he could give them some very real offensive line depth when he is off injured reserve, especially in the context of the Jaguars' swing tackle spot.
Mekari has nearly 2,000 career snaps at the tackle positions since joining the NFL in 2019, giving him a significantly larger sample size at the tackle position than any of the Jaguars' other in-house options for swing tackle. Mekari has been a disappointment with the Jaguars since becoming their highest-paid free agent of the new regime in March 2025, but the loss of Harrison could give him the chance to prove his worth.
Mekari of course has to get healthy first, but once he is healthy he should give the Jaguars a boost in terms of a versatile and experienced depth option. Considering the Jaguars' top swing tackle, Walker Little, is now the team's starting left tackle, then Mekari has suddenly become much more valuable to the Jaguars than he was at the start of the season.
The Jaguars have not had a ton of need for Wyatt Milum to step into the lineup since they drafted him in the third-round of the 2025 NFL Drafft, but he now looks like he is one snap away from likely becoming the Jaguars' starting right tackle. Milum was set to be the Jaguars' top swing tackle at the start of the season if Cole Van Lanen was set to miss time at the start of the year, which of course did not end up happening. But the Jaguars are now right back into the same situation with Harrison out for the year.
Milum has played just 122 snaps on offense in his career thus far, with many of those snaps coming as an extra offensive lineman in jumbo packages. That is a good bit different than potentially lining up at offensive tackle against some of the best pass-rushers in the NFL, but that is the scenario the Jaguars have now found themselves in. Milum went from a luxury player to a critical part of the depth chart now that Harrison is sidelined for the rest of 2026.

title: 3 Most Important Takeaways on Anton Harrison's ACL Injury and What it Means for Jaguars
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have been dealt their toughest injury blow of the 2026 season.
According to reports, the Jaguars are set to be without left tackle Anton Harrison for the rest of the 2026 season after he reportedly sustained a season-ending ACL injury, and now the next natural step is simple: what's next?
So, what does the Harrison injury mean for the Jaguars moving forward, and for other members of the roster as well? We break it all down below.
Jaguars left tackle Walker Little has become a very important piece of the Jaguars' offense, and the Jaguars deserve some credit for showing restraint here. The reason I say that is because Little was an unusually highly-paid non-starting offensive lineman before the Harrison injury, and the Jaguars could have easily moved him for draft picks at any time over the last two seasons. Once the Jaguars paid Cole Van Lanen to be a long-term piece at offensive tackle, Little could have easily become an expendable piece, but the Jaguars never let that happen.
We now know why. The Jaguars were obviously content with fitting Little's price tag on the pay-roll in the event of a rainy day, and it has become time to get the umbrellas and ponchos. Little could have easily been one of the most sought after offensive tackles on the trade market in the time since the offseason began, but the Jaguars never seemed like they were going to trend in that direction. Now, we see the Jaguars set to benefit from the decision.
Not many teams may have been able to show that kind of restraint, but the Jaguars clearly made their offensive line depth a major piece of their roster-building. As a result, the Jaguars are in the rare position where they can sustain the impact of losing their blindside left tackle, something not many other teams could say.
The downside for the Jaguars and Harrison's injury was always going to be what it meant for Harrison's long-term future, especially when it comes to the left tackle spot. Harrison was entering his fourth NFL season with the chance to establish himself as the Jaguars' long-term answer at left tackle, which obviously would have made him a very, very rich man whenever it came to his contract extension down the road. Now, a wrench has been thrown into those details.
For one, the Jaguars likely still simply needed to see more from Harrison before comitting big money to him. He would have had at least another 11 games, plus any potential playoff games, at the left tackle spot to prove himself in 2026 before entering his fifth-year option season in 2027. Now, Harrison will be entering 2027 coming off an ACL injury, which very well could naturally change the entire timeline of his extension, and whether one now happens.
This is brutal timing for both Harrison and the Jaguars. Harrison will be back next year, but he had a lot riding on this season, and so did the Jaguars. Now, both parties are set to enter 2027 with a lot more questions than answers.
If this injury hurts the Jaguars anywhere, it is at the swing tackle position. That goes without saying when most teams lose a starting offensive tackle, but in most cases teams have to turn their attention to the vacated starting role. The Jaguars can feel perfectly fine about the left tackle position with Walker Little, though, which means their focus should now go to the swing tackle spot that Little occupied for the first month-plus of the season, and for at times last season. The swing tackle spot is critical considering the situation the Jaguars are now in, and there are some questions.
The most likely swing tackle as of today is second-year offensive lineman Wyatt Milum, who took reps at the tackle spot during training camp when Cole Van Lanen was missing time. Milum was a college left tackle with years of starting experience at West Virginia, but all but three of his snaps in the NFL have come either at guard or as a sixth-offensive lineman in jumbo packages. The Jaguars do also have Daniel Faalele (182 career snaps at tackle) and eventually Patrick Mekari (1,895 career snaps at tackle) as other options as well.
Perhaps the Jaguars look at external options with the trade deadline a few weeks away. But as things stand today, it feels more likely the Jaguars will have to lean on the offensive line depth chart that they have been building over the last two seasons.

title: Final Anton Harrison Injury Update Gives Jaguars a Bye Week Loss
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The bye week is not often kind to the Jacksonville Jaguars, and the trend has repeated in 2026
Bye weeks, or at least bye week-adjacent weeks, have normally brought bad news for the Jaguars over the years and this year that news comes in the form of left tackle Anton Harrison, who is now out for the season.
"Jaguars starting LT Anton Harrison was revealed to have suffered a torn ACL during his surgery yesterday, sources say," NFL Network's Ian Rapoport said on Friday. "The hope was just an arthroscopic procedure, but instead there was more damage. Harrison, who is already on Injured Reserve, is now out for the season."
The hope when Harrison was injured, of course, was that he would potentially be able to return this season if the Jaguars were able to avoid the worst-case scenario. But the worst-case scenario is now year and, for the second year in a row, a Jaguars' offensive tackle has sustained a serious knee injury after Cole Van Lanen suffered a similar injury in January in Week 17 of the 2025 season.
Van Lanen was able to attack rehab and be ready to return for the season-opener on Sept. 13 this year against the Cleveland Browns, though he has still had to work himself back into form. The timeline of Harrison's injury does suggest that he should be back by Week 1 next season as well, but that is little comfort for the Jaguars when it comes to their playoff push this season.
With Harrison out, the Jaguars only have a few real options. The most obvious and likely of those options is for the Jaguars to turn back to former left tackle Walker Little, who has started 40 games in his NFL career, with the bulk coming at left tackle. Little started for the Jaguars at left tackle last week against the Houston Texans and played well against Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, and he will now have to man the blindside spot to give the Jaguars a chance to win the AFC South and go on a deep run.
“I probably can't overstate how important it is because we really are fortunate to not have to play a backup in a situation when a tackle goes down. I don't look at Walker as a backup tackle or a backup guard," Jaguars offensive coordinator Grant Udinski said last week.
"We have seven, eight starter-caliber offensive linemen, and I know that's an incredibly rare luxury to have that type of depth at the offensive line. So, it totally changes the way you gameplan, it changes the way you attack the run game, it changes the way you attack pass protection, so to have that luxury, like I said, is really unimaginable in many other places in the NFL."
The Jaguars have the luxury of being able to sustain Harrison's injury, but that doesn't change the fact that the Jaguars just got dealt a loss during their bye week ... once again.

title: One Curious Offensive Concern the Jaguars Must Clean Up After Bye Week
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars offense is playing well ... very well. But, they could still be better.
Trevor Lawrence is playing some of the best football of his career, Bhayshul Tuten looks like an ascending star, and the Jaguars have several rookies making a big impact on the offensive side of the ball. But there is one issue that has hurt the Jaguars' offense in recent weeks: drops.
The Jaguars curiously had 5 drops recorded against the Texans in Week 6: 2 from Parker Washington, two from Brian Thomas Jr,, and one from Jakobi Meyers. This also comes a week after the Jaguars had similar issues against the Philadelphia Eagles, with Washington having an uncharacteristic drop against Philadelphia in Week 5 and Thomas also having two passes hit his hands in the end zone that he failed to complete.
Would the Jaguars have defeated the Texans if they curbed their drops? Perhaps, perhaps not. But it was a sign of the Jaguars’ self-inflicted mistakes once again holding them back from hitting their offensive potential.
Drop Yards Lost in Week 6 NE 74 JAX 68 SEA 67 GB 60 NO 40 Data: @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/3fEihsBKRr
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen was asked after the Texans' loss about the Jaguars' drops in the 34-31 loss in Week 6 , and he did not seem overly concerned based on the context of the game, from the conditions of the field with the weather and even with some of the passes.
"I couldn't tell on a few; if it was, like, the one across the middle, Jakobi [WR Jakobi Meyers] I thought it was a little lower. It was wet for sure out there early on I felt the drops. I couldn't really tell if we just didn't connect on that deep corner ball to Parker [WR Parker Washington] there towards the end. I couldn't tell if we could have made the play or not. From where I was standing, I couldn't tell. But, yeah, we got to find a way in those moments to be able to make some of those plays," Coen said Sunday.
But regardless of Coen's concern level, the Jaguars have to make this an emphais before they take the field in Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts. Drops loomed over the Jaguars at times a year ago, and they have somehow crept back up after the Jaguars seemed to rid themselves of the issue during the second-half of last season.
Washington and Meyers are normally sure-handed receivers, and the same can be said for tight end Brenton Strange, who has also had a few drops during the first six weeks. Thomas has had issues with drops dating back to last season, and the Jaguars have seemingly reached the end of their rope with him. But when the team’s best and most reliable pass-catchers are putting the ball on the ground in key moments, the Jaguars are going to find it tough to not get into one-score games week in and week out.
The margin for error is truly that small in the NFL. The Jaguars’ offense is exceptional, but it can, and should, be better. After the bye week, that will largely depend on whether the Jaguars have solved their newfound drops issue.

title: Andy Reid on Chiefs OT Josh Simmons Hitting Injured Reserve: ‘We’ll Buy a Little Time'
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs placed Josh Simmons on Injured Reserve this week due to a back injury that has hampered him since training camp. Fans were given reason for optimism when Simmons was listed as a limited participant in three practices last week, but head trainer Rick Burkholder said yesterday that he had "plateaued" in his recovery and that a new course of action was required.
Although Burkholder provided a detailed explanation of Simmons' injury and the decision to place him on IR, Chiefs reporters were still looking for answers when Andy Reid met with the media today. "We were making sure that you give him a chance to sort it out with family, agents, all that," Reid said about why it took some time for the Chiefs to conclude that Simmons hitting the IR was the right move.
"And when you're dealing with backs, that's a little different animal. That can go either way, and I thought Rick and his crew have handled it well, and so has Josh. He's been in here every day, doing his rehab."
Reid stressed that Simmons' doctors will ultimately determine the best strategy. Burkholder did clarify that a second opinion and follow-up MRI showed the bulging disc had improved, leading to a recommendation for continued rehab rather than surgery. Still, Reid acknowledged that some back injuries eventually require an operation. "Doctors are involved, so they're the ones who end up making the decision with Josh," Reid continued. "Backs are complicated, we all know that. Sometimes, time works. It might be a longer time. Sometimes, you have to have the surgery. So I think we'll buy a little time, see how things work on the rehab part."
This leaves KC in a standstill as Simmons continues his hiatus from football. The Chiefs are hoping additional rest will help him ramp back up to full health, but Reid's comments made it clear that the team has not ruled out other options if the wait-and-see game does not produce the necessary progress.
Reid's patience with the topic also appears to be wearing thin. After fielding several questions about Simmons, he grew visibly frustrated and left his press conference early, telling reporters that he wanted the focus to return to the players preparing to play. "Rick's got the plan for that. They'll stay in touch," Reid said. "I hope this isn't asked to me every week. I mean, this is like — let's put this to rest. You guys, this isn't that big of a story. Let's focus on the football team and the guys playing."
🚨THIS IS A VERY WEIRD SITUATION🚨 #Chiefs head coach Andy Reid was extremely ANGRY with reporters after being asked AGAIN about the mysterious situation surrounding former first-round pick Josh Simmons. “I hope this isn’t asked to me every week. Just put this to rest. This… pic.twitter.com/SgpWqgEA15
Simmons' recovery has now stretched across more than two months, with no real timetable for his return. Reid first acknowledged the bulging disc in late September , but prior to that, Chiefs supporters were left guessing about the entire situation.
He is eligible to return in Week 11 versus the Arizona Cardinals, though that is the earliest he can come off IR, not a confirmed target date. If rest does not solve his injury and it lingers much longer, surgery this late in the year would wipe away any chances of Simmons playing in 2026.
With right tackle Jaylon Moore in the concussion protocol , Joshua Ezeudu is expected to start at right tackle Sunday night against the Seattle Seahawks. Ezeudu arrived in Kansas City in an offseason trade with the New York Giants. Meanwhile, Kahlil Benson will continue to man the left tackle spot in Simmons' absence.

title: Chiefs Rule Out Two Offensive Starters for Sunday Night Showdown in Seattle
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs will be exceptionally thin at wide receiver and offense tackle for Sunday Night Football against the Seattle Seahawks.
On Friday, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid announced that wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring) and right tackle Jaylon Moore (concussion protocol) will both miss Sunday's primetime showdown, dealing blows to a pair of already-depleated position groups.
Wide receiver Tyquan Thornton has been on injured reserve (IR) since suffering a dislocated ankle in Week 4, which is reportedly set to sideline him until at least late-December . Meanwhile, left tackle Josh Simmons was placed on IR after weeks of rehab "plateaued" this week.
When Moore left last week's win over the Los Angeles Chargers, veteran offensive lineman Joshua Ezeudu stepped in at right tackle, and he projects to start on Sunday night. Ezeudu held his own against Los Angeles, though the Seahawks' pass rush is far more fierce . With Simmons sidelined for the foreseeable future, undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson is expected to continue as the Chiefs' left tackle.
Without Rice last week, the Chiefs relied heavily on Xavier Worthy as their top pass catcher , as Worthy took 84% of the offensive snaps and caught all seven of his targets for 73 yards. Rookie Cyrus Allen caught two passes for 27 yards, while second-year receiver Jalen Royals caught two for 24. Andrew Armstrong also recorded his first NFL catch for a 13-yard gain.
Royals was second in wide receiver snaps (45, 74%) while Armstrong was third (42, 69%).
On Friday, Reid also revealed that second-year running back Brashard Smith "hurt his hamstring" on Thursday, knocking him out for Sunday night. In Smith's absence, Reid said that rookie practice squad running back Jaydn Ott "will be the one that works into his spot."

title: ESPN Matchup Predictor Analyzes Chiefs vs. Seahawks Sunday Night Showdown
full_text:
Following a gritty 22-6 victory over the Chargers last week, the Kansas City Chiefs are set to return to the primetime stage for the first time since Week 2. They will compete in a Sunday Night Football matchup for the second time in 2026 as they head to Seattle to take on the reigning Super Bowl champions.
While Andy Reid's squad has yet to drop a game, the Seahawks have struggled to get their offense going in the post-Kenneth Walker era . Amid their two-game losing streak, quarterback Sam Darnold has tossed four interceptions, including one that ultimately gave the Broncos a free victory last week in overtime. Sportsbooks have labeled Seattle as a slight home favorite, but what does the ESPN Matchup Predictor think? Here's what their computer model projects a few days before kickoff.
This is technically the second meeting between these two teams this year, following an ugly preseason tie in August that featured mostly second and third-string players.
ESPN Matchup Predictor Chances at Victory: Chiefs 52.8%, Seahawks 46.8%.
While Seattle boasts one of the best home-field advantages in the sport, the matchup predictor still gives the undefeated Chiefs a slight edge to maintain their perfect record.
Usually, the matchup predictor closely mirrors what traditional betting lines are forecasting. However, that isn't the case for this contest.
This was undoubtedly circled as one of the more difficult challenges on the Chiefs' schedule heading into the season, and that stands true despite Seattle's early shortcomings. They have the same defensive playmakers who made them a force to be reckoned with in last year's postseason. Even with Darnold's inconsistencies through the air, Jaxon Smith-Njigba remains a premier wide receiver in the league. He leads the NFL in receptions, receiving yards, and receiving touchdowns in spite of the shaky quarterback play.
Seattle's passionate 12s will undoubtedly come out in full force, as this game means a lot more to them than it does to the Chiefs. Kansas City obviously wants to preserve its flawless record, but a loss that drops Seattle to 3-4 would likely take the Seahawks out of the division race moving forward.
Walker's homecoming to the team he spent his first four years with is a major storyline. He'll be looking to prove why Seattle should have paid him as he continues to establish himself as one of the best running backs in the NFL.
The Chiefs have had plenty of breaks go their way and won't stay undefeated forever, but the Seahawks will have a tough time overcoming turnovers from Darnold if they want to win. Unlike some of their past opponents, Patrick Mahomes will make them pay.
