title: Division Clincher, "Fail Mary" Highlight List of Best Dolphins Road Victories vs. the Jets in the 2000s
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' first road game against the New York Jets in the 2000s produced one of the wildest fourth-quarter comebacks in NFL history — or worst fourth-quarter collapses, depending on your viewpoint.
It was part of a very rough start for Miami in those away games against their AFC opponents from the New York/New Jersey area in the new millennium, though the Dolphins have evened things out at 13 wins apiece heading into their 27th matchup of the 2000s in the Northeast this Sunday at MetLife Stadium.
Here is our countdown of the Dolphins' top five of those 13 victories at Giants Stadium, Meadowlands Stadium or MetLife Stadium against the Jets in the 2000s.
We start our countdown with one of those rare games — the only one we can remember, actually — where the punter was the difference-maker. In this game under cloudy skies, the Dolphins offense was brutal to the tune of 131 total yards and two turnovers, not to mention going 3-for-15 on third downs. The defense did hold New York to 280 yards, but the difference was Brandon Fields averaging 56.4 yards with an absurd net of 49.6 yards. A big example of Fields' brilliance that day came with Miami leading 10-3 on the second play of the fourth quarter and having to punt from its 7-yard line. Fields unleashed a 69-yard punt and even after an 11-yard run, that produced a 58-yard net that had the Jets starting at their own 35.
The term "Hail Mary" had been used before to describe the fiasco produced by an apparent (or obvious) officiating mistake that changed the outcome of a Green Bay-Seattle game on a, you guessed it, Hail Mary. But it was more appropriate here because this was a bad player fail, with the culprit being future Dolphins QB Tim Boyle and the hero/beneficiary being former Dolphins safety Jevon Holland. For those who don't remember, the Dolphins were in full control leading 10-0 against the Jets heading toward halftime until a pick-six gave New York some life. Holland's touchdown off a brilliant return basically ended all suspense.
Talk about coming up big as a backup quarterback. With the Dolphins in the midst of a playoff run, Matt Moore had to start this Saturday night game after Ryan Tannehill went out the previous week with a knee injury, and he lit up the Jets for four touchdown passes. Those came after a pair of future Dolphins — QB Bryce Petty and WR Robbie Chosen — connected on a 40-yard touchdown pass to give the Jets an early 7-0. The Dolphins' other touchdown came on a blocked punt return by Walt Aikens, which we bring up because ...
Yep, more special teams fireworks, this time courtesy of Ted Ginn Jr. The Dolphins' controversial 2007 first-round pick — who absolutely was overdrafted, but still had a productive NFL career — made NFL history with not one but two kickoff returns for touchdowns in the third quarter alone. Oh, and that third quarter also featured a 48-yard fumble return for another Miami touchdown by Jason Taylor. Those big plays allowed the Dolphins to score 30 points and steal a victory despite the offense being held to a meager 104 total yards.
As the Dolphins going through this rebuilding 2026 season, it's always nice to look back on those days when the team was able to win the AFC East title. It hasn't happened in 18 years, but it was an oh-so-satisfying capper to an improbable run just one year after the Dolphins were 1-15 — and certainly a measure of hope for fans going through the pain of 2026. That seven-point win against the Jets in 2008 was highlighted by defensive end Phillip Merling's pick-six in the second quarter, but don't forget about QB Chad Pennington — maybe the most important player in the amazing turnaround after the Jets discarded him for Brett Favre and the Dolphins gladly scooped him up in August of that year — converting a massive fourth-and-1 with a run that basically clinched the victory and the division title.

title: Would the Dolphins Really Consider Trading Jordyn Brooks?
full_text:
It seems everybody, or just about everybody is fair game when it comes to the NFL trade deadline and the Miami Dolphins.
It was expected that we would see the names of Zach Sieler and Austin Jackson mentioned among trade candidates given their contract status and age, plus the obvious situation in which the franchise finds itself.
That one, we have to say, surprised us when we saw him included in a list of top 50 trade candidates put together by The Athletic.
Yet there was Brooks at number 21, between Jets edge defender Will McDonald IV and Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley.
"The Dolphins are executing their tank effectively," writer Daniel Popper began. "They have remained moderately competitive while still losing five straight games to begin the season. Their rookie class looks promising. The next step would be accruing some more draft capital for 2027. One issue, though, is they do not have many tradable players. Brooks, a reliable veteran off-ball linebacker, is one of the few. He signed a three-year extension in July and has close to $13 million in guaranteed salary in 2027, so any acquiring team would be making a multiyear commitment. The Dolphins would take on $15.6 million in dead money in 2027 if they traded Brooks. This regime, with coach Jeff Hafley and GM Jon-Eric Sullivan, has not been afraid of dead money thus far."
Brooks' name came in trade speculation in the offseason, with the Dallas Cowboys and Cincinnati Bengals mentioned as logical suitors, and Popper mentioned the Cowboys, Bills and Steelers are potential trade partners now.
But the big question here is simple: Why would the Dolphins trade Brooks only a few months after giving him a contract extension that included a $20 million signing bonus?
If they were to trade Brooks, the Dolphins would be on the hook for Brooks' bonus when it comes to the cap space on top of already having signed that check.
After the Dolphins signed Brooks to his extension after doing the same with De'Von Achane and Aaron Brewer, GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and head coach Jeff Hafley both spoke of making sure to hang on to franchise "pillars," good players who do things the way the Dolphins want them done.
Hafley also talked about showing players that the franchise will reward those who produce and do things the right way.
What kind of message would it send to sign Brooks to an extension and then trade him in the middle of a season that's gone not too far from where the organization figured it would or could go after they dumped high-profile veterans and saddled themselves with $180 million of dead space to clear the books for future years.
Sure, Sullivan has shown a willingness to take dead cap money if it accomplishes a goal, but what goal would be accomplished by dumping Brooks if the Dolphins can't get a premium pick in return.
And that's what it boils down, as always, because there's no player for whom the Dolphins shouldn't entertain an offer too good to be true.
But what could the Dolphins realistically expect to get for Brooks?
In terms of his appeal and market value, he probably was more valuable in the offseason coming off his All-Pro season than he is right now after dealing with an injury in training camp and then leaving the Week 5 game against the Cincinnati Bengals with a foot injury.
Would a third- or fourth-round pick in 2027 be more valuable to the Dolphins than having Brooks next season and the one after, both in terms of talent but also in terms of intangibles — Brooks' leadership plus keeping the player you just extended?
The bottom line is stranger things have happened, which is why we'll never say never, but a Brooks trade seemed a lot more likely then than it does now because making a deal months after giving a player an extension and giving him $20 million in signing bonus just doesn't compute.

title: Examining the Pending Dolphins UFAs Who Could Be Playing Their Way to an Extension
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins roster has a lot of new faces this year, and it figures to be the same thing next season as they continue the rebuilding project that began with the regime change.
The Dolphins have 22 players currently on their roster who are scheduled to become free agents in 2026 and the questions is how many of them will be back for another go-around.
The breakdown of free agents includes 12 UFAs free to sign with any other team barring the Dolphins using the franchise tag, which we already can tell you is highly unlikely given the financial commitment to a single player; five RFAs, who require a qualifying tender for the right to match an offer they might receive from another team; and and five ERFAs, who the Dolphins basically will keep if they want because any qualifying tender gives them exclusive rights to those players.
The 13 pending UFAs are T Austin Jackson, TE Greg Dulcich, CB JuJu Brents, P Bradley Pinion, CB Darrell Baker Jr., WR Jalen Tolbert, EDGE Joshua Uche, LB Willie Gay Jr., S Zayne Anderson, LB Ronnie Harrison Jr., EDGE Malik Herring and EDGE Robert Beal Jr.
The five pending RFAs are OL Jarrett Kingston, LB Shaka Heyward, TE Cole Turner (who's on IR), WR Jared Wayne and C Andrew Meyer.
The five pending ERFAs are LS Tucker Addington, LB Jackson Woodard, T Chukwuebuka Godrick, CB Reese Taylor and QB Kyle McCord.
As we evaluate the outlook for those players and their status with the team, we should not it's entirely possible — if not downright probable — that some of them will be gone before the end of this season.
But, for now, here are our best projections as to which players will be back in 2027, understanding that for UFAs it's a two-way street that requires both the team and the player to want to continue working together.
CB JuJu Brents — This is a player the Dolphins should prioritize because he still continues to perform at a high level and plays a premium position. The ability to stay healthy has been the issue so far in Brents' career, but he hasn't missed a game yet (knock on wood) so far in 2026.
TE Greg Dulcich — The Dolphins showed they valued him by giving him considerably more than most of their other free agents when they re-signed him in the offseason, though they did make it a one-year deal. But he's still pretty young, has good upside, and it's not like the Dolphins are swimming in high-end tight ends.
EDGE Joshua Uche — While he's been around a bit, Uche still is only 29 years old and he's been easily the second-best edge defender on the team, if not the best. The biggest question with him is whether the Dolphins will resist the temptation to move him before the trade deadline if a team offers a draft pick in a trade.
P Bradley Pinion — Yes, this might sound weird, particularly since Pinion is 33, but the fact is he's punted well all season — we can forgive him that blip when he dropped the ball proceeding to get into his punting motion — he's not expensive and punters can work in the NFL into their late 30s with no issues.
T Austin Jackson — Despite his poor Pro Football Focus standing (he's dead last among all NFL tackles), Jackson is a solid veteran tackle who's simply off to a bad start. The issue with Jackson is how it would cost to bring him back in what probably wouldn't be a starting role and whether he even would be interested in that idea after being asked to take a pay cut this year.
WR Jalen Tolbert — It's hard to imagine the veteran wide receiver wanting to come back to Miami after he found himself behind not only Malik Washington but the team's three draft picks at the position — Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr.
S Zayne Anderson — The special teams specialist got his big chance when he was in the starting lineup at safety in the opener, but he's now gone back to his previous role of working mostly in the kicking game. He's also 30 years old, which won't make him a priority to bring back.
LB Ronnie Harrison Jr. — Harrison was one of the latest free agent acquisitions in the offseason and he made the 53-man roster after a strong training camp showing. But he's been out since Week 1 because of a hamstring injury and he's also 30 years old.
The lowest qualifying tender for restricted free agents in 2026, which simply gave teams to right to match an outside offer with no compensation if declined, was $3.5 million. None of the pending RFAs signed for more than $1.1 million this year, so it's highly unlikely — if not an outright foregone conclusion — the Dolphins will not be extending any qualifying offers.
That means the Dolphins then would have to decide which to try to bring back, and we've got three we've got pegged as most likely to return.
OL Jarrett Kingston — Kingston, claimed off waivers from the Houston Texans, had a solid outing in relief of Jonah Savaiinaea in the Week 5 game against Cincinnati.
OL Andrew Meyer — The Dolphins have been developing Meyer for three years now and offensive linemen always are a valuable commodity.
TE Cole Turner — That the Dolphins placed Turner on injured reserve in training camp and didn't simply waive him injury suggests they think he's got potential worth investigating.

title: Examining the Mestemaker-to-Miami Draft Opinion Surge
full_text:
There's a lot of time until the 2026 season is over for the Miami Dolphins, but a good chunk of the fan base has already has moved on to next season's NFL Draft, which can shape the future of the franchise depending on who they select.
Any position on the team can receive an upgrade with what will likely be a very high draft pick, if not the first overall. But if the Dolphins were to pull the trigger at quarterback, t hey have a few options to choose from, but one name is standing out as of late.
And, no, it's not Arch Manning, the son of Cooper Manning and nephew to both Peyton and Eli Manning. After a pair of unsuccessful outings for him as of late, the focus has shifted to a redshirt sophomore in the Big 12 Conference.
Drew Mestemaker didn't even begin his football journey as a quarterback. He was a dual-threat option at both punter and safety in high school before making the change to QB when he walked on at North Texas. With the Mean Green, he had one of the best seasons at the position in 2025, recording 4,379 passing yards, 34 touchdowns, and nine interceptions.
When UNT head coach Eric Morris took the job at Oklahoma State ahead of 2026, Mestemaker followed suit, and he hasn't lost a beat despite the tougher competition in the Big 12. Their loss to Tulsa to begin the season has only become more confusing, since they proceeded to take down Oregon the week after, who was ranked ninth in the nation.
The Cowboys then rattled off three more wins before a tough loss on the road to 20th-ranked Houston. Through it all, Mestemaker has had an excellent season with 1,940 yards and 16 touchdowns, but six interceptions through six games, three picks away from his 2025 total, with at least six more games to go.
Regardless, the national consensus has been overwhelmingly positive on Mestemaker and believes he has what it takes to be the first QB picked in the 2027 draft. The following outlets believe the Miami Dolphins will select him with their pick, which is expected to be somewhere in the top three.
CBS (Josh Edwards) - #1 Overall
ESPN (Field Yates) - #2 Overall
SI (Gilbert Manzano) - #2 Overall
Athlon Sports (Luke Easterling) - #3 Overall
Bleacher Report (Brent Sobleski) - #3 Overall
All of these mock drafts have been done within the past seven days, with Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith ending up on either Tennessee or the Los Angeles Chargers. It's worth noting that the biggest outlet that doesn't think Miami is selecting Mestemaker is USA Today, with Michael Middlehurst-Schwartz predicting the Dolphins will select Smith with the first overall pick.
Mestemaker feels like a jack-of-all-trades quarterback, being able to achieve whatever North Texas and Oklahoma State have asked of him. He has a powerful, accurate arm that coincides with smart decision-making for someone who's only 20 years old. On top of that, he's surprisingly mobile, having rushed for 142 yards and two touchdowns this season.
As mentioned earlier, he has thrown a considerable number of interceptions. It feels like the bad decisions he makes come from trying to do too much, spearheaded by the Cowboys' defense, which gives up 358.2 yards and 23.7 points per game, both on the lower end of the Big 12.
The other big knock on Mestemaker is that there isn't much film to go off of. He didn't play QB at all in high school and has clocked one and a half seasons at the position in college. Granted, what we've been able to witness is a lot of good, but the experience isn't quite there.
With that said, any team that drafts Mestemaker might be better off sitting him for a season, learning from NFL quarterbacks about what to do and what not to do. Look towards Fernando Mendoza, learning from Kirk Cousins and taking the occasional snap during blowouts. Yes, if he's drafted by Miami, that likely means one more season of Malik Willis.
In reality, Mestemaker having a quality season isn't the only reason he's emerged as a top QB in the draft. The other big reason is how Arch Manning has regressed in his senior season. Both he and Texas looked promising, with a 24-23 win over Ohio State, taking the top spot in the nation from the Buckeyes.
After losing to Oklahoma in the Red River Rivalry, then to Florida at home the week after, Texas is currently 19th in the nation. Manning has had a pedestrian season with 1,295 yards, 11 touchdowns, and five interceptions. Granted, he's faced extreme, maybe unfair expectations because of his last name, but this isn't the best time to have a mediocre season with the draft around the corner.
The falloff of Manning has painted a picture of how volatile the position is at college. The outlook on a draft hopeful at any position can drastically change with one bad performance, especially at quarterback. Right now, Mestemaker is the front-runner, but there's no guarantee he'll stay that way after a few weeks, at the end of the regular season, or when a champion is crowned in the CFP.
In the event he isn't, there are a handful of other quarterbacks who could make their case to be a top pick. That includes Miami's Darien Mensah, a Heisman front-runner who's led the top-ranked Hurricanes to an undefeated season up to this point, but he's coming off his worst performance against Florida State. The Canes will hope that this is a one-time occurrence before their premier matchup against Notre Dame on November 7.
Not far behind Mensah is Trinidad Chambliss, who began his college career at Division II Ferris State before leading the Rebels all the way to the Fiesta Bowl last season. Unlike Mestemaker, Chambliss has film for days as a sixth-year senior, but there might be too much, as he's already 24 years old. Only four quarterbacks aged 24 or older have ever been drafted in the first round: Phil Simms, Jim Druckenmiller, Brandon Weeden, and Bo Nix.
One final first-round hopeful (Assuming that Manning continues to struggle) is C.J. Carr. Notre Dame's QB is as smart on the field as he is in the classroom, but he only has 17 starts to his name in college. He'll need a quality performance against a top-rated opponent to become a true top candidate, which could come against the aforementioned Hurricanes in early November.

title: Why the Dolphins Should Keep an Eye on Their Former Head Coaches
full_text:
It's starting to look like it could be only a matter of time before former Miami Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel becomes former Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator, and it's a situation the team he led for four seasons (and their fans) should monitor.
McDaniel's offense turned in yet another poor performance during a Week 6 loss at Kansas City that dropped the Chargers to 0-6 on the season, leaving them as one of only two teams this season without a win.
The other, of course, is the Dolphins, who will take an 0-5 record into MetLife Stadium coming off their bye next Sunday.
The Chargers scored a season-low six points against the Chiefs on Sunday, the fifth time in six games they failed to score more than 17 and it doesn't take long watching them to see how disjointed and dysfunctional the whole offensive operation looks, from a badly regressing Justin Herbert at quarterback to an offensive line that's again among the worst in the NFL and dealing again with injuries to their quality starting tackles, Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt.
Things haven't improved one bit since a shocking loss against Arizona in the opener and it might be that Jim Harbaugh will have no choice but to fire McDaniel to, if nothing else, inject some life into an offense that has shown little while the defense keeps battling.
Harbaugh's comments after the loss at Kansas City and heading into the Chargers' bye didn't sound great for McDaniel when he said he would have to evaluate things when asked whether McDaniel would continue calling plays.
And, of course, where it gets fun for Dolphins fans is that the logical replacement for McDaniel based on play-calling experience is the man who preceded McDaniel's predecessor, Adam Gase.
Gase had been out of the NFL since he was fired by the New York Jets after the 2020 season when the Chargers hired him as a pass game specialist, and the question is what kind of changes he might make to the offensive scheme if he were to take over.
This is important because McDaniel's complex scheme clearly isn't a fit with Herbert and the rest of the offense with its complicated verbiage, shifts and motions, and timing-based offense. That scheme worked for a while in Miami, and it's fair to ask how much of that was the presence and skill set of Tua Tagovailoa at quarterback and how much was prime Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle overwhelming defenses with their speed.
The reality is that if the Chargers don't make a change, it's difficult to envision them winning many games navigating a schedule that's about as tough as that of the Dolphins.
It does seem at the moment as though a major revamping is needed for the Chargers to have offensive success and win some games.
As it stands Monday morning, the Chargers hold the first position in the 2027 draft order and it could be that it comes down to them or the Dolphins for that No. 1 spot.
And it very well might be that the status quo would benefit the Dolphins in this instance, and that status quo is the Chargers keeping McDaniel.
Meanwhile, McDaniel's three coordinators from last season all are enjoying some team success this season.
Former offensive coordinator Frank Smith now is an assistant head coach with the Minnesota Vikings, who at 5-0 stand as one of the three undefeated teams in the NFL — though it should be pointed out that team's success has a lot more to do with the defense coordinator by Brian Flores.
Former defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver is handling the same role with the Baltimore Ravens, who are in a three-way tie atop the AFC North, although the team just squandered a 13-3 fourth-quarter lead in a last-second loss against divisional foe Cleveland on Sunday.
Lastly, special teams coordinator Danny Crossman now works for the team tied for first at 4-2 in the AFC North, the Pittsburgh Steelers.

title: 10 Stats That Help Explain the Dolphins' Tough Start (And What Can Be Done About Them)
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins sat out the Week 6 action of the 2026 NFL regular season before getting back to work Monday looking to bounce back after an 0-5 start.
While stats often can be deceiving stats, we've come up with 10 numbers that help explain the winless start along with some analysis as to how to move those numbers in the right direction.
29.5 — That's the gap in completion percentage for Malik Willis from his 2025 season with the Green Bay Packers (85.7) and his first five games with the Dolphins (56.2)
Nobody should expect a full-time quarterback to come close to an 85 percent completion rate, but 56 percent isn't good enough and Willis can help himself by simply being willing to accept and take the safe, short completions.
10.1 — That's Willis intended air yards per pass attempt, according to Pro Football Reference. That figure leads the NFL, with Lamar Jackson second at 9.8.
This goes right to our first point. The Dolphins maybe need to stop taking shots down the field with a less-than-stellar wide receiver group.
3.2 — That's the average yards of separation for Malik Washington, which is the highest figure of any Dolphins player. That figure is tied for 35th-best in the NFL. The next-best Dolphins player in that category is tight end Greg Dulcich at 2.6, all the way down to tied for 79th in the NFL.
And this number illustrates, only in part, the issues with the wide receiver group.
3:09 — That's the Dolphins' rushing average on first-and-10 rushing attempts, tied with the Philadelphia Eagles for second-worst in the NFL, with only the Green Bay Packers doing worse.
Ollie Gordon II is coming off two productive games in relief of De'Von Achane, so maybe this number will improve organically after the bye without having to make any kind of schematic adjustments.
3:09 — That's Ollie Gordon II's NextGen Stats efficiency number, which measures the yards ran per yard gained, with the lower the number the most North-South the runner is. Gordon's figure is second-best in the NFL behind only the 3.01 of the Chicago Bears' Kyle Monangai.
This is what we're talking about with Gordon ... maybe the Dolphins need to give him more first-down carries.
76.0 — That's the completion percentage allowed by the Dolphins, which is on track to set a dubious NFL record. The record currently belongs to the 2016 Detroit Lions at 72.7 percent, according to StatMuse.
We get that part of Jeff Hafley's defensive scheme involves a willingness to give up short completions, but at some point the coverage needs to tighten up, particularly if the pass rush doesn't start getting to the quarterback.
4 — That's the number of sacks for the Dolphins through five games, their lowest total at this stage since at least 1981. They had five sacks in the first five games of 2019.
And that brings us to this, though it's never all about sack numbers but also affecting the quarterback. And the Dolphins have come up short on both ends. This might require more blitzing, which will leave the secondary more vulnerable to big plays, but getting nickel-and-dimed to death as they were against Cincinnati last week might not be much better.
41.27 — That's the Dolphins offense's third-down conversion rate, 12th-best in the NFL through Week 5. The only time since 2010 the Dolphins have finished a season with a higher conversion rate was in 2023 (the 11-6 season) when they were at 42.08.
Imagine how much better it could be if the Dolphins did better with their first-and-10 rushes. This also is one positive for Willis in the midst of all the criticism (some of it warranted) thrown in his direction.
34.1 — That's the kickoff return average allowed by the Dolphins, which puts Miami dead last in the NFL. It's on pace for the Dolphins' worst showing since 2023 when they finished 32nd by allowing 30.5 yards per kickoff return.
The Dolphins have used 53 different players on special teams, and the only way this gets better is continuing to churn the roster to find answers because we're thinking (at this point) it's not a schematic issue.
0 — That's the number of leads the Dolphins have held this season, one short of the NFL record of six games to start a season without a lead, a mark that belongs to the 2005 Houston Texans.
And we close with maybe the most painful stat of all, and will repeat our suggestion from last week that the Dolphins should elect to receive if they win the coin toss. Yes, it's usually preferable to defer to be able to potentially get the back-to-back possessions, but desperate times call for desperate measures. And there are times when playing with a lead or a deficit changes game strategy. And it would be nice for the Dolphins not to be chasing the game all the time, like they did against Cincinnati when they won the toss, deferred, gave up an 81-yard kickoff return and were down 7-0 before a minute of game action had expired.

title: Vikings Week 7: Potential Trade Targets Among Most Important Things to Watch for vs. Colts
full_text:
Fans will once again fill the stands at U.S. Bank Stadium on Sunday as the Vikings return from a much-needed bye week break to host a Colts team desperate to turn their season around .
While everything suggests this should be a straightforward matchup for Minnesota, longtime fans know they can never write off an opponent . Let’s break down three key things to watch as the Vikings look to achieve their first 6-0 start since 2009.
The NFL trade deadline is rapidly approaching, and the Vikings are possible buyers. The Colts, meanwhile, fired their general manager six weeks into the season, signaling that anything short of a rapid change of fortune on the field could lead to a fire sale .
The Colts have several players who could be targets for a contender like the Vikings. Names floated over blogs, podcasts and social media include defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, left guard Quenton Nelson and even a possible reunion with former Vikings safety Cam Bynum.
The hottest name, though, is three-time Pro Bowl running back Jonathan Taylor.
While Minnesota may have no interest in acquiring any of the players listed, Sunday’s game gives general manager Nolan Teasley a chance to evaluate whether he wants to take a swing or two. If Teasley likes what he sees, a decisive Vikings win may be the nudge the Colts need to start answering phone calls.
Minnesota’s offense finally showed some life before the bye week, and the return of some familiar faces may take it to the next level. Thursday’s injury report listed every player on the 53-man roster as a full participant, providing a massive sigh of relief for Vikings fans everywhere (h/t: Vikings).
Barring setbacks, the team should see the return of Christian Darrisaw, Jordan Addison, Jordan Mason, and T.J. Hockenson.
Thursday's #Vikings injury report pic.twitter.com/EVmLOt2D49
While Minnesota is still dealing with the season-long losses of Donovan Jackson and Josh Oliver, Sunday will be the closest the offense has been to “full strength” since Week 1. The opportunity for the offense to gel against a spotty defense could not come at a better time as they prepare to face a gauntlet of top-end teams over November.
If the offense looks sluggish with a full slate of weapons, it may be time to worry about how sustainable that side of the ball could be.
Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier. Magic Johnson and Larry Bird. Tom Brady and Peyton Manning. These are just some of the greatest matchups in sports history, and Sunday’s Colts-Vikings game will feature the next great battle of titans, as kickers Spencer Shrader and Will Reichard battle for supremacy.
In all seriousness, this game could very likely turn into a special teams shootout. Shrader and Reichard are both at the top of their craft, with Shrader’s 66 points scored through six games currently leading the NFL. His 11 points per game put him just above Reichard’s average of 10.6 over five games played (h/t: NFL Films ).
Don't mess with Will the Thrill 😮‍💨 @Vikings | @InsideTheNFL pic.twitter.com/n1CmRxSRje
Reichard’s 34-made-field-goal streak dating back to last season puts him just two kicks away from breaking Gary Anderson’s franchise record of 35. Hall of Fame kicker Adam Vinatieri holds the NFL record with 44.

title: Vikings Have No Excuse to Keep Sidelining Forgotten Rookie Amid Safety Concerns
full_text:
The Vikings have a real problem at safety . Veterans Harrison Smith and Josh Metellus are ranked among the ten worst safeties in the NFL this season, ranking dead last and sixth-worst, respectively, on Pro Football Focus . Despite the success of defensive coordinator Brian Flores's unit, a change is needed.
That said, the answer to Minnesota's safety issues might already be on the team's roster—a 2026 NFL Draft pick has yet to make an impact this season.
The Vikings selected Jakobe Thomas with the 98th overall pick in April, yet he hasn't played a single snap this season. The 6'1", 211-lb defensive back was inactive for each of Minnesota's five games before the bye, which doesn't bode well for his chances against the Colts in Week 7 .
Thomas played in one preseason game after working hard to recover from a back injury sustained during training camp. In that exhibition game against the Broncos, he had five tackles, three of which were solo efforts. His 79.4 tackling grade ranked second-best among Vikings defenders that game, according to PFF , while his 66.0 run defense grade was seventh-best.
Now that he's healthy and the safety room needs all the help it can get, Thomas needs to be active on game day.
Even if he only gets started on special teams, getting the former Miami (FL) and Tennessee defensive back some on-field experience could go a long way in preparing him for the future.
On Friday, Andrew Krammer of the Minnesota Star Tribune shared an article about Thomas that included a quote from Vikings special teams coordinator Matt Daniels. Apparently, the rookie safety has been asking when he will finally get on the field in a regular-season game.
The 23-year-old safety is chomping at the bit to get some reps this season. Considering how Smith and Metellus have struggled this season , it is imperative that the Vikings find a way to take pressure off Theo Jackson.
Jackson has played 191 defensive snaps for Minnesota this season and has the highest PFF grade among Vikings safeties this year, at 63.7. That's still not great, since it ranks him 41st out of 98 qualifying safeties across the NFL.
It is time to see Thomas finally play some snaps for the Vikings, and that should start in Week 7. He needs to be active on game day to prepare for a future where he steps into a defensive role for the Purple and Gold and helps keep Flores's defense among the NFL's most feared units.

title: Jordan Mason's Return Brings Much-Needed Changes to Vikings' RB Room in Week 7
full_text:
After spending the last four weeks on injured reserve with a thumb issue, Vikings running back Jordan Mason is now healthy and ready to suit up against the Colts on Sunday.
Mason enters the game with a questionable injury designation (h/t Vikings), but that's mostly just semantics, as he still technically needs to be activated off of injured reserve. So, assuming he kept his thumb wrestling to a minimum over the last month, Mason should have essentially no restrictions for Sunday.
With Aaron Jones still battling through a sprained MCL , how should the Vikings handle their freshly reformed backfield and the potential changes Mason's return could bring?
During Week 1—and the only game so far this season that the duo has played together—the Jones-Mason tandem notched a near 50/50 split, with Mason getting 15 carries to Jones's 12. That's been the plan along for Minnesota, and something similar could be in store for Sunday, but how well conditioned Mason is after the break, and how well Jones's knee is holding up could boost or drag these numbers in either direction.
Presumably, though, the answer to both of those questions is: good enough.
That means it's doubtful Mason gets put on a snap count, and equally doubtful that the Vikings completely put Jones on ice either despite running him ragged the past month. Mason averaged a pedestrian 3.9 yards per carry against Green Bay in the season opener, but the Colts' run defense ranks a hum-drum 22nd in the NFL this year, so he may find some more opportunity to get back on track after a month away.
And without reliable production coming from either DeeJay Dallas or Demond Claiborne, both starters should once again see double-digit touches. Look for Mason to get work on early downs, while Jones takes on more of a third-down back role, thanks in part to his pass-catching ability.
Speaking of Dallas and Claiborne, the return of Mason now means that the Vikings are rostering four running backs. That doesn't feel like something general manager Nolan Teasley wants to last, especially since the Vikings may look to bolster their depth elsewhere with the NFL trade deadline approaching on Tuesday, Nov. 10 .
With a possible deal to bring in more talent along the offensive line, secondary or even at running back, one of these reserves could be getting the boot.
Dallas has some special teams appeal, so rookie sixth-round pick Claiborne could be the one on the outside looking in sooner rather than later. He's logged just six carries for 13 yards on the season, and it likely wouldn't be too difficult to pass a late-round pick with no production down through waivers to the practice squad. It'll be something to monitor moving forward.
How the backs fare against Indianapolis will likely determine some of those plans, and if Mason looks sluggish, or Jones's condition deteriorates, anything could be on the table over the course of the next three weeks.

title: 5 Pending Vikings Free Agents Already Deserve Contract Extensions
full_text:
The Vikings are surprising everyone with their hot start to the season. The team's 5-0 record has fans dreaming about an NFC North title and a deep playoff run, which makes the future look bright for the Purple and Gold.
Several key contributors on the Vikings' roster have contracts expiring at the end of the 2026 NFL season. Those players will need an extension to stay in Minnesota; otherwise, they will seek a role with another franchise.
There are five players for Minnesota who will become unrestricted free agents if they aren't re-signed. The problem is that the Vikings are estimated to have approximately $37.5 million in salary cap space , according to Spotrac , but still need to re-sign players and add talent to replace any players who are lost.
The offseason is a ways away, but here's a look at the players who have earned contract extensions to stay with the Vikings past the 2026 NFL season.
Pairing Andrew Van Ginkel with Dallas Turner as the Vikings' edge rushers has been a recipe for success this year. To stay with Minnesota, Van Ginkel signed a one-year, $23 million deal and has rewarded the Purple and Gold by racking up 14 combined tackles, eight quarterback hits, four sacks, a forced fumble, and an interception in five games.
The 31-year-old edge rusher has played 249 defensive snaps this season and has a Pro Football Focus grade of 74 . His 78.4 pass-rush grade is highlighted by 18 pressures that have kept opposing quarterbacks on their toes.
T.J. Hockenson will be 30 years old next season, but he has been one of the few players to step up offensively this season for the Vikings. In five games, he has caught 23 of 27 targets for 202 yards and a touchdown, earning a 77.5 PFF grade that ranks him fifth among all qualifying tight ends.
Hockenson is playing the 2026 season on a one-year deal worth $10.25 million, and the two-time Pro Bowl pass-catcher will likely get a similar deal at the conclusion of this season. He hasn't dropped a single pass and has accumulated 80 yards after the catch so far this season, so he shows no signs of slowing down.
The combination of Eric Wilson and Blake Cashman as Minnesota's interior linebackers has been stout. Cashman is in the final year of his three-year, $22.5 million contract, and the 30-year-old Minnesota native will likely be one of the team's top priorities to re-sign this offseason.
Cashman has played 281 defensive snaps this year on his way to a 73 PFF grade. His solid grade was earned by being a statistical monster this season. He leads the team with 42 combined tackles while having seven hits on opposing quarterbacks, four tackles for a loss, 2.5 sacks, a pass defense and a fumble recovery.
Minnesota trusted Isaiah Rodgers to be a breakout player when the team signed him as a free agent, and he has delivered. He is likely going to get a significant raise from the two-year, $11.045 million contract he signed, based on his playing over 90% of the defensive snaps.
This season, Rodgers has played in all five games so far, getting 15 combined tackles, four pass defenses, an interception, and a fumble recovery. His stellar 87.9 PFF grade shouldn't be a surprise to any fan who has watched him play this season.
The Vikings are probably moving on from Aaron Jones Sr. at running back after this season, which makes bringing Jordan Mason back even more important. Minnesota's RB2 has missed time recovering from surgery on an injured thumb.
Mason hasn't played enough snaps to qualify for a PFF grade this season, but he had 15 carries for 59 yards and a touchdown in Week 1 against the Packers. The 27-year-old rusher will get a raise from his previous two-year, $10.5 million contract when general manager Nolan Teasley re-signs him during the offseason.

title: 3 Vikings Lineup Decisions I'd Make If I Were Kevin O'Connell vs. the Colts in Week 7
full_text:
The bye week provided a perfect opportunity for the Vikings to get healthy and regroup.
Now, in Week 7, the Vikings have plenty of things to figure out ahead of the upcoming NFL trade deadline , and this matchup against the Colts may be the ideal platform to determine the best path forward .
So with a 6-0 start and potential future deals on the line, here are three changes I would make if I were in head coach Kevin O'Connell's shoes against the Colts this weekend.
Jordan Mason has logged multiple full practices this week, and looks like a full go for Sunday after spending the last four weeks on injured reserve with a fractured thumb. With the recent news that Aaron Jones's banged-up knee is actually a sprained MCL , there's really no reason not to lean on Mason heavily against Indianapolis.
Giving Mason a good look on Sunday is more than just letting Jones get a breather; it's also a chance to see if the Vikings duo can perform well enough to hold off on a trade deadline deal . If Mason returns with some energy, Minnesota potentially strides past the Nov. 10 deadline without adding another back.
Either way, getting Mason involved again will be a huge boost to the work-in-progress offense.
Beckham has been coming along just fine since joining the Vikings two weeks ago, according to O'Connell, but he should take another back seat in Week 7 for one very good reason.
Despite the temptation to see what Beckham can do, the Vikings still need to find out whether Jauan Jennings will be part of this team going forward. Trying to work Beckham in while also implementing some looks for Jennings is just too convoluted.
Ideally, Jennings shows some juice and leaves Beckham as some valuable veteran insurance down the road. But if the disappointing free agent drops another dud, the Vikings may look to fire up the trade machine .
Beckham, meanwhile, has no trade value, and the Vikings shouldn't be in a rush to put him on the field. He can sit and learn the playbook for another week while O'Connell and general manager Nolan Teasley figure out Jennings' situation.
The second-rounder has played just seven defensive snaps this season, but after some strong special teams play, it might be time to give rookie linebacker Jake Golday some run on defense.
Golday forced a fumble on a kickoff return against the Saints, and may parlay that into a bigger role. Typically, Ivan Pace Jr. has been the first linebacker off the bench, but after logging just five and then two snaps over the last two contests, he may be falling out of favor. Enter Golday, who has seen action at both edge and off-ball linebacker and should now be in line for possibly double-digit snaps on defense.
The Vikings' rookie class hasn't been incredibly impactful in 2026 , but maybe Golday can change that trend, starting this week against the Colts.

title: Analyzing What a Jonathan Taylor Trade Could Look Like for the Vikings
full_text:
The Nov. 10  NFL trade deadline is fast approaching, and Vikings general manager Nolan Teasley will face some incredibly difficult decisions. With minimal input on the current roster after being hired in June, the coming weeks will be his first chance to shape the organization's present and future. While there are a few paths to choose from, one potential home run swing has become a dream scenario for many Vikings fans.
Colts running back Jonathan Taylor has quickly become a name to watch as a possible trade candidate after the firing of general manager Chris Ballard signaled a possible fire sale in Indianapolis. Luckily for Teasley and the Vikings, they’ll get a close look when Taylor and the Colts come to town this weekend.
But could the Vikings even pull off a move this big? Heck, is there even a need for it? Let’s break down what a deal could look like and if it’s worth pursuing.
Taylor is fresh off signing a two-year, $44 million extension in August that carried him through the 2028 season. Now, the Colts must decide on their long-term future.
As it stands, trading Taylor before June 1 would hit the Colts with over $7.5 million in dead money in 2026 , per Spotrac . That dead money rises to $10 million in 2027 before dropping to $5 million in 2028. Simply put, trading Taylor wouldn’t remove him entirely from Indy’s books, but it would free up over $8.6 million in cap space this season that the Colts wouldn't have.
Now, Minnesota’s side of the equation comes into play.
According to Spotrac , the Vikings have $4.1 million in cap space available for 2026 , far less than Taylor's current cap hit of approximately $16.19 million before any offsets. Teasley and executive vice president Rob Brzezinski would need to find creative ways to create more cap space through restructures, extensions, or trading away other players. Their projected $37.5 million in cap space for 2027 will likely increase once the NFL announces the final cap number for the year, but several impending roster holes will make things tricky.
Let’s say the financials can be worked out—now it’s time to talk trade compensation.
Acquiring a player of Taylor’s pedigree will not come cheap, and other suitors will likely only drive the price up further. Minnesota will likely need to offer its 2027 second-round pick to close the deal. There are clearly numerous hoops to jump through for any of this to work, but the question is: is it worth it?
With Aaron Jones off to the best start of his career and Jordan Mason returning from injury, a running back acquisition does not exactly seem like a top priority. But with Jones and Mason both in the final years of their current deals, finding a talented long-term upgrade now could prove to be the best decision. The announcement that Jones has been playing through a sprained MCL adds even more urgency to find stability at the position.
With Teasley fresh off a Super Bowl win in Seattle led by Kenneth Walker, I have a hard time thinking he doesn't at least make a call or two about Taylor. The ultimate decision will come down to his assessment of the 2026 Vikings. If he believes this roster can truly win it all, he may take the swing and go all in.
If his priorities are long-term roster construction, Teasley will likely retain his draft picks and see where the current roster can go.

title: Demond Claiborne's Vikings Future Could Be Crystal Clear After Week 7
full_text:
There's no sugarcoating it: Vikings rookie running back Demond Claiborne has been a huge letdown early in the 2026 NFL season . The preseason hype built around his excellent training camp, where he showed great speed and athleticism, has not translated into regular-season success.
Claiborne played in four of the Vikings' first five games, but the rookie running back has only six rushing attempts for 13 yards and two catches for eight receiving yards. He has played 18 offensive snaps for the Purple and Gold this season despite Jordan Mason being on injured reserve and Aaron Jones Sr. playing through a knee injury , further hammering home that the Vikings don't trust the first-year runner.
If head coach Kevin O'Connell trusted Minnesota's sixth-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft more, he would receive more opportunities. Instead, the 23-year-old rookie is finding himself on the sidelines instead of on the field, and it might not be much longer before his future with the Vikings becomes crystal clear.
After sitting out Week 1 against the Green Bay Packers, Claiborne has struggled to get playing time. He hasn't played double-digit snaps in a game yet, but came close in Week 4 against the Miami Dolphins when he played nine snaps.
Demond Claiborne offensive snaps
That said, Mason—who had 15 carries in Week 1—is expected to return from injured reserve now that his thumb has healed, which means Claiborne could be used even less moving forward. Even then, the rookie will still be splitting RB3 work with DeeJay Dallas, making those opportunities even more scarce.
Dallas's seven years of experience have led to him having a bigger offensive role than Claiborne this season. He also knows general manager Nolan Teasley from their days in Seattle. The veteran running back has played 40 offensive snaps this year, carrying the ball three times for 10 yards and catching four passes for 34 yards.
At this point, it seems unnecessary to keep Claiborne on the 53-man roster for any reason other than the fear of another team claiming him off waivers or signing him off the practice squad. It might be too early for Minnesota to give up on him or risk losing him, so it is understandable not to gamble with his future.
The most logical move for the Vikings moving forward might be to keep Claiborne inactive on game day until there is a role for him on offense. Keeping him dressed and active when he isn't contributing as a running back and has played only four special teams snaps doesn't make sense.
Keep a close eye on Claiborne's role in Week 7 against the Indianapolis Colts . If he doesn't get involved on the field or blows any limited chances he gets, expect the Vikings to change how they'll handle the rookie's development moving forward.

title: Vikings' Biggest Need Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline Is Painfully Obvious
full_text:
The undefeated Vikings need to decide how aggressive they will be before the 2026 NFL trade deadline , which takes place on Tuesday, Nov. 10. If the Purple and Gold feel they are truly contenders, general manager Nolan Teasley should do what he can to strengthen the roster and prepare for a potential playoff run.
The Vikings have been fortunate to lean on defensive coordinator Brian Flores's unit and the strong leg of kicker Will Reichard through the first five games of the season, but teams will soon start exploiting any weaknesses Minnesota's roster could have.
Much of the trade talk around the Purple and Gold involves offensive players ,  as Vikings fans want to see the team trade for a weapon to help put points on the board. That said, the team's biggest weakness is actually a defensive position that desperately needs more depth.
The strong play of other defenders, particularly close to the line of scrimmage, has hidden the Vikings' struggles at safety fairly well. At one time, the combination of Harrison Smith and Josh Metellus was enough to carry the position, but that duo has struggled to be effective this year .
Smith is 37 years old and in his ninth season as a pro. For the first time in his career, he is playing less than half of Minnesota's defensive snaps. Even in his limited role, he has been the worst safety in the league , earning a 31.5 Pro Football Focus grade—dead last among 98 qualified players.
Metellus isn't much better than Smith when it comes to PFF . The 28-year-old defensive back's 40.2 grade ranks him 93rd while allowing a 145.8 passer rating to opposing quarterbacks.
Even Theo Jackson (63.7 PFF grade) and Jay Ward (59.9 PFF grade) have been just okay. However, Ward has only played two defensive snaps, while Jackson has been attempting to pick up the slack with 191 defensive snaps.
The Vikings have rookies Jacob Thomas and Jakobe Thomas on the roster to insert into the lineup when they are ready, but Minnesota needs to do something to get better play at the safety position this year.
Don't be surprised if the Purple and Gold explore trade options before the Nov. 10 deadline. To keep the defense strong for the rest of the season, adding an experienced safety to Flores's aggressive unit would prove that the Vikings are serious about being contenders this season.

title: Surprise Aaron Jones Injury Update Gives Vikings Even More Reason to Bolster RB Depth
full_text:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline was always going to be an interesting time for the Vikings, but things are already changing with some recent running back news.
On Thursday, ESPN 's Kevin Seifert reported that Vikings running back Aaron Jones Sr. has actually been playing with a sprained MCL . Despite suffering the injury in Week 2 against the Bears, Jones has carried the ball 90% of the time since Jordan Mason went down after the season opener.
I spoke with Aaron Jones about the career-high burden he has carried in 2026, at age 31 and with a sprained MCL. It was a lot. "They can measure your weight. They can't measure your heart." On the Vikings' "warrior" as they return to a backfield rotation: https://t.co/DCn9ZIW1xB
While Jones's toughness was never questioned, the string of various running back signings and cuts over the last few weeks was clearly some attempt at insurance for their RB1.
With Mason now expected to return , Jones should get some much needed rest as the duo once again splits the workload, but his injury does add some fuel to the fire of a potential trade for another rusher.
Clearly, Jones was able to carry the entire burden of the Vikings' rushing attack over the last few weeks, racking up 410 yards on the season, but could Minnesota look to make a splash in their backfield at the deadline ?
Jones is nearing 32 years old and is essentially playing hurt the rest of the way, while Mason is fresh off an injury himself that cost him four weeks. Looking beyond 2026, neither back is under contract for next year, so the Vikings could look to add both a short- and long-term solution with one swing of the bat.
Rookie Demond Claiborne clearly isn't ready for that role , and may never be, so Minnesota may do something drastic to take advantage of their hot start and dirt-cheap quarterback.
Big names like Saquon Barkley or Jonathan Taylor have been thrown around as possible fits, but those aren't perfect options either. Barkley has been banged up himself this year and will turn 30 in February. It's just hard to be a top producer at running back at that age, and even Dalvin Cook was just 27 when the Vikings decided to move on.
Meanwhile, Taylor is two years younger, but also already has over 1,600 carries on his legs, 400 more than Cook did at this age. Obviously both Taylor and Barkley at this point would be upgrades over the current Minnesota stable, but the cost will determine if the Vikings bite.
If Mason returns with some juice and Jones can manage his injury, the Vikings may opt for a deal for a committee-type back or stand pat altogether. Conversely, there's no question that if either Jones or Mason goes down again, this team may struggle in the playoffs.
So do the Vikings get ahead of those issues now with a trade, or let things unfold how they may?
How the backfield performs against the Colts will be the first step in determining a plan. If the run game is effective over the next week or two, it'll be hard to see general manager Nolan Teasley pulling the trigger on a big-name RB using valuable picks. That doesn't rule out some more palatable options like Kenny Gainwell or James Conner.
At the same time, the Vikings can't roll into the playoffs hoping Claiborne or DeeJay Dallas can move the needle if either starter has to miss time. It'll be interesting to see Teasley & Co.'s next RB-related move, to say the least.

title: 3 Bold Vikings Predictions as Kyle Murray & Co. Host the Colts in Week 7
full_text:
The Vikings will host a game at U.S. Bank Stadium on Sunday for just the third time this season as they welcome the 2-4 Colts to the Twin Cities in Week 7 . Minnesota looks to remain undefeated coming off an early Week 6 bye, while Indy will be scratching to salvage a start that has already led to the firing of general manager Chris Ballard .
Needless to say, these are two teams currently heading in completely different directions.
With a beast of a November schedule looming, here are my predictions for a Vikings team looking to put together a dominating performance.
While the early bye provided desperately needed injury relief for the Vikings, there are fair concerns that the break may have disrupted the progress Kyler Murray and the passing game were starting to make.
Murray’s performance in New Orleans was especially promising, mainly due to the fact that the offense entered the game without wideout Jordan Addison and left tackle Christian Darrisaw, and then lost tight end T.J. Hockenson to a concussion early. With all three looking to return this weekend, I see Murray having his best day yet in purple.
Indy’s 351.2 yards allowed per game rank ninth in the league, and Murray’s abilities through the air and on the ground make him especially hard to stop (h/t: Ian Hartitz).
Next-Gen Stats fastest ball carrier speed in Week 5: Kyler Murray (20.82 MPH) Also the fastest ball carrier speed by a QB this season. pic.twitter.com/GSZ61DBqzc
After totaling 280 total yards against the Saints (229 passing, 51 rushing), I predict Murray will finish with over 300 total yards on Sunday.
The Vikings’ season started with a bang, scoring 39 points in the season opener against the Packers. Since then, they have not scored more than 23 points in a game.
Sunday is the perfect opportunity for that to change.
The Colts have given up 27.3 points per game so far this season, the sixth-highest average in the league. Minnesota, meanwhile, is looking for its first truly dominant offensive showing as it prepares for the hardest stretch of its schedule.
The returns of Hockenson and Addison should open up passing options, and Jordan Mason’s possible return to the backfield could elevate a run game that Aaron Jones has carried almost entirely on his own so far. The Vikings’ offense needs to prove it can score consistently before facing some of the league's toughest opponents, and the Colts’ shaky defense may give them plenty of opportunities.
Franchise legend Harrison Smith has had a relatively quiet start to his 15th NFL season .
Smith announced his return a week before the Vikings kicked off their 2026 campaign and has mostly been a rotational piece in defensive coordinator Brian Flores’s ever-evolving defense. Even though “The Hitman” is clearly past his prime, he’s still one of the smartest defenders in the game, and I expect that to pay off this weekend.
Smith recently confirmed to Richard Sherman that this will be his last season , so there is no better time to snag his 40th interception than now (h/t: "Richard Sherman Podcast").

Colts quarterback Daniel Jones has thrown six interceptions this season, tied for the third-most in the league , and anyone who's watched him through his career knows he’ll eventually throw a duck or two (h/t: NFL).
Smith’s football IQ and Jones’s occasional recklessness may just be the perfect combination to get the NFL’s active interception leader his next pick.

title: An Oral History Of Patriots WR Kyle Dixon's 'Twisted' Collegiate Baseball Career
full_text:
Kyle Dixon , the 26-year-old wide receiver from Carlinville, Illinois, was a multi-sport athlete in high school. He was a fantastic wide receiver, a fantastic defensive back and an even better pitcher.
His journey out of Carlinville High School started on the mound. It's now taken him onto the sidelines for the New England Patriots .
How in the world did that happen?
When you ask Dixon — now on the Patriots practice squad — he still doesn't really know. He can try to explain his winding road to the NFL, but there's so many stops along the way that sometimes he forgets a few things. So here's everyone else he's crossed paths with to help fill in the puzzle.
Kyle, born in 2001 to Tim and Monica Dixon, played baseball, football and wrestled in high school. He was excellent in everything he did. His coaches rave about his athletic abilities, almost to a fault.
Don Borgini, former Carlinville baseball head coach: "He was a fierce competitor."
Monica Dixon, Kyle's mother: "He excelled in all of his sports, but was looking for ways to improve his skills. He was always looking online for new training techniques."
Kyle Dixon: "Baseball was a little bit more special for me."
Maybe it was just the athletic juices in his veins, but Kyle always lived for the moment. The homemade pitchers mound that Kyle and his grandfather made in his backyard certainly helped. Once high school rolled around, baseball is where he found his groove.
Borgini: "Every coach on Earth wants a kid that wants the ball in the moment, and Kyle is certainly that guy."
Monica Dixon: "When he did get to pitch, I had a lot of anxiety. His dad could always handle that pressure better than me."
Kyle Dixon: "It was something I really enjoyed a lot."
Borgini: "In a sectional game, he had 19 strikeouts of the 21 batters and it was a tremendous performance by him that I won't forget. ... It is the top (game) for me as far as a pitcher goes (that I've ever seen)."
Kyle Dixon: "It might have been the last game I ever played (in high school). ... We ended up losing that game."
Borgini: "He was attracting a lot of attention."
Monica Dixon: "As parents, it was nice to see his hard work pay off when he got his scholarship. He earned it."
Kyle officially committed to Southern Illinois after a coach at a local JUCO help connect the two parties. But he had committed when Ken Henderson was the head coach. Henderson was fired and the abrupt change caught Kyle — who was on his way to vacation — off guard. Still, from the first day on campus, he stood out.
Lance Rhodes, Southern Illinois baseball head coach: "He wasn't the typical high school-sized kid that was coming to college. He was very put together, just a good looking kid. He definitely looked the part."
Kyle Dixon: "You don't really know what to expect as a freshman, especially with the new staff that didn't recruit you. It was an interesting start to college."
Rhodes: "He (was) just as big as the seniors. He had a ton of ability and he threw extremely hard."
Kyle Dixon: "I was off to a pretty good start my freshman year and then we stopped. We couldn't go into our facility to train with it being COVID. We couldn't go to a lot of the gyms or anything to work out."
His freshman year was mangled by the pandemic, where he only played in eight games. He pitched in four more as a sophomore, but a 22.50 earned run average plagued him. It was a pair of trying years for Dixon. He watched pro pitchers like Max Scherzer and Aroldis Chapman to try and figure out his form.
Kyle Dixon: "I became very focused on looking at MLB pitchers' mechanics and then trying to figure out how I wanted mine to look in regards to that. ... I think I became too focused on mechanics."
Monica Dixon: "I think he started putting more pressure on himself to be perfect and it just wasn't happening. As a parent, it was hard to watch."
Rhodes: "Kyle was always one of those guys that the feel of pitching was something that he needed to develop and work on, and I really think the COVID break in action ... was probably the toughest thing for him."
Kyle Dixon: "I kept thinking if I just keep figuring out whatever mechanical thing it is, then it's gonna play, then it's gonna click. The reality, that was the problem in and of itself."
He didn't want to stick around. After his scholarship was pulled, Southern Illinois Edwardsville — who did research on him coming out of high school — came calling.
Sean Lyons, SIUE baseball head coach: "I had a local umpire stop by our baseball office, come in and tell our staff there's this really good arm pitching, high school kid, not too far from here. ... When Kyle decided to transfer from (Southern Illinois) Carbondale, we kind of had a connection."
Monica Dixon: "We just went with the flow. He would always talk to us about moving and the reasoning for it."
Kyle Dixon: "Ironically, the pitching coach there was the one who recruited me to Carbondale. I was really comfortable with him."
But that coach would later take the head coaching gig for SIUE's softball program, and so Dixon was left with another surprising staff change. Still, his stuff on the mound never left.
Lyons: "He could throw the baseball in the lower-to-mid 90s. Sometimes command and where the location of that was sometimes a mystery for him. But when it was right, man, it was really good."
Kyle Dixon: "I wouldn't say I had a good year, but it was a better year. It wasn't good, but it was progress compared to the year before."
Lyons: "He had a skillset on the mound that could have possibly given him the option ... to play professionally as a baseball player."
Kyle Dixon: "Without a doubt."
Maybe it was time to get out of Illinois. Kyle called Lyons to let him know that he would be entering the transfer portal, a decision that he think took his coach by surprise. After having some summer league teammates hype up Georgia Gwinnett, Kyle then made the trip down south to a team that would go on to make eight-straight NAIA World Series appearances, a streak still active.
Jeremy Sheetinger, former Georgia Gwinnett baseball head coach: "When you see a kid that looks like Kyle and he's built like an Adonis, you know that there's something in there. ... We just feel like sometimes Division I schools, if a kid doesn't gave it, they get pushed to the side. We could spent a little bit more time with them."
Braxton Meguiar, former Georgia Gwinnett second baseman (who played baseball with Mike Vrabel's son, Carter, at Wabash Valley Community College in 2021): "I always remember Kyle's work ethic being different. He never changed. He never wavered, even when he wasn't having success."
Like the previous two schools, it just wasn't in the cards. Kyle had the yips, most commonly associated when throwing a baseball accurately becomes a chore. He'd walk away from sports entirely at the end of the season.
Kyle Dixon: "I was still kind of holding out optimism that I was going to be able to figure it out and turn it around."
Sheetinger: "He was good for a hit an inning, a strikeout an inning and a walk an inning. ... Kyle didn't make our postseason roster."
Meguiar: "He was having some control problems."
Sheetinger: "He's a guy that didn't impact us on the field, but he impacted with the kind of kid he was."
Kyle Dixon: "I just tried to be as good as a teammate as I could and really just not let what was happening to me affect my teammates. It's never fair to them. I think I was partially being myself and then having a little awareness about how not to act."
Monica Dixon: "We were sad for him. His love for the sport had faded. He was done completely."
Sheetinger: "Our pitchers threw footballs. But more people started watching the way Kyle would go catch footballs. You could see it coming together."

title: 4 Postive Takeaways From Patriots' Thursday Night Loss to Bears
full_text:
After falling to the Chicago Bears (5-2) on Thursday Night Football, many are quick to pick apart what went wrong for the New England Patriots and what needs to improve. Those conversations are centered around third down defense, tackling, wide receiver play, and other scrutinies from the Patriots 30-24 let down.
However, like most games, the Patriots still put out good tape, despite the outcome. Here's what New England did well on Thursday night and what we learned about this team moving forward:
With a diminished wide receiver room, the Patriots had to rely on other skill position players to push the ball through the passing game. One of the few that stepped up on Thursday was rookie tight end Eli Raridon.
Raridon hauled in 3 catches for 56 yards, including a 30-yard touchdown reception on a seam route in the third quarter. Maye targeted Raridon earlier in the game but was intercepted in the redzone.
Raridon now has more receiving yards (168) and touchdowns (two) this season than Kyle Williams, Efton Chism III, and A.J. Brown. The third-round pick out of Notre Dame has turned out to be a great investment by the Pats, and will carry the team's pass game well after Hunter Henry retires or moves on from New England.
The Patriots are among the top teams in the NFL for players listed as inactive on reserve lists. Entering Thursday night, the Patriots had 22 players on reserve lists, with nine of those players being starters.
Most notably, the Patriots were missing four guards on Thursday, and were forced to start Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor . While the two players struggled, New England's offensive line had a decent performance, only allowing two sacks on quarterback Drake Maye.
Additionally, the Patriots had three inactive cornerbacks on Thursday, including starter Carlton Davis. Christian Gonzalez was also listed as questionable ahead of the game with an illness, but played every defensive snap.
Lastly, the Pats were limited to just four wide receievers, with Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs on the injured reserve.
With Chicago being one of the NFL's top teams, and last year's second ranked NFC team, New England's competitive showing was impressive, considering the diverse roster they were forced to use.
Similar to the last point, injuries have been a major hurdle the Patriots have had to overcome this season. Each game, the Pats leave with more diagnoses than they entered with.
Last night, the Patriots stayed relatively healthy. With depth being an issue, the health of New England's team was crucial to staying in yesterday's game.
The only significant injury was suffered by defensive linemen Christian Barmore, who appeared to sustain an upper-body injury after sacking Caleb Williams late in the game.
With 10 days until they travel to Miami, Patriots players will have plenty of time to recover from past injuries.
Running back Rhamondre Stevenson was one of the best players on the field Thursday night, and was crucial to New England's ability to stay in the game.
The sixth-year player only ran for 22 yards against the Bears defense, but carried the ball six times, which is twice the amount of his counterpart, TreVeyon Henderson.
Most notably, Stevenson impacted the game through his pass-catching. He hauled in 5 receptions for 93 yards and was New England's leading receiver. His 48-yard touchdown reception to end the first half kept the Patriots within scoring distance of the Bears for the rest of the game.
RHAMONDRE STEVENSON‼️ 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/heXDiTFnzW
This season, Stevenson has 25 more carries than Henderson and has notched 82 more yards than the second-year player. While Henderson has dealt with an ankle injury over the past two weeks, the only action he's missed was Week 1 against Seattle.
Stevenson's production and usage points to continued increase in carries and impact plays from the veteran Patriot.

title: Drake Maye's Interception Wasn't The Reason The Patriots Lost
full_text:
CHICAGO — The New England Patriots didn't win on Thursday Night Football, and yet, their quarterback had yet another great performance.
Drake Maye threw for 300 yards for the second time in three weeks, scored 3+ total touchdowns for the fourth-straight game and used his legs to extend plenty of plays behind a banged-up offensive line.
Did he throw a bad interception in the first half that took points off the board? Yes.
Was that play the biggest reason for the Patriots' 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears ? Nope.
Maye was hard on himself after the game, taking the brunt of the blame for the bad interception he threw to Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson. He was trying to hit Eli Raridon for a touchdown to cut into Chicago's 13-7 lead. Instead, he didn't put enough air on the throw and it was turned over.
“It definitely was a huge point in the game. It’s those plays, I talk about all the time," Maye said. "And those plays that can swing the game, can impact the game, and that was definitely one of them right there. I wish I definitely had that one back and a lot of plays.
"But got to give credit to them. They had a good plan on a short week and they got after us. ...  I know that was a big turning point in the game and I know I let my team down."
But the Patriots had a bigger reason for the loss, and it was from the other side of the ball. The Patriots really couldn't tackle all night, and according to Pro Football Focus, they missed 16 tackles. That's the most they've had in a single game since Super Bowl LX. Marcus Jones led the Patriots with five.
Chicago controlled the ground game with D'Andre Swift (22 carries, 78 yards, 1 rushing touchdown) and beat the Patriots' zone coverages all night.
“The tackling wasn’t good enough, not against this team," head coach Mike Vrabel said. "We knew coming in, certainly against this team, whether it’s Swift, (Luther) Burden, the quarterback. It just leads to extra yards and conversions. But, we fought. I would say that we need to turn the ball over and tackle better and those are fundamental skills."
Caleb Williams hit eight passes for 20+ yards, really stressing the secondary that was down three cornerbacks coming into the game.
Ultimately, the Patriots lost the game, not because of Maye's play, but because of everything around it. There wasn't a lot of production from the ground game or the wide receivers, penalties ran rampant and the defense struggled to bring anyone down.
And yet, Maye kept them in it. He shouldn't be the one receiving the pointed finger.
"He gave us a chance. He competed and I know he’d like to have that throw back to Eli but, I thought he really competed," Vrabel said. "Whether that was running around and scrambling or finding good places to go with the football. He gave us a chance. I know he’d like to have that one back and he’ll learn from it like he always does. I’m glad he’s ours."

title: Patriots' Rhamondre Stevenson Details 'Momentum' Last-Second TD Scamper
full_text:
CHICAGO — The Chicago Bears had just scored, with Luther Burden weaving his way into the end zone. They were up 20-7 over the New England Patriots and looked like they might run away with the game at halftime.
And yet, in a blink of an eye, the Patriots stormed into the locker room trailing by just one possession.
After hitting A.J. Brown on an 18-yard in cut, the Patriots quickly called a timeout with three seconds left. Then, lining up in a Hail Mary-like formation (three receivers spread out wide to one side), Drake Maye checked it down to Rhamondre Stevenson out of the backfield.
Brown came across the field to help clear out room for Stevenson, who'd use a big block from DeMario Douglas to pick up what turned into a 48-yard touchdown run to close the first half.
RHAMONDRE STEVENSON‼️ 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/heXDiTFnzW
It was a play that's been in the Patriots' back pocket for the last few seasons.
"I was just trying to make a play, put my team in a position to swing the game a little bit as much as we can," Stevenson said after the Patriots' 30-24 loss to the Bears on Thursday Night Football .
"We've been working on that play for a long time and came in handy today. Executed on that play, so felt good to do that."
What was Stevenson's mindset during the play?
"Score. Score," he said. "I felt like it brought us some momentum. Felt like it brought us some momentum, but obviously, not enough, you know? We didn't come out with the win."
That play was part of Stevenson's career-high 93 yards through the air, the most on the team. The running game wasn't really working for the Patriots all night, but Stevenson was able to impact the game through the air.
"Just trying to give us a chance to go down and run. And I think it’s hard when those things, I kind of had a feeling they were going to come after me and blitz," Maye said on the play. "So when it leaves, we get five out in the pattern and they bring five. We got really five, four blockers, and Mondre with the ball, and they got six defenders, and it all takes one cut. So that was pretty cool. How you draw it up. That’s how we drew it up all. We’ve been practicing that play since OTAs. So, it definitely brought us some life at halftime, and then just didn’t really swing for us in the fourth quarter."
As a runner, Stevenson carried the ball six times for 22 yards. It wasn't much better for the other running backs on the roster either. TreVeyon Henderson was rarely used (three carried, nine yards), while Corey Kiner (four carries, 13 yards) appeared to be second-in-command for most of the first half .
"We didn't run the ball well enough, but moved it however we needed to move it, which sometimes you're going to have days like that," head coach Mike Vrabel said. "I though we'd be able to run it a little better. We didn't. ... We'd like to run the ball a little better, but it didn't happen tonight."
Stevenson has been on some really good Patriots teams and some really bad Patriots team. That play, although it didn't spark a comeback on Thursday, could be a sign that there's something below the surface for this year's group that's ready to come out.
"We know this team's gonna fight," he said. "We got some relentless people in this locker room. That's great, that's great. We just gotta come out and win games though, that's the main thing. We just gotta watch the film and see what we did well. We had shots to win the game. Bunch of credit to them, that's a great team. But we had shots to win the game, I think."
