title: Patriots Stock Report: Which Position Groups Rose, Fell vs. Bears?
full_text:
The New England Patriots' battle with the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on Thursday night had the visiting team flash plenty of inconsistencies.
Many of New England's positions shined, or struggled, as a collective. Here are the stock reports on the groups which had the biggest impacts in either regard.
New England's wide receiver room may have been the biggest contributor to the team's loss on Thursday night. A.J. Brown, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism and Kyle Williams combined for just seven receptions on 12 targets. Those catches went for 87 yards and no touchdowns.
As the primary target at wide receiver, Brown struggled once again. He has caught just three passes in each of his trio of games as a Patriot.
"I think (the Bears' defense) did a really good job," Brown said after the game. "Early on, (offensive coordinator) Josh (McDaniels) tried to do a really good job of getting me involved and Drake just was taking what they were giving. They were trying to take me away early on, and that's just kind of how the game played."
What the Patriots lacked in production from its wide receivers, it made up for with its tight ends. Veteran Hunter Henry tallied seven receptions for 71 yards, including multiple crucial first down conversions. Also, rookie Eli Raridon got on the board for three receptions, 56 yards and a touchdown.
The main highlight from those two? Raridon's 30-yard score late in the third quarter.
Drake Maye DIME to Eli Raridon 🪙 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/ajUvbcD8Oo
"(He's) great, man," Henry said on Thursday about Raridon. "Just continuing to get better and growing that confidence. A lot of fun to play with."
To address the elephant in the room, yes, Drake Maye's interception was borderline unacceptable. After being turnover-free in his last two games, the third-year signal caller reverted back to his early-season struggles by tossing a pick in the red zone.
Other than that, however, Maye was near-perfect on the evening. He finished 24/31 passing for 321 yards and two touchdowns, alongside the interception. On the ground, he added an extra 26 yards and a score.
In a game where he was constantly pressured, and his receivers were struggling to get open, Maye was one of the lone reasons why New England had any chance of beating Chicago.
"He gave us a chance," Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said about Maye after the loss. "He competed. And I know he'd like to have that throw back to Eli, but I thought that he really competed. Whether that was running around and scrambling or finding good places to go with the football, he gave us a chance."
The Patriots' pass defense was borderline non-existent on Thursday. Their completion percentage allowed (66.7%) was largely aided by a few bad drops by Bears receivers. Plus, Caleb Williams tossed for over 300 yards and two touchdowns.
While the defense as a whole improved in the second half, the secondary struggled immensely in the first 30 minutes against dynamic wide receiver Luther Burden III. The second-year pass catcher hauled in four receptions for 130 yards and a touchdown — all coming in the first half of play.
New England's running back room struggled immensely in the ground game, but helped make up for the wide receivers' struggles in the pass game. Rhamondre Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson and Corey Kiner combined for only 13 carries and 44 yards, and played a significant role in the Patriots' slow start to the night.
However, Stevenson also ended the night with five receptions for a team-high 93 yards and a touchdown. The score came on a 48-yard catch-and-run with no time remaining in the first half to cut the Bears' lead to one possession.
Crazy things happening 🤯 @budlight | 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/QdmQ1DOPPX
Between penalties, pressures allowed on Maye and an inability to find momentum in the run game, the Patriots offensive line combined for a perfectly imperfect performance on Thursday.
Offensive tackle Morgan Moses was called for a hold to back New England up from 2nd-and-2 to 2nd-and-12. Plus, he allowed three pressures and a sack on the evening, per PFF. Every other starter on the line allowed one pressure and was called for a penalty, except for center Jared Wilson who had a clean sheet in both regards.

title: Patriots, Bears QB Duel Lived Up To The Hype
full_text:
CHICAGO — It lived up to the hype, that's for sure.
The second-ever meeting between Drake Maye and Caleb Williams was far better than their first one two seasons ago. The young quarterbacks for the New England Patriots and Chicago Bears had excellent days for their respective sides on Thursday Night Football, with Williams' Bears grabbing the 30-24 win in the final moments .
"Shoulda, woulda, coulda," Maye told reporters postgame. "I'm proud of the guys for the effort. I think we did some good things, we've got a lot of stuff to clean up."
But that loss wasn't on Maye's shoulders, at least not entirely. The 24-year-old went 24-for-31 for 347 total yards and three total touchdowns (two passing, one rushing). It was a fantastic effort by Maye, who kept the Patriots offense in the game all night.
And yet, it was Williams' scrambling and elite arm talent that led the Bears. He finished the night going 22-for-33 for 308 yards and two passing touchdowns, and hit Rome Odunze on a pair of first downs that started to break the Patriots' proverbial defensive back.
It was two juggernauts dueling it out.
"Drake's a competitor, man," tight end Hunter Henry said in the locker room. "That's what he does. We always got a chance when 10's back there, that's for sure."
"He did a great job extending plays," A.J. Brown, who caught three passes in the loss, said. "He did great."
Maye's one blip on his radar was a bad interception in the first half. Looking to hit rookie Eli Raridon in the end zone, he didn't put enough air on his pass and Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson picked it off. It was Maye's third INT thrown in the end zone this season, the most in the entire NFL.
On the other side of the field, Williams completed eight passes of 20+ yards, tied for the most by any quarterback in 2026. He didn't turn the ball over and used his legs to buy some time for his receivers, which hurt the Patriots secondary's ability to defend "the second play."
"We talked about it all week," Christian Gonzalez said. "He's very gifted with how he can run and how he can extend plays. ... You gotta defend the second play. There's a play and then there's a second play with a quarterback like Caleb."
"Anytime a quarterback that's as mobile as him gets out of the pocket, they definitely put stress on the DBs," Charles Woods told Patriots On SI. "It's definitely difficult, but that's what we signed up."
Williams ran for just 18 yards, but his legs helped set up some of the game's biggest plays. He rolled out to find Colston Loveland on a 12-yard touchdown in the third quarter. He escaped the pocket to help pick up big conversions late in the fourth. He was the victor in Week 7, and deservingly so.
If this was the type of matchup these two young quarterbacks can provide , watch out NFL. Instead of rookie gunslingers on bad teams in 2024, these were two grown quarterbacks that offer plenty of skills under center. It was a fun one to watch at Soldier Field.
"I just appreciate we have him back there and (to) be able to block for him," Walter Rouse, who started his first game of the season at left guard, told Patriots On SI. "Drake's an awesome, great guy."
The loss wasn't the outcome the Patriots had hoped for, but it was a gutsy effort by their quarterback. It's just the latest in a string of them, and it's proving why he's the face of this franchise.
"He gave us a chance," Mike Vrabel said. "He competed. ... He'll learn from it like he always does. I'm glad he's ours."

title: Patriots Defense Struggles, and 6 More Takeaways From Groggy TNF Loss to Bears
full_text:
CHICAGO — At some point, the New England Patriots ' three game-winning streak was going to end. That happened at Soldier Field Thursday, as they ran into a Chicago Bears-shaped buzzsaw and couldn't get anything cooking.
Struggles upfront on an injury-depleted offensive line, penalties and an inability to stop the chunk play was what caused the Patriots to drop this one 30-24 to the Bears on a national stage. They kept it close in the final frame, but several long first downs from Rome Odunze wiped that dream away.
Drake Maye (23-for-29, 305 passing yards, two total touchdowns) was efficient, but couldn't will his team to the win. Instead, it was Caleb Williams (22-for-33, 308 passing yards, two passing touchdowns) who emerged victorious, handing the Patriots their first loss in the city of Chicago since 2000.
Here's what happened, and what it means moving forward.
The Patriots lost Alijah Vera-Tucker (who was placed on IR pregame) and Ben Brown last week in their win over the New York Jets. So they had to turn to Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse to step into the starting lineup.
it didn't go that well. The Bears continued to dial up pressure — both up the middle and off the edge — to make life difficult for Maye in the pocket. Chicago really got into the backfield consistently, allowing just 70 yards on the ground. They also sacked Maye twice.
The Patriots would get on the board with a seven-yard rushing touchdown from Maye, but for the most part, the ground game was not the way to go. They consistently lost battles in the trenches and it really took the running attack out of the playbook down the line.
For the entire first half, the Patriots struggled to stay on Burden in coverage. The speedy wideout — who came into the game with just 361 receiving yards on the year — tallied 130 receiving yards with a touchdown.
A 58-yard catch-and-run early helped set up a four-yard D'Andre Swift touchdown in the first quarter, and he'd hit paydirt himself on a weaving 24-yard score. The Patriots would soon adapt, and Burden would be shut down in the second half and held without a catch.
After several weeks of playing nearly-flawless football, Maye made his first bad decision in a while. Driving down the field, he tried to hit Eli Raridon in the end zone in the second quarter. He didn't put enough juice on the throw, and it was picked off by Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson.
That was the third time in seven games that Maye has been intercepted in the end zone this year, the most by any NFL quarterback. Other than that, the Patriots quarterback was good at getting the ball out to his open receivers.
He could have had A.J. Brown deep down the sideline , but the perfectly thrown ball was deflected by Malik Muhammed in coverage. Brown's night ended with just three catches and he's yet to make that big play the Patriots need him to make .
After Burden ran his way in for a touchdown and a 20-7 lead, it looked like the Patriots were heading into the locker room on life support. But somehow, someway, they made something out of nothing.
Maye connected with A.J. Brown on his first reception of the game, good for 18 yards. The Patriots would call a timeout with three ticks left and line up for appeared to be a Hail Mary attempt.
Instead, they checked it down to Rhamondre Stevenson out of the backfield. He would run and pick up some yardage against a Chicago defense playing pretty soft coverage. Then he'd cut back and pick up some more yardage. And more, until the Patriots running back waltzed into the end zone untouched. That 48-yard pickup was the longest play by New England all night, and got them back into the game.
On the Bears' opening drive of the second half, they'd pick up chunk play after chunk play to drive deep into New England territory. Williams would roll out and hit tight end Colston Loveland — who'd power his way into the end zone and give the Bears the 27-14 lead.
But not so fast. Maye and the Patriots go on an impressive drive of their own in response. They drive 80 yards on nine plays, and it ends with Maye hitting Rairdon down the right seam for a 30-yard touchdown.
After back-to-back drives where both offenses sputtered out, the Bears would try to extend their lead with a Cairo Santos field goal. That 53-yard attempt would hit the right upright, giving the Patriots a chance — a chance they'd squander away after giving up a big sack on second down.
All night, the Patriots defense was just getting gashed . Whether it was a long pass from Williams to Odunze or a crisp off-tackle run for Swift that picked up a first down, it was difficult for the Patriots to make life difficult for the home team. The Bears had more than 400 total yards of offense, and that was even converting just four third downs.
But they were oh so close plenty of times. Kevin Byard nearly broke up a pass, but a dart from Williams to Odunze turned into a 21-yard pickup. Neither Milton Williams nor Christian Barmore — the team's top stars on the interior — could muster up any consistent pressure. Williams' ability to move in the pocket and scramble if needed really limited the impact that the Patriots could have done.
Barmore would sack Williams on a third down with 1:39 left, but Santos would drill a 58-field goal one play later to essentially put the nail in the coffin. Barmore would also get banged up on the play and leave the game.
The Patriots lost to the Bears, but they also kept beating themselves.
They were flagged 10 times for 71 total yards, and consistently put themselves behind the 8-ball. A false start from Pryor turned what would have been a fourth down conversion attempt into a punt, and a Cory Durden encroachment flag gave the Bears a first down after the final two-minute warning.
It wasn't just the Patriots, though. The Bears were also called for eight penalties for 56 yards.
The Patriots, after playing two games in five days and now sitting at 4-3, will now have the next three days off.

title: Patriots Week 7 Inactives vs. Bears: Breaking Down What to Expect at OL Tonight
full_text:
CHICAGO — In under 90 minutes, two teams with Super Bowl aspirations will duke it out in front of a national audience. The New England Patriots and Chicago Bears , both sporting 4-2 records, will do battle on Thursday Night Football — but not at full strength.
The Patriots have taken a beating in recent weeks . They've had to put a number of players on injured reserve this season, including wide receiver Romeo Doubs this week. It hasn't been easy sledding for the defending AFC champions, and a short week certainly won't help that.
Here's a look at the inactives from both sides, including key offensive linemen who won't be able to dress:
QB Behren Morton (emergency third QB)
QB Case Keenum (emergency third QB)
RB Kyle Monangai (thumb/toe)
CB Channing Canada (hamstring)
CB Karon Prunty (hamstring)
For the Patriots, there isn't any surprises. Head coach Mike Vrabel shared all of these names (other than Behren Morton and Joshua Farmer) at his final press conference of the week on Wednesday.
Rookie offensive tackle Dametrious Crownover will return to the lineup after being inactive for the last  five games. Behren Morton, who's been the third quarterback all season, won't be able to play unless Drake Maye and Tommy DeVito leave with injuries.
For the Bears, losing their downhill running back in Kyle Monangai is a break for the Patriots — who have struggled against the run in recent weeks. They'll still have to deal with D'Andre Swift , who had two touchdowns on 44 yards a week ago against Atlanta.
"Their runners or anybody that touches the ball is going to be a physical player, is going to be a tough tackle," Vrabel said. "We'll have to be great tacklers."
After Alijah Vera-Tucker and Ben Brown went down a week ago, the Patriots got inspiring outings from their backups. Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor , the last two active linemen on the game day roster, stepped up to fill in at both guard spots. They'll now be in the starting lineup tonight, with Rouse handling the left side and Pryor the right.
It's just another offensive line combination that the Patriots will need to navigate through . They lost Mike Onwenu early in the season, and then lost his backup Greg Van Roten one week later. Just a few games later, and we're seeing two players who didn't spend the summer in New England starting a primetime game. Vera-Tucker was placed on IR prior to kickoff , ruling him out for the next four games.
Vrabel was asked Wednesday about the possibility of rookie tackle Caleb Lomu, who's gotten reps on both sides of the line the last two weeks, potentially kicking inside at guard.
"We have a lot of consideration," he said. "We go through things, different scenarios. We're going to go with where we finished on Sunday and see what that looks like, and then have everybody else ready to go."
The Patriots are also down three cornerbacks, the biggest name being Carlton Davis. He's been dealing with a neck injury for a lot of the season, and this will be his fourth missed game of the year. They're also down rookies Channing Canada and Karon Prunty, who both have hamstring injuries.
Davis is the team's second-best cornerback and easily their top one when it comes to playing the run. But he's struggled to stay healthy in 2026, and while he was spotted at practice for the first time in three weeks leading up to this game, the Patriots still didn't feel comfortable rolling him out there.
The Patriots will have four active cornerbacks for this matchup against a high-flying Bears offense, with Christian Gonzalez, Marcus Jones, Charles Woods and Kindle Vildor ready to go. Second-year safety Elliott Davison has also gotten snaps at cornerback this season in a reserve role.
The Patriots nearly got a scare at cornerback, as Gonzalez was downgraded to questionable pregame with an illness. However, he was warming up on the field and will suit up.
The Bears come into this matchup with one of the league's best defenses — especially against the run. But they rank 14th in the NFL in passing defense through six games, and with a few players banged up in the secondary, the Patriots can try to push the ball through the air.
Chicago will be without cornerback Tyrique Stevenson, who was ruled out with a hip injury. They'll also line up without Nick McCloud (who's played in just two games this year) on the field. They do have Kyler Gordon back, who played last week after opening the year on the PUP list, but he's still trying to knock the rust off.
If the Patriots want to try and air the ball out against a secondary that isn't at full strength, they could end up putting up a bunch of points in a hurry. Avoiding a stout Bears run defense, especially early in drives, could be beneficial.

title: Key Patriots Starter Goes to IR, Pair of Practice Squad Elevations for TNF
full_text:
Ahead of Thursday night's game against the Chicago Bears, the New England Patriots have announced that guard Alijah Vera-Tucker has been placed on the injured reserve . Vera-Tucker suffered a hamstring injury in Sunday's win over the New York Jets .
Vera-Tucker is a former first-round NFL Draft selection, who spent his first four years with the Jets. This past offseason, the 6-foot-4, 308 pound linemen signed with New England on a three-year contract worth up to $48 million.
The Patriots starting left guard has had a career riddled with injuries. Since entering the league six years ago, Vera-Tucker has only played 55.1% of offensive snaps. Vera-Tucker becomes the 22nd player to be placed on a reserve list for the Patriots this year, and is the ninth projected starter to miss at least four weeks with an injury.
Vera-Tucker will be eligible to return in Week 13, four games after his IR designation.
The Patriots will rely on players listed deep in the depth chart at the guard position against the Bears. With Ben Brown ruled out, and both Greg Van Roten and Mike Onwenu on injured reserve, the Patriots will start Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse — their fifth and sixth options, at guard .
In addition to Pryor and Rouse, New England will have lineman Xavier Newman-Johnson available Thursday night, as he's been announced as a practice squad elevation.
Newman-Johnson has been with the Patriots since Week 2 of the NFL season, and will be on the Patriots game roster for the first time. It's his first of three elevations for the season
A fifth-year player, Newman-Johnson got his start in Tennessee while Mike Vrabel was the head coach. He then spent three seasons in New York with the Jets, with extended time on the team's 53-man roster. Newman-Johnson will serve as a a back-up to Pryor and Rouse at both guard positions.
The Patriots have placed LG Alijah Vera-Tucker on IR with a hamstring injury. They also elevated OG Xavier Newman-Johnson and LB Benton Whitley to the game day roster from the practice squad.
The Patriots have also elevated linebacker Benton Whitley. Whitley has been with the Patriots for just under a month, and will also be seeing his first game action as a Patriot on Thursday night.
A Holy Cross graduate, Whitley is in his fifth year in the NFL after bouncing around to multiple teams, six of which he was signed to the 53-man roster. He'll be making his seventh appearance in an NFL game on Thursday night, and will supplement a linebacker room consisting of Robert Spillane , Christian Ellis, Namdi Obiazor, Darius Muasa, and Erick Hunter.

title: Saints Fans Should Know These 3 Things About the Steelers Before Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (2-4) enter Sunday's historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) at Stade de France, looking to build momentum after their 34-27 win over the New York Giants .
However, Pittsburgh presents a considerably different challenge.
Under first-year coach Mike McCarthy , the Steelers have established themselves as a competitive AFC North contender, winning four of their first six games despite an offense that has struggled to consistently produce explosive plays.
Pittsburgh enters Sunday's contest averaging 22.8 points and 320.5 yards per game, ranking 18th and 21st in the NFL, respectively. However, its defense has been considerably more effective, allowing 307.5 yards per game, the ninth-fewest in the league.
For Saints coach Kellen Moore , Sunday's matchup offers a chance to secure consecutive wins for the first time this season before the team's Week 8 bye.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Steelers.
While 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers continues to anchor Pittsburgh's offense with his elite ability to read defenses and capitalize on errors, the Steelers' aerial game has produced fairly modest results.
Across six games, Rodgers has completed 61.4% of his pass attempts for 1,487 yards, throwing 12 touchdowns against five interceptions.
Despite these respectable individual metrics, Pittsburgh ranks just 18th in the league through the air, averaging 221.3 passing yards per contest.
Physical wide receiver DK Metcalf gives Rodgers a dependable downfield threat capable of winning contested balls and creating opportunities on intermediate routes.
However, Rodgers' statistical split against specific zone schemes presents a critical storyline for this matchup.
NFL Next Gen Stats reveals that Rodgers has struggled against Cover 3, registering a 32.9% success rate—the third-lowest figure among qualified quarterbacks—compared to a 52.9% success rate against all other zone schemes.
This dynamic is especially relevant given that New Orleans deploys Cover 3 on 55.9% of defensive dropbacks, leading the entire NFL.
Consequently, defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must balance disciplined zone coverage with an effective pass rush to contain Pittsburgh's passing attack.
While Rodgers draws significant focus, the Steelers' ground attack could pose a greater threat to New Orleans.
Running back Jaylen Warren has rushed for 460 yards on 84 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt.
His ability to gain yards after contact, identify lanes and contribute in the passing game gives Pittsburgh multiple offensive options.
That creates a difficult matchup for New Orleans.
The Saints allow 138 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the NFL, while Pittsburgh averages 99.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 20th.
Despite Pittsburgh's modest team average, Warren's efficiency indicates the Steelers can exploit the Saints' run defense.
While returning veteran linebacker Kaden Elliss should bolster the Saints' run defense, containing Warren remains a critical priority. Allowing Pittsburgh to establish its ground game early will open up play-action opportunities for Rodgers.
While Pittsburgh's offense has experienced inconsistencies, its defense remains the team's most reliable strength.
The Steelers enter Sunday's matchup allowing 21.3 points and 307.5 yards per game, ranking 12th and ninth in the NFL, respectively.
A key part of its defense has been its ability to defend the pass as the Steelers have surrendered just 204.3 yards per game, the eighth-fewest in the league.
Pittsburgh has also recorded 16 sacks and six interceptions through six games, contributing to a plus-three turnover differential.
Outside linebacker T.J. Watt , who has a team-high 4.5 sacks, remains one of the league's most disruptive defensive players.
Alex Highsmith provides another formidable presence on the edge, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward anchors the interior.
The Steelers also one of the league’s top cornerbacks, eight-time Pro Bowler Jalen Ramsey , giving their secondary an experienced playmaker who can create turnovers.
For Saints quarterback Tyler Shough , protecting the football will be especially important.
Shough has thrown for 1,443 yards, 12 touchdowns and five interceptions this season, but his performance against zone coverage presents a potential concern.
According to Next Gen Stats , Shough has thrown five interceptions against zone coverage this season, tied for the second-most among qualified quarterbacks.
Pittsburgh has utilized zone coverage on 82.8% of opposing dropbacks, with five of its six interceptions occurring against zone concepts.
This creates a compelling schematic test between Moore's offense and Pittsburgh's defense.
If Pittsburgh generates pressure without compromising coverage, Shough may struggle against an opportunistic unit. To build on last week's win, New Orleans will need to establish the run, avoid clear passing downs, and minimize turnovers.

Running back Alvin Kamara and starting offensive guard Cesar Ruiz headline New Orleans' injury report, while Pittsburgh is monitoring several key defensive players, including T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Jalen Ramsey.
According to the Saints' official Thursday injury report , 11 New Orleans players were listed Thursday, with three missing practice and three participating on a limited basis.
The Saints (2-4) are looking to build momentum following Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, which snapped a three-game losing streak. Meanwhile, Pittsburgh (4-2) enters the matchup seeking its second consecutive victory.
Both teams have several injury situations worth monitoring before Friday's final practice report.
The Saints' biggest offensive concerns involve Kamara and Ruiz, who have been dealing with back and knee injuries, respectively.
Kamara was limited for the second consecutive practice Thursday, leaving his availability worth monitoring heading into Sunday's game.
The veteran running back remains an important part of Kellen Moore's offense, particularly as New Orleans attempts to establish a more consistent rushing attack.
Ruiz's situation is potentially more concerning. The veteran offensive lineman missed practice Wednesday and Thursday because of a knee injury, raising questions about his availability against Pittsburgh's defensive front.
However, Jeremiah Wright played well in his absence during New Orleans’ win over the Giants last week.
Meanwhile, linebacker Kaden Elliss (calf) and edge rusher Anfernee Jennings (knee) were limited for the second consecutive day. During today's player roundtable , Elliss was asked if he would be available to play Sunday, and he said, "Yes."

Shough, who appeared on the report with a left-hand injury, participated fully in both practices. Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry (head) and defensive lineman Nathan Shepherd (illness) also practiced without limitations.
Running back CJ Donaldson (shoulder) improved from limited participation Wednesday to a full practice Thursday.
Kicker Daniel Carlson missed his second consecutive practice because of a personal matter unrelated to injury (he and his wife are having a baby), while defensive lineman Davon Godchaux received a rest day Thursday.
Backup quarterback Spencer Rattler was added to Thursday's report with a knee injury but participated fully.
Pittsburgh is also dealing with significant injury concerns, particularly on defense.
The most notable development Thursday was star edge rusher T.J. Watt, who was limited with a calf injury after sitting out Wednesday's practice for rest.
Watt's status matters, given the Saints' offensive line concerns. The former NFL Defensive Player of the Year has 4.5 sacks through six games.
Fellow pass rusher Alex Highsmith remained limited with a groin injury, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward missed his second straight practice for rest.
The Steelers also received encouraging news about star cornerback Jalen Ramsey, who returned to practice on Thursday, albeit in a limited capacity. He missed Wednesday's session with a wrist injury.

title: Saints Stock Up: 3 Heroes From New Orleans' Win Over Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints earned a much-needed victory over the New York Giants as they broke a three-game losing streak.
Now, the Saints are in Paris as they turn their attention to the Pittsburgh Steelers to win consecutive games for the first time this season. However, it will be a tough task: Pittsburgh still has a solid quarterback in Aaron Rodgers at 42, and the offense has plenty of weapons; on defense, they have a solid pass rush.
After fully reviewing the Saints’ win over New York and looking at which players have been trending upward, here are three players whose stock is rising.
The Saints historically produce standout special teams performers, including Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis , and Steve Gleason .
Linebacker Isaiah Stalbird has continued that tradition this year, keying special teams unit success and executing the decisive sequence of the game.
Down 10-3 late in the second quarter, New Orleans seemed poised for a halftime deficit before Stalbird made a game-altering play on coverage.
The second-year backer stripped the ball from Charlie Jones on a kickoff return, which tight end Oscar Delp recovered to set up New Orleans inside the red zone.
Shough converted the takeaway into points, finding rookie Bryce Lance for a game-tying touchdown right before the break.
That turnover shifted game momentum entirely and helped spark a 31-point unanswered run that gave New Orleans a 34-10 lead before the Giants mounted a furious fourth-quarter comeback.
Cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. posted his top outing of the year in the 34-27 victory, accumulating seven tackles, two interceptions, and four pass breakups.
His effort earned an 88.4 defensive rating and a 90.2 coverage rating from Pro Football Focus, leading all team defenders in Week 6. Emerson was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his efforts.
Emerson held opponents to four catches on 10 targeted passes while picking off throws from Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy . The performance provided valuable depth after Kool-Aid McKinstry exited due to a migraine.
Rookie guard Jeremiah Wright capitalized on unexpected playing time against New York, filling in when starter Cesar Ruiz left with a knee injury in the second quarter.
If one thing is certain, the run game started to click when Wright went into the game as he added toughness to the interior line, anchoring a run game that piled up a season-best 175 yards. If you want to know how much of an impact Wright had? When the Saints ran to the right, they averaged just over 5 yards per carry. When they ran to the left? 3.1-yards a clip.
The fourth-round selection surrendered just a single QB pressure in his most extensive action of the season.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly: Saints Finally Win, but Major Problems Remain
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints finally have a reason to celebrate. Their 34-27 victory over the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on Sunday was far from seamless, but it brought a much-needed end to a troublesome stretch.
Riding a three-game losing streak and facing mounting questions about the franchise's direction, New Orleans desperately needed a win. The Saints delivered by overcoming an early 10-0 deficit, though they nearly squandered a commanding 24-point lead late in the second half.
Quarterback Tyler Shough completed 16 of 30 passes for 144 yards and three touchdowns, guiding an offense that showed encouraging progress on the ground. Meanwhile, the defense created three interceptions despite struggling to contain New York's passing game.
The win gives head coach Kellen Moore 's squad welcome breathing room, after the team entered the week under heavy scrutiny following critical remarks from franchise icon Drew Brees and owner Gayle Benson .
Still, the team's inability to comfortably close out the game after building a 34-10 advantage underscores ongoing concerns about their consistency and ability to finish strong.
Here is a look at the good, bad and ugly from the Saints' victory over the Giants.
Following weeks of criticism regarding a stagnant ground attack, the Saints may have uncovered a workable formula.
New Orleans ran for a season-high 175 yards, offering vital balance to an offense that had relied far too heavily on Tyler Shough to make plays.
Kendre Miller paced the backfield with 70 yards on 20 carries, while C.J. Donaldson added 39 yards on six attempts. Alvin Kamara chipped in 34 yards on seven carries, and Shough contributed 32 yards along with a rushing touchdown.
This collective output was an encouraging sign for a unit that had failed to establish any momentum during its three-game slide.
However, the Saints still have considerable work ahead.
Even so, efficiency remains an issue; Miller averaged just 3.5 yards per carry, reflecting the play-to-play inconsistency that still lingers.
Lineman Jeremiah Wright provided a notable spark after replacing the injured Cesar Ruiz at right guard. His presence was felt in the second half, as the Saints repeatedly—and successfully—ran behind the right side of the line.
To sustain this progress, the offensive line must open cleaner lanes up front rather than depending on backfield effort to gain positive yardage.
While far from dominant, Sunday's performance marked a meaningful step toward a more balanced attack.
Despite forcing three interceptions, the Saints' defensive backfield repeatedly yielded big plays during New York's late comeback bid.
Receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely caused major problems throughout the contest.
Nabers hauled in 12 receptions for 165 yards, while Likely added six catches for 99 yards and a touchdown.
After replacing starter Jameis Winston , backup J.J. McCarthy threw for 243 yards in just over 11 minutes, orchestrating three straight touchdown drives to cut a 34-10 deficit to seven points.
New Orleans did deliver key playmaking moments: Martin Emerson Jr. picked off two passes, Julian Blackmon intercepted another, and the pass rush brought down Winston four times.
However, surrendering 461 total yards (377 passing) highlights persistent pass-coverage issues that defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must resolve.
For three quarters, the Saints looked poised for their most convincing win of the year—a strong statement following three straight home defeats.
Instead, they nearly suffered a catastrophic fourth-quarter collapse.
After trailing 10-0 early, New Orleans reeled off 34 unanswered points using balanced rushing, opportunistic turnovers, and efficient red-zone execution.
Shough's 18-yard touchdown strike to Chris Olave early in the fourth quarter pushed the lead to 34-10, prompting the Saints to begin rotating in reserves.
However, the momentum quickly shifted.
With McCarthy at quarterback, New York scored 17 unanswered points over the final 11 minutes, exploiting defensive breakdowns and stalling offensive possessions.
An offense that had scored on four straight drives suddenly went cold, finishing an alarming 4-for-15 on third down.
Meanwhile, the defense surrendered multiple scoring drives as New York steadily chipped away at the deficit.
The Giants eventually cut the lead to 34-27 and drove deep into New Orleans territory. The Saints survived only when McCarthy's fourth-down pass to Likely fell incomplete near the end zone.
For a Saints team already facing criticism over its lack of consistency, nearly blowing a 24-point advantage raises legitimate questions about its ability to finish games.
Moore and his staff deserve credit for halting the losing streak, but nearly letting a 24-point lead slip away shows that New Orleans still has significant work ahead to compete with top-tier opponents.

However, the Saints' inability to put away the Giants after building a 24-point advantage demonstrated why significant questions remain about their consistency and ability to finish games.
Here are four instant reactions from New Orleans' much-needed victory.
The Saints always have at least one special teamer that becomes a star whether it’s Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis or Steve Gleason .
This time, it has been linebacker Isaiah Stalbird , who has been valuable on special teams all year, and he made the biggest play of the game.
Trailing 10-3 with less than a minute remaining in the first half, New Orleans looked set to enter halftime with another double-digit deficit. However, Stalbird delivered arguably the biggest play of the afternoon on special teams.
The rookie safety forced a fumble on Charlie Jones 's kickoff return, allowing tight end Oscar Delp to recover the football and give New Orleans possession deep in Giants territory.
Shough capitalized on the turnover, connecting with rookie Bryce Lance for a touchdown that tied the game at 10 with one second remaining before halftime.
The sequence completely changed the momentum.
After struggling offensively throughout much of the first half, the Saints suddenly found themselves in position to take control. New Orleans carried that momentum into the third quarter, scoring 24 additional unanswered points to build a commanding advantage.
Although Stalbird's contribution won't receive the same attention as Shough's four-touchdown performance or Martin Emerson Jr. 's two interceptions, his forced fumble was arguably the game's most important play.
After weeks of heavy criticism in regard to its horrendous rushing attack, the Saints may have figured out the formula.
New Orleans finished with a season-high 175 rushing yards, providing much-needed balance to an offense that has frequently relied on too much on Shough to generate production.
Kendre Miller led the charge with 70 yards on 20 carries, while C.J. Donaldson contributed 39 yards on six attempts. Alvin Kamara added 34 yards on seven carries, and Shough chipped in another 32 yards and a touchdown run.
The production was particularly encouraging considering New Orleans had struggled to establish a reliable ground game during its three-game losing streak.
However, the Saints still have considerable work ahead.
Miller averaged just 3.5 yards a carry, highlighting the inconsistency that continues to plague the rushing attack despite the improved overall numbers.
Another player worth monitoring is offensive lineman Jeremiah Wright , who came in for the injured Cesar Ruiz at right guard. His impact became noticeable as it was a trend that the Saints ran the ball to the right a solid amount in the second half and with success.
The Saints need their offensive front, including Wright when he is involved, to create more consistent running lanes rather than relying on individual efforts to generate positive yardage.
Sunday's performance was hardly a dominant rushing effort, but it represented a meaningful step forward for an offense desperately searching for balance.
Despite grabbing three interceptions, the Saints' secondary once struggled once again against a solid receiving corps in coverage during New York's fourth-quarter comeback.
Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely torched New Orleans’ secondary all game.
Nabers recorded 12 catches for 165 yards, while Likely had six catches for 99 yards and a touchdown.
After replacing Jameis Winston, J.J. McCarthy threw for 243 yards in just over 11 minutes, sparking three straight touchdown drives to trim a 34-10 deficit to seven points.
Still, the defense created crucial takeaways: Martin Emerson Jr. had two interceptions (one off McCarthy), Julian Blackmon picked off Winston, and the pass rush logged four sacks on Winston.
Yet, allowing 461 total yards (377 passing) highlights the already serious concerns on whether or not the secondary can slow so. Defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must fix these coverage breakdowns to prevent future collapses.
Few teams entered Week 6 under more pressure than the Saints.
Following three consecutive losses, including a disappointing 23-13 defeat against the Minnesota Vikings , New Orleans found itself under intense scrutiny from fans, former players and ownership.
Former Saints quarterback Drew Brees, who called the game for Fox and was inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor at halftime during the loss to the Vikings, criticized the team's offense and Moore's play-calling .
A few days later, Saints owner Gayle Benson publicly expressed her frustration with the team's 1-4 start during a speaking engagement at the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club, making it clear that recent performances were unacceptable.
Benson specifically challenged the team's leadership, including Moore and general manager Mickey Loomis , to address the mistakes that had contributed to the disappointing start.
Those comments placed additional pressure on Moore, whose second season as head coach has been defined by inconsistent performances and questions about the team's direction.
Sunday's victory provided a much-needed response.
The Saints showed resilience after falling behind 10-0, capitalized on turnovers and demonstrated the offensive explosiveness that had been largely absent during their losing streak.
More importantly, they found a way to win.
Yet blowing nearly all of a 24-point fourth-quarter lead highlighted the issues behind Benson's criticism. With execution and closing troubles nearly turning a blowout into a loss, the 2-4 Saints face major questions before playing the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris. Snapping the streak offers short-term relief, but New Orleans must show real growth to make this a true turning point.

title: Postgame Live Blog: Saints Survive Late Rally from Giants to Break Losing Skid
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints survive a furious comeback from the New York Giants to pull off a much-needed 34-27 win and break a three-game losing skid.
The Saints will now travel to Paris to take on the Pittsburgh Steelers on Oct. 25.
The New Orleans Saints survive a furious comeback from the New York Giants to pull off a much-needed 34-27 win and break a three-game losing skid.
After leading 34-10 early in the fourth quarter, New Orleans nearly squandered its 24-point advantage before a final fourth-down incompletion ended New York's comeback attempt.
The Saints appeared headed toward another disappointing first half Sunday before a late rally erased a double-digit deficit against the Giants at MetLife Stadium.
SAINTS WIN! #Saints | @Gatorade pic.twitter.com/L3rLoA34Cg
Trailing 10-0 early, New Orleans mounted a crucial 10-point rally to tie 10-10 by halftime. The turnaround gave the team vital momentum as it looked to end its three-game losing slump. and a coach trying to extinguish the fire on his seat.
The Saints (1-4) struggled offensively for much of the opening half, with quarterback Tyler Shough facing consistent pressure from an aggressive Giants defense, which is ninth in the NFL in total defense. New Orleans struggled to sustain drives, while former Saints quarterback Jameis Winston helped New York build an early advantage.
Winston opened the scoring with a 17-yard touchdown pass to running back Tyrone Tracy Jr. in the first quarter. Tracy caught the pass near the line of scrimmage and capitalized on a missed tackle before reaching the end zone.
New York extended its lead to 10-0 when Dominic Zvada nailed a 34-yard field goal with ease late in the second quarter.
Meanwhile, New Orleans continued to squander scoring opportunities, including Daniel Carlson 's missed 55-yard field goal attempt earlier in the quarter.
However, the Saints finally broke through when Carlson drilled a 58-yard field goal with 1:18 remaining before halftime, cutting the deficit to 10-3.
On the ensuing kickoff, linebacker Isaiah Stalbird laid one on Giants returner Charlie Jones to force a fumble and rookie tight end Oscar Delp recovered the football to give the Saints.
A few plays later, Shough would find a wide-open Bryce Lance in the endzone on fourth-and-two, tying the game and giving Lance his first career touchdown reception.
Shough to Lance: TD Saints 🙌 #Saints | 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/bMW0CKYTSP
That led to a Saints scoring spree.
Shough connected with Alvin Kamara on a 31-yard touchdown pass to give New Orleans its first lead, 17-10. The scoring play also helped Kamara reach the historic milestone of 5,000 career receiving yards, adding to his more than 5,000 rushing yards.
AK ALL THE WAY!!! #Saints | 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/ftWZuuSHFX
Shough later scored on a 1-yard quarterback sneak before Carlson added a 51-yard field goal, extending the advantage to 27-10.
Shough Sneak ⚜️ #Saints | 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/oNfCm0szhE
New Orleans' defense continued creating opportunities, with Martin Emerson Jr. recording two interceptions and Julian Blackmon adding another.
Blackmon's interception set up Shough's 18-yard touchdown pass to Chris Olave, pushing the lead to 34-10 early in the fourth quarter.
Shough ➡️ Olave 🙌 #Saints | 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/qS5PI0R1jR
With Winston struggling, New York turned to JJ McCarthy , who immediately provided a spark.
McCarthy directed a touchdown drive capped by Tracy's 5-yard scoring run and a successful 2-point conversion. He later connected with Isaiah Likely for a 24-yard touchdown before Zvada's 41-yard field goal reduced New Orleans' lead to 34-27.
After forcing a Saints punt, McCarthy drove the Giants deep into New Orleans territory before the final fourth-down incompletion ended the comeback attempt.
Despite the fourth-quarter collapse, New Orleans produced a season-high 175 rushing yards and received its most productive touchdown performance of the season from Shough.
The victory offers some relief for second-year coach Kellen Moore after owner Gayle Benson publicly criticized the team's disappointing start .
Wild NFL games. They're always coming in different shapes and sizes. Proud of our guys to find a way to win this game. That's ultimately your No. 1 objective going on the road.
Obviously, we'll extend this road trip here shortly tonight, but proud of our guys to find a way to win.
From a medical standpoint, Cesar had a knee injury. He didn't finish. Quincy had that neck issue at the end. I think we're OK. Kool-Aid had a little bit of a migraine thing going on. Everyone else was able to play and was good to go.
Q: In hindsight, how do you feel about the decision to start pulling your starters?
A: Obviously, looking back on it, they got things going and were able to score a lot. We had to get back into that thing. It's just a couple guys who are managing some stuff, guys who are sore, and we tried to get a few guys out. Obviously, it didn't work.
Q: Was that a quick decision after the score?
A: Yeah, after the turnover. Obviously, it was a 24-point game, and we were just trying to give a couple of our guys a break. It was really Eric and Tyler. Everyone else was playing. Then we obviously had the fumble.
Q: Did Kool-Aid McKinstry's migraine develop at halftime, or when did that become an issue?
A: Just during the game. We'll work through the details of that.
Q: What changed with the running game in the second half that allowed you to have so much success?
A: I think ultimately our guys' physical play. The runners ran really hard. I thought they finished well.
Again, when you don't beat yourself with penalties and negative plays, you're able to get more rush attempts and get into the rush game and some action game off it.
I thought our guys just did a better job of playing in those mixed downs more.
Q: Did Jeremiah Wright bring something different to the running game?
A: Jeremiah, certainly. He's a really good runner — or really good blocker, excuse me. He's a physical player. We saw that through camp and all those different things, and we feel great about him.
We feel like he can go contribute and play. I thought those other guys, though, Dave, Cee's, I thought those guys did some good stuff as well.
Q: What did you like about Martin Emerson's performance?
A: Just physical football. Playing corner in this league, you've got to play physical.
I think the stat I had was two interceptions, four PBUs, seven tackles. You're just getting involved in the plays.
Just proud of him because he's had to navigate an injury, rotation, and you're trying to find your groove, so to speak. I thought he took advantage of those opportunities.
Q: Emerson had a moment on the sideline after colliding with Quincy. Was he injured?
A: He just got the wind knocked out of him. Popped back in there.
Q: There was a report before the game that Tyler Shough had two broken bones in his left hand. What can you tell us about that?
A: His hand, he's battling. Again, he's doing a great job. He's able to do everything for us.
Q: What ultimately turned the game around after falling behind 10-0 late in the first half?
A: I thought that field goal was big, and then really the special teams.
To me, all three phases at that point. That was a huge turnover, Stallberg creating that forced fumble. We're able to score right there, tie the ballgame up, and then come out of the second half and just play.
I thought a really good middle part right there. I thought it was a big, important part of this game.
Q: Was the three-running back rotation what you envisioned coming into the game?
A: Yeah, just rotate those guys. They have different roles and opportunities. Some plays are specific to players, and some are based on who's out there.
I thought they all ran hard. I thought Alvin's catch on the sideline, then to stay in bounds and get upfield, was an incredible play.
You guys probably saw his statistics. He's the sixth player in NFL history now with over 5,000 receiving and…

title: Saints vs. Giants: Can New Orleans Snap Its Losing Streak? Our Staff Predicts
full_text:
The pressure continues to mount on the New Orleans Saints as they head to the Meadowlands for Sunday's Week 6 showdown against the New York Giants , desperately searching for answers amid a disappointing start to the season.
Following a frustrating 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , the Saints (1-4) have dropped three consecutive games, raising questions about the team's direction under second-year head coach Kellen Moore.
The struggles have even drawn the attention of team owner Gayle Benson , who recently expressed frustration with the organization's performance and made it clear that continued losing would not be tolerated without consequences.
With expectations rising and patience wearing thin, New Orleans faces another difficult challenge against a surprising Giants team that has emerged as an early contender in the NFC East.
Here are our predictions for Sunday's game.
This is the Saints' first road game since Week 2, and it’s a strategic one at that, as the Saints will immediately fly out of New York for their game against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris next week. However, this is a critical game for coach Kellen Moore , and maybe even longtime general manager Mickey Loomis .
I don’t think Tyler Shough will have many games like he did last week in the loss to the Vikings, but he will have another matchup against a top-10 defense as the Giants are ninth in total defense. The strength of the defense is its ability to defend the pass, allowing only 199.7 yards per contest, which is good for seventh in the NFL, and have forced six interceptions, which is good for fourth.
While I think Shough will do much better, the Giants have the players needed to at least limit Shough, and New Orleans’ rushing attack is one of the NFL’s worst and will be ineffective. While the Giants have struggled to stop the run, they will have no trouble stopping the Saints.
Defensively, I think the Saints will do enough to keep the game close but not enough to win. The Giants aren’t the greatest offense in the world, but Cam Skattebo is a decent running back, while the receiving threats of Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely are going to give the Saints’ defense a heap of trouble.
I predict a one-score game in the Meadowlands with the Giants pulling it out.
Which Saints club will show in the Meadowlands today? Will it be the one from the first three weeks of the season, or the one from the last three?
We know this: those leading this organization have been put on notice by the woman that holds the checkbook. For the first time as owner of the Saints, Gayle Benson is faced with a situation that will require resolve and a possible move that will force her to make decisions that will be uncomfortable. She has put her trust and belief in those in charge. After seeing where her club has gone in the last few weeks, and the fan reaction to that direction, Mrs. Benson is having to rethink that trust.
Meanwhile, a two-week road trip followed by the Saints open/bye week may be just what the doctor ordered for Moore and his troops: a chance to regroup and rethink where things are.
Being a "glass-half-full" kinda guy, I'm getting this feeling this may be the first step to Moore, his coaches, and his players turning things around. However, don't bet the house on who I choose to win today. I've only been right once in five prognostications this year.

title: Giants 2027 NFL Draft Watch: Four Prospects to Track This Weekend
full_text:
As the New York Giants (3-2-1) prepare for a Week 7 matchup against the Houston Texans (2-4) at NRG Stadium, several Big Blue scouts will be watching closely as college football’s Week 8 slate unfolds.
After the Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints, this could be a good time to scout potential targets as they make their cases for selection in the 2027 NFL Draft.
Beyond their need at running back, the team’s biggest needs remain along both the offensive and defensive lines. Coach John Harbaugh and his staff may also want to add a player who can bolster the return game on special teams.
Here are four players the Giants may keep an eye on this weekend.
As the Giants keep searching for in-season answers to their running-game woes, Lacy may be a wise investment for the future.
The 5-foot-11, 205-pound running back has both the speed and field vision to be an elite rusher at the pro level.
Given his ability to quickly read defensive sets, Lacy is a threat as a vertical runner, and the 20-year-old is well-equipped to provide the production currently lacking in East Rutherford.
After dealing with minor hamstring and shoulder injuries earlier in the week, Lacy is no longer listed on the SEC availability report, clearing him for action in his home state of Texas.
As such, look for him to add to his 352 rushing yards and five rushing touchdowns through five games this season.
While Brown could interest the Giants as a yards-after-catch weapon out of the slot, their interest would likely hinge on his exceptional speed.
As one of the nation’s leading special teams prospects, Brown leads the FBS with an average of 24.3 yards per punt return.
Given his rare ability to accelerate from the moment he fields the ball, the 5-foot-8, 170-pound receiver could be a top-tier returner at the pro level.
With the Hokies set for a prime-time matchup against Clemson in Week 8, Brown will look to showcase his talents, especially to a Giants team that may need an upgrade in the return game for 2027.
While New York’s running woes have been blamed on the lack of a dedicated, three-down workhorse, the interior offensive line could also use help blocking for the ground game.
With John Michael Schmitz likely heading to free agency after being replaced in the starting lineup by Bryan Hudson, the 6-foot-4, 295-pound Hawkeyes interior lineman could be an intriguing option for New York, with the versatility to play either guard or center.
Pieper is best known for his top-level movement and high football IQ. His blend of fluidity and strength gives him the chance to be an immediate force in zone blocking, a trait he is likely to showcase in Iowa’s Week 8 matchup against the Minnesota Golden Gophers.
If Pieper can improve his balance, especially in the run game, he could be a solid fit in New York’s offensive scheme.
If the Giants want an upgrade at run defense, they may not need to look any further than Holmes.
The highly touted Red Raiders defender has already earned PFF credit for 11 solo tackles against the run this season.
He has also logged 27 total pressures as a pass rusher, including five sacks, 17 hurries and five quarterback hits. Still, the 6-foot-3, 300-pound defender is at his best as a disruptive interior run defender.
New York’s depth behind nose tackle D.J. Reader and defensive lineman Shelby Harris has been scarce this season.
Holmes is a high-octane defender with a frame sturdy enough to withstand opposing double teams.
If Texas Tech hopes to neutralize the Cincinnati Bearcats’ offense in Week 8, Holmes will need to play a major role on defense.

title: Giants Mailbag: Skattebo, the Run Defense and Winston’s Misses
full_text:
Welcome to the weekly New York Giants On SI mailbag! From offseason moves to game-day strategies, we'll do our best to answer your questions. (Some questions have been edited for brevity and clarity.)
From Mike A. (via e-mail): Do you think Cam Skattebo is doing too much outside of football with all these endorsements that it's affecting his performance? Or is he just overrated?
Very interesting question, Mike. While I believe a player has every right to pursue as many opportunities as he can during his heyday, I also think there is such a thing as oversaturation. And I think that’s what we’re seeing with Skattebo.
I don’t want to sound like I’m picking on him because I’m not. I like him when he’s being himself and  I’ve had quite a few great chats with him about football and common interests, like our shared love of caring for rescue dogs.
That said, sometimes I wonder if he’s lost the plot and is trying to do too much too soon. He has the opportunities he does because of football and his big personality, but in this town, if you don’t produce, you’ll lose your audience and your appeal quickly.
I’d rather he focus more on football, to be honest, and become a better fit in the system than try to play hero ball and get a charge out of the fan base by trucking over a defender with a stiff arm.
But I get why he’s doing it. There’s a small earning window, and you never know when your career will end or when the next big personality/advertiser’s dream will come along.
From Adam B. (via e-mail) What are the chances we see Darius Slayton back with Big Blue?
@Patricia_Traina hi, you might be better at this then me,but I think the OL hasn't been right in weeks. Even last week,it looked off,pushed around,no gaps. Today they couldn't open a good lane in seemed.  Just wanted your thoughts. #AskPTrain .
I think it's a combination of factors. First, with no real running threat from the quarterback, defenses have been loading up the box with eight or more defenders against the Giants.
New York has faced a loaded box on 77 of their rushing attempts this season, tied for sixth most in the league. That said, the O-line hasn't been sharp at all in run blocking.
Guys are not sustaining their blocks (biggest culprits remain the interior guys). It's my hope, and I suspect the coaches', that inserting J.J. McCarthy, a more mobile quarterback, will discourage teams from loading up the box against the run.
What would you say are the most  realistic expectations for the Giants leading up to the trade deadline?
Brian, if the decision were mine, I would get a defensive tackle in here yesterday, especially now that Tremaine Edmunds is lost for the season.
In my opinion, the run defense's inconsistency has been the biggest problem on this team, and the guys behind starters Shelby Harris and D.J. Reader haven't stepped up. You now throw in the loss of Tremaine Edmunds, and that run defense has taken another huge hit.
I understand the O-line and running backs haven't played well, but I suspect switching to J.J. McCarthy may help both, though we’ll see.
But as I have said repeatedly, what good is having a dangerous pass rush if you’re never really in a position to unleash it fully? And the way you fully unleash it is to stop the run, which this team has struggled to do consistently.
I’d like to see them call the Chargers and see if they can pry Dalvin Tomlinson away for one of their two sixth-round picks. We’ll see what direction they go, but that’s what I would do.
Curious for your perspective on why the Giants extended  Runyan this past offseason. He seemed like a poor fit for Harbaugh’s vision, not a people mover.   So far this season that has played out.  When can they reasonably move on from him?
Kris, the Giants can move on from Runyan after next year.
As to why they extended him, I think part of it was to open up cap space, which the extension did, and the other part of it was that, rather than have to replace both his spot and center, they prioritized center.
Does this mean Bryan Hudson hasn't played well enough? Not necessarily. I think they're looking to see how he does with extended action, and he hasn't been bad.
But is there any doubt they'll move on from John Michael Schmitz after this season and need another center?
On Winston’s performance, what is your impression of the disconnects? Inaccuracy? Bad reads? Miscommunication? Drops? Being too conservative in trying to put the ball where his receiver is the only player with a chance to grab the ball? What stands out the most? #AskPtrain

title: Giants’ Cam Skattebo Eager to Play Against Texans After ‘Learning a Lesson’
full_text:
New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo says he has learned a lesson.
After being held without a single carry during Big Blue’s 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints in Week 6, the second-year running back is set to return to the Giants’ ground-game mix after what head coach John Harbaugh described as a “heck of a week of practice.”
Though it was a valuable experience, he’d rather not repeat it.
“I got taught a lesson,” Skattebo said. “I don’t know if that’s from them or from myself. I had to kind of step back and look at it and figure out why — why I was doing the things I was doing, what was happening?
“I came to practice, worked on those things, and corrected them,” he added. “I’m ready to go back out there and play ball.”
While Skattebo has spent much of his young career atop the Giants’ running back depth chart, he has struggled to hold his spot as the team’s lead back.
Through the first six games of this season, the 5-foot-11, 215-pound rusher has carried the ball 81 times for 294 yards (3.6 yards per carry) and one touchdown.
Still, Skattebo’s season has largely been defined by his four fumbles, the last of which landed him in Harbaugh’s doghouse.
New York’s fourth-round selection (No. 105 overall) in the 2025 NFL Draft lost a key fumble in overtime of the club’s eventual 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders.
As a result, Skattebo was temporarily demoted from his starting role in favor of now-former Giant Najee Harris, and the team settled into a committee-style approach to its ground game.
That strategy ultimately proved ineffective, as its trio of running backs (Harris, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary) combined for just 34 rushing yards against the Saints. In fact, Harris was released just two days after voicing his displeasure with the Giants’ running back rotation.
For Skattebo, Harris’ release only solidified the harsh realities of pro football.
“Nobody’s safe. It’s as simple as that,” he said. “When we go on the field and we perform, if we’re not performing, we understand there’s a possibility of not being here.
“If I don’t perform, I know there’s a possibility of me not being here. We came in this week. We continue to work. We know where we’re at. We know what we have. If we put that on display, we’re going to be just fine.”
As the Giants’ Week 7 showdown with the Houston Texans approaches, Skattebo realizes that the running game will be especially vital to the team’s success.
With the newly installed J.J. McCarthy set to make his first start at quarterback, Big Blue’s rushers will be called upon to take some of the burden off him.
After all, the Texans defense has 18 total sacks, 10.5 of them from pass rushers Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter.
To complete the turnaround, Skattebo knows that he and his teammates must step up their respective games.
“We have guys that can do it,” Skattebo said. “The three of us (Skattebo, Tracy and Singletary) in the backfield are working together. We came out to practice this week with the right mindset and were ready to go.
“Whoever is going to carry the ball knows that the other two guys have their back,” he continued. “When that guy comes off the field, the next guy in is going to perform. The vibes have been great. We’ve been talking. We’ve been staying on the same page.”
As for whether he has regained his starting role for the foreseeable future, Skattebo is wisely focusing on this weekend’s game at Reliant Stadium.
“I didn’t do anything yet,” Skattebo said cautiously. “I took care of the ball during practice, and whatever my role is on Sunday is going to be my role, and I’m going to give it everything I’ve got.”

title: Harbaugh Explains Why the Giants Cut Najee Harris
full_text:
No sinister motives or acts of revenge drove New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh’s decision to release veteran running back Najee Harris earlier this week.
Harris was named the starter last week over Cam Skattebo, who had struggled with ball security, but he carried the ball just four times for two yards.
After the loss to the Saints, Harris admitted to being perplexed over the lack of consistent carries, noting that it was hard to get into a rhythm without that consistency.
When Harbaugh was asked about the comments on Monday, he bluntly said no running back had stepped up to claim the RB1 spot, and he challenged the players on the roster to do so.
On Friday, Harbaugh offered more detail on the decision to release Harris.
“It’s hard to carry four backs,” he said. “There were some other moves we had to make to get guys on the roster. And I just felt like in this situation, like I told him, nothing against what he did.
“I thought he ran super hard. I didn’t think he had a lot of room, in all fairness, in the plays he happened to have in the last couple of weeks, but it was just the direction we decided to go at this time going forward. So, nothing that he did or didn’t do.”
Harbaugh said the plan is to go with the three backs remaining on the 53-man roster: Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary. He didn’t address why the team bothered to add Harris in the first place, a move made before the season, though perhaps it was because no one stepped up to claim the job.
Skattebo, who said after the loss to the Saints that he was punished for his fumbling problem, has taken the lesson in stride and vowed to put his ball-security issues behind him.
Still, Skattebo said the decision to release Harris sends a message that “nobody’s safe” and that it’s all about performing.
“If we’re not performing, we understand there’s a possibility of not being here,” he said on Friday. “If I don’t perform, I know there’s a possibility of me not being here. We came in this week. We continue to work. We know where we’re at. We know what we have. If we put that on display, we’re going to be just fine.”

title: Tremaine Edmunds Reportedly Out for Season as Giants Finalize Injury Statuses for Week 7
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ final injury report for Week 7 is out. In yet another crushing blow, the team will reportedly be without inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds (shoulder) for the rest of the season.
Edmunds was said to have innjured his shoulder in last week’s loss to the New Orleans Saints and did not practice the entire week.  ESPN reported that the veteran linebacker actually tore a muscle in his chest that had hoped to play through. But according to The Athletic , the injury is believed to be season-ending .
Micah McFadden is believed to be the next man up behind Edmunds, and rookie Jack Kelly is also likely to see more snaps on defense. The Giants also have inside linebacker Zaire Barnes, who could be plugged in if needed.
“I think I said early on we have three starters,” head coach John Harbaugh said when asked about McFadden. “So, when and if that happens, Micah is ready. He’s a starter, and he’ll play really well. He’ll be excited for his opportunity.”
Still, the loss of Edmunds is a gut punch to the Giants, who are already without quarterback Jaxson Dart on offense and outside linebacker Brian Burns on defense for the rest of the season.
With Edmunds heading to IR, a roster spot opens for cornerback Paulson Adebo (knee), whose 21-day window opened this week. Harbaugh said Adebo has looked good in practice this week, and with starter Greg Newsome II (concussion) ruled out, Adebo will step into the starting lineup.
“He’s looking good. Yeah, he’s ready to go,” Harbaugh said of Adebo’s week of practice.
“He’s a legit corner. He’s a cover corner; he tackles. He’s been a high-end corner in this league. I think he’s really determined to play that way. I think he’s finally probably healthy and ready to go.”
As for the rest of the Giants’ injury report, tight end Theo Johnson (neck) was listed as doubtful after his practice status was downgraded from limited on Thursday to did not practice on Friday.
If, as is expected, he misses Sunday’s game, it will be his second straight missed game.
Other Giants listed as questionable include right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor, safety Tyler Nubin, safety Jevon Holland and offensive tackle Marcus Mbow.

title: Giants Special Teams Coordinator Chris Horton Calls Unit’s Mistakes “Embarrassing”
full_text:
Lost in the shuffle of the quarterback change, the roster tweaks, and the defensive struggles is the fact that the New York Giants ’ special teams unit, which started the season well, has also hit a rough patch.
Costly turnovers, penalty yardage that has wiped out decent returns, and, of course, at least four instances when the unit was a man short on a play have given opponents a decided advantage.
In short, the last few weeks haven’t been good enough, and assistant head coach and special teams coordinator Chris Horton knows it.
“One of the things we talk about the most is going out there and playing winning football, and I believe in all phases we didn’t do that collectively as a group,” he said this week.
“It’s not a lack of effort, I can tell you that. The guys are flying around. The guys are playing hard. We just got to make sure we get back to playing winning football.”
The most glaring problem has been the shortage of players on the field, which Horton called “embarrassing.”
“I believe we do a great job throughout the practice, and we’re rotating a lot of guys. But, man, that thing starts with me. It’s making sure that I’m communicating to the guys.
“Then it’s also the players understanding, being in the flow of the game, being in the moment. We’ve got to get out there, we’ve got to make calls, and we’ve got to have everybody up. We’ve got to put an end to that. I can assure you that.”
“It’s a part of being just in tune to the game. We’re out there, we’re making calls. When the phases are up, we need every guy up on the field,” he said.
“Sometimes there are guys that are on the field that have got to make sure that they don’t come off the field. It just goes back to those little things. Again, we’re working on those things, and we’re going to get them fixed.”
And what about the costly Charlie Jones fumble last week against the Saints, which turned the tide of the game?
“Just got to take care of the football, right? We’re in traffic. Protecting the ball. Two hands on the football,” Horton said.
“Guys came free. Again, we’ve got to block. We’ve got to make sure no one’s in his way. But at the end of the day, we’ve got to take care of the football.”
The penalty yardage, meanwhile, is something the coaching staff has tried to address.
“The penalties in the return game, those are things that we try to coach against, and we try to make sure that we’re not on the receiving end of those things,” Horton said.
Horton said the unit will start cleaning things up this weekend against the Houston Texans, and he is confident it is on the right track.
“At the end of the day, I’m always bringing it back to my guys. If we play the kind of football that we need to play, which we played the last few weeks up until this game, we’ll be fine,” he said.
“There are opportunities to make sure that those things don’t happen,” Horton said. “And, again, it comes back to playing winning football and pure execution of the plays.”
